articles.title: Powers of a weighted adjacency matrix sum the weights of walks
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
semiring, let $k$ and $n$ be natural numbers, and let $A$ be a $k \times k$ matrix over $R$ with
rows and columns indexed by $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, viewed as the weighted adjacency matrix of a
weighted digraph on these $k$ vertices. Then for all vertices $i$ and $j$,

$$(A^n)_{ij} = \sum_{p} \prod_{t=0}^{n-1} A_{p_t p_{t+1}},$$

where the sum runs over all sequences $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ of vertices with $p_0 = i$ and
$p_n = j$, that is, over all walks of length $n$ from $i$ to $j$, each weighted by the product
of the entries of $A$ along its edges.

The source states $n \ge 1$; the case $n = 0$ is included, where both sides equal $1$ if
$i = j$ and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Thomas Koshy, "A Graph-Theoretic Model for a Generalized Fibonacci Gem," Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.4.1, Theorem, lines 128–130, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Koshy/koshy7.tex

articles.title: Andrásfai graph
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, the Andrásfai graph is the Cayley graph of
the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/(3k+2)\mathbb{Z}$ whose connection set $C$ consists of the residues
whose representative in $\{0, 1, \dots, 3k+1\}$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $3$: two distinct
residues $x$ and $y$ are adjacent when $y - x \in C$ or $x - y \in C$.

articles.title: $s$-arc digraph
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite graph and $s$ a natural number. For an
$(s+1)$-arc $\gamma = (x_0, \dots, x_{s+1})$ of $X$, its *head* is the $s$-arc
$(x_1, \dots, x_{s+1})$ and its *tail* is the $s$-arc $(x_0, \dots, x_s)$. If $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ are $s$-arcs of $X$, then $\beta$ *follows* $\alpha$ if there is an $(s+1)$-arc of $X$
whose tail is $\alpha$ and whose head is $\beta$. The *$s$-arc digraph* $X^{(s)}$ is the directed
graph whose vertices are the $s$-arcs of $X$, with an arc from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ if and only if
$\beta$ follows $\alpha$.

articles.title: $s$-arc regular graph
articles.statement:
A finite graph $G$ is $s$-arc regular if it has at least one
$s$-arc and, for any two $s$-arcs $(u_0, \dots, u_s)$ and $(v_0, \dots, v_s)$ of $G$, there is
exactly one automorphism $\varphi$ of $G$ with $\varphi(u_i) = v_i$ for every $i \le s$.

articles.title: $s$-arc transitive graph
articles.statement:
A finite graph $G$ is $s$-arc transitive if its automorphism
group acts transitively on its $s$-arcs: for any two $s$-arcs $(u_0, \dots, u_s)$ and
$(v_0, \dots, v_s)$ of $G$ there is an automorphism $\varphi$ of $G$ with $\varphi(u_i) = v_i$
for every $i \le s$.

articles.title: $s$-arc
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite graph and $s$ a natural number. An *$s$-arc* in $X$ is a
sequence $(v_0, \dots, v_s)$ of vertices of $X$ such that $v_{i-1}$ and $v_i$ are adjacent for
$1 \le i \le s$, and $v_{i-1} \ne v_{i+1}$ for $0 < i < s$.

articles.title: Diagonal ballot numbers are Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the ballot
number $B(n, n)$ equals the $n$-th Catalan number $C_n$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Section 1.

articles.title: Ballot numbers with second index zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the ballot number
$B(n, 0)$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Section 1.

articles.title: Ballot numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the ballot number $B(n, k)$ is the
integer part of $\max(n + 1 - k, 0) \binom{n+k}{n} / (n + 1)$. For $k \le n + 1$ the division
is exact, so $B(n, k) = \frac{n - k + 1}{n + 1} \binom{n+k}{n}$ (OEIS A009766), and
$B(n, k) = 0$ for $k > n + 1$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Section 1.

articles.title: Smooth structures on coconut trees with two leaves
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$ and let $(d, r)$ be a
smooth arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p, 2)$, whose path is
$v_1, \dots, v_p$ and whose two leaves are attached to the central vertex $v_p$. Then
$d(v_p) \le 1$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Corollary 7.

articles.title: Ancestors of labelings of coconut trees
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a pair of vertex labelings $(d, r)$
of the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ and $y$ a pair of vertex labelings of $CT(q, t)$. Then $y$ is an
ancestor of $x$, and $x$ a descendant of $y$, when $y$ is obtained from $x$ by a finite,
possibly empty, sequence of smoothings, each performed at a vertex where the current
$d$-label equals $1$: either at a path vertex other than the central vertex, or at a leaf.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 3.7 (ancestors and descendants; arXiv numbering).

articles.title: The coconut count term with second argument zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $x$, the
term $A(x, 0)$ of the coconut tree count equals the Catalan number $C_{x-1}$, read as $C_0$
when $x = 0$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Terms of the coconut tree count
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x$ and $y$, the term $A(x, y)$ is
defined by $A(x, 0) = C_{x-1}$, $A(x, 1) = C_{x-1} - C_{x-2}$ and, for $y \ge 2$,

$$A(x, y) = \sum_{i=y+1}^{x} B(x - y - 1, x - i) \, |\mathrm{SArith}(CT(i - y, y))|,$$

where $C_n$ is the $n$-th Catalan number (a negative index is read as $0$), $B$ is the ballot
number, and $|\mathrm{SArith}(CT(m, y))|$ is the number of smooth arithmetical structures
$(d, r)$ on the coconut tree $CT(m, y)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Smoothing a leaf preserves arithmetical structures
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $s$ be natural numbers
with $p + s \ge 2$, let $(d, r)$ be an arithmetical structure on the coconut tree
$CT(p, s + 1)$, and let $\ell$ be a leaf with $d(\ell) = 1$. Then the labelings $(d', r')$
obtained by smoothing $(d, r)$ at $\ell$ form an arithmetical structure on $CT(p, s)$.

The hypothesis $p + s \ge 2$ excludes the single-edge tree $CT(1, 1)$: there $d = r = (1, 1)$,
and smoothing the leaf gives $d' = 0$ at the remaining vertex, which is not an arithmetical
structure.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 3.6.

articles.title: An example of smoothing at a path vertex and at a leaf
articles.statement:
On the coconut tree $CT(4, 4)$,
write a labeling as (values at $v_1, \dots, v_4$ | values at the leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_4$).
Take $d = (1, 3, 2, 3 \mid 2, 2, 3, 1)$ and $r = (2, 2, 4, 6 \mid 3, 3, 2, 6)$. Smoothing at the
path vertex $v_1$ and then at the leaf $\ell_4$ gives the labelings $d' = (2, 2, 2 \mid 2, 2, 3)$
and $r' = (2, 4, 6 \mid 3, 3, 2)$ on $CT(3, 3)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Example 3.5 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Smoothing at a leaf of a coconut tree
articles.statement:
Let the coconut tree $CT(p, s + 1)$ have path
vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$, central vertex $v_p$ and leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_{s+1}$, let $d$
and $r$ be labelings of its vertices by natural numbers, and let $1 \le k \le s + 1$. Smoothing
$(d, r)$ at the leaf $\ell_k$ gives the labelings $(d', r')$ of $CT(p, s)$ obtained by deleting
$\ell_k$ and renumbering the remaining leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_{k-1}, \ell_{k+1}, \dots,
\ell_{s+1}$ in order as $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_s$. Every remaining vertex keeps its value of $r$
and its value of $d$, except that $d$ drops by $1$ (truncated at $0$) at the central vertex $v_p$
when $p \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 3.4 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Path smoothing preserves arithmetical structures on coconut trees
articles.statement:
Let $s \ge 1$ and let
$(d, r)$ be an arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p + 1, s)$, whose path vertices are
$v_1, \dots, v_{p+1}$ with central vertex $v_{p+1}$. If $d(v_k) = 1$ for some non-central path
vertex $v_k$ (that is, $1 \le k \le p$), then smoothing $(d, r)$ at $v_k$ gives an arithmetical
structure on $CT(p, s)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 3.3 and Proposition 3.6 for `i = 1`.

articles.title: Example of smoothing a coconut tree at a path vertex
articles.statement:
List a labeling of a coconut tree as
its values on the path vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots$, then $\mid$, then its values on the leaves.
Smoothing the labelings $d = (3, 1, 3, 2, 2 \mid 2, 2, 4)$ and $r = (1, 3, 2, 3, 4 \mid 2, 2, 1)$
of $CT(5, 3)$ at $v_2$ gives the labelings $d' = (2, 2, 2, 2 \mid 2, 2, 4)$ and
$r' = (1, 2, 3, 4 \mid 2, 2, 1)$ of $CT(4, 3)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Example 3.2 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Smoothing at a path vertex of a coconut tree
articles.statement:
Let the coconut tree $CT(p + 1, s)$ have
path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_{p+1}$, central vertex $v_{p+1}$ and leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_s$,
let $d$ and $r$ be labelings of its vertices by natural numbers, and let $1 \le k \le p + 1$.
Smoothing $(d, r)$ at $v_k$ gives the labelings $(d', r')$ of $CT(p, s)$ obtained by deleting
$v_k$ and renumbering the remaining path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_{k-1}, v_{k+1}, \dots, v_{p+1}$
in order as $v_1, \dots, v_p$. Every remaining vertex keeps its value of $r$ and its value of $d$,
except that $d$ drops by $1$ (truncated at $0$) at the path neighbours $v_{k-1}$ and $v_{k+1}$
of $v_k$, where they exist.

The paper applies it only at a non-central vertex ($k \le p$) with $d(v_k) = 1$: for $k \ge 2$
this is the degree-2 smoothing of Definition 3.1 and for $k = 1$ the smoothing at $v_1$ of
Definition 3.4.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definitions 3.1 and 3.4 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Subdivision preserves arithmetical structures on coconut trees
articles.statement:
If $(d, r)$ is an
arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$, whose path vertices are $v_1, \dots, v_p$,
then for every $1 \le k \le p$, subdividing $(d, r)$ at position $k$ (inserting a new path vertex
just before $v_k$) gives an arithmetical structure on $CT(p + 1, s)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 3.11.

articles.title: Example of subdividing a coconut tree
articles.statement:
List a labeling of a coconut tree as its values on
the path vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots$, then $\mid$, then its values on the leaves. Subdividing the
labelings $d = (2, 2, 2, 2 \mid 2, 2, 4)$ and $r = (1, 2, 3, 4 \mid 2, 2, 1)$ of $CT(4, 3)$ at
position $2$ gives the labelings $d' = (3, 1, 3, 2, 2 \mid 2, 2, 4)$ and
$r' = (1, 3, 2, 3, 4 \mid 2, 2, 1)$ of $CT(5, 3)$. These are the labelings of Example 3.2, whose
smoothing at $v_2$ is $(d, r)$, so here subdivision undoes that smoothing.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 3.9 and Example 3.2 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Subdivision at a path vertex of a coconut tree
articles.statement:
Let the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ have path
vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$ and leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_s$, let $d$ and $r$ be labelings of
its vertices by natural numbers, and let $1 \le k \le p$. Subdividing $(d, r)$ at position $k$
gives the labelings $(d', r')$ of $CT(p + 1, s)$ obtained by inserting a new path vertex $w$
just before $v_k$, so that the path becomes $v_1, \dots, v_{k-1}, w, v_k, \dots, v_p$, with
$d'(w) = 1$ and $r'(w) = r(v_{k-1}) + r(v_k)$, where $r(v_0) = 0$ (so $r'(w) = r(v_1)$ when
$k = 1$). The path neighbours of $w$, namely $v_{k-1}$ (when $k \ge 2$) and $v_k$, get
$d' = d + 1$; every other vertex keeps its value of $d$, and every vertex other than $w$ keeps
its value of $r$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 3.9 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Monotonicity criteria for arithmetical structures on coconut trees
articles.statement:
Let $(d, r)$ be an
arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ with path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$, and
write $d_k = d(v_k)$ and $r_k = r(v_k)$. The following are equivalent: (1) $d_k \ge 2$ for
$1 \le k \le p - 1$; (2) $0 < r_2 - r_1 \le r_3 - r_2 \le \cdots \le r_p - r_{p-1}$; (3)
$r_1 < r_2 < \cdots < r_p$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Adjacent path vertices of a coconut tree
articles.statement:
Let the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ have path
vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$. Two path vertices $v_a$ and $v_b$ are adjacent if and only if
$|a - b| = 1$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.2 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Adjacency of leaves and path vertices in a coconut tree
articles.statement:
Let the coconut tree
$CT(p, s)$ have path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$, with central vertex $v_p$. A leaf of $CT(p, s)$
is adjacent to a path vertex $v_k$ if and only if $k = p$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.2 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Leaves of a coconut tree are pairwise nonadjacent
articles.statement:
No leaf of the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$
is adjacent to a leaf.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.2 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Coconut tree
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $s$, the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$ is the
graph whose vertices are the path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$ and the leaves
$v_{\ell_1}, \dots, v_{\ell_s}$, in which $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}$ are adjacent for $1 \le i < p$, every
leaf is adjacent to $v_p$, and there are no other edges. For $p = 0$ it consists of $s$ isolated
vertices.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.2 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Path length of a smooth arithmetical structure on a coconut tree
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be the
Euclidean chain function, let $p \ge 1$, and let $(d, r)$ be a smooth arithmetical structure on
the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$, with path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$ and leaves
$v_{\ell_1}, \dots, v_{\ell_s}$. Then $p = F(r(v_{\ell_1}) + \dots + r(v_{\ell_s}), r(v_p)) - 1$.

The source states this for the smooth arithmetical structure that Proposition 7 constructs from
labels $a_1, \dots, a_s$ and $c$; every smooth arithmetical structure is the one constructed from
its own labels $a_j = r(v_{\ell_j})$ and $c = r(v_p)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Corollary 6.

articles.title: The leaf labels of a smooth arithmetical structure on a coconut tree are coprime
articles.statement:
Let
$(d, r)$ be a smooth arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$ with leaves
$v_{\ell_1}, \dots, v_{\ell_s}$. If a natural number $g$ divides $r(v_{\ell_j})$ for every
$j = 1, \dots, s$, then $g = 1$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Euclidean chain function under adding multiples
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x \ge 1$, $y$ and
$k$, the Euclidean chain function $F$ satisfies $F(x + k y, y) = F(x, y)$ and
$F(x, k x + y) = F(x, y) + k$.

The source quotes this result from Archer et al.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 6.

articles.title: Euclidean chain function when the first argument divides the second
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$x, y \ge 1$ with $x \mid y$, the Euclidean chain function $F$ satisfies $F(x, y) = 1 + y / x$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Recursion for the Euclidean chain function
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x$ and $y$ with $y \ne 0$,
the Euclidean chain function $F$ satisfies $F(x, y) = 1 + F(y, (-x) \bmod y)$, where
$(-x) \bmod y$ is the least nonnegative residue of $-x$ modulo $y$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 4.12 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Euclidean chain function at one
articles.statement:
For every natural number $y$, the Euclidean chain
function $F$ satisfies $F(1, y) = y + 1$, and for every natural number $x \ge 1$ it satisfies
$F(x, 1) = 2$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Corollary 5.

articles.title: Euclidean chain function of 13 and 60
articles.statement:
The Euclidean chain function $F$ satisfies
$F(13, 60) = 8$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Example 4.13 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Euclidean chain function with second argument zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $x$, the
Euclidean chain function $F$ satisfies $F(x, 0) = 1$.

For $x = 0$ this is the value given by the recursive definition of $F$, not a count of positive
terms.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 4.12 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Euclidean chain function
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x_1$ and $x_2$, the Euclidean chain
$x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ is given by $x_{i+1} = (-x_{i-1}) \bmod x_i$ (the least nonnegative
residue) while $x_i \ne 0$, and by $x_{i+1} = 0$ once $x_i = 0$. The Euclidean chain function is
defined by the recursion $F(x, 0) = 1$ and $F(x, y) = 1 + F(y, (-x) \bmod y)$ for $y \ne 0$. For
$x_1 > 0$, $F(x_1, x_2)$ is the number of positive terms of the Euclidean chain.

For $x_1 = 0$ the recursion also counts the first term $0$: $F(0, 0) = 1$ and $F(0, 1) = 2$,
although the chains $0, 0$ and $0, 1, 0$ have $0$ and $1$ positive terms.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 4.12 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Smooth coconut structures with prescribed labels
articles.statement:
Let $s \ge 1$ and let $c$ and
$a_1, \dots, a_s$ be natural numbers with $a_i > 0$, $a_i \mid c$ and $a_i < c$ for every $i$, such
that the only natural number dividing $c$ and all of $a_1, \dots, a_s$ is $1$. Write $CT(p, s)$ for
the coconut tree with path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$ and leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_s$ adjacent
to $v_p$. Then there is exactly one $p \ge 1$ such that $CT(p, s)$ carries a smooth arithmetical
structure $(d, r)$ with $r(\ell_i) = a_i$ for every $i$ and $r(v_p) = c$. Moreover, for every
$p \ge 1$, any two smooth arithmetical structures $(d, r)$ and $(d', r')$ on $CT(p, s)$ with
$r(\ell_i) = r'(\ell_i) = a_i$ for every $i$ and $r(v_p) = r'(v_p) = c$ are equal.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 7.

articles.title: Unique smooth ancestor
articles.statement:
Let $s \ge 1$ and let $(d, r)$ be an arithmetical structure on the
coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ with $d(\ell_j) \ge 2$ at every leaf $\ell_j$. Then there is exactly one
pair consisting of a number $q$ with $1 \le q \le p$ and a smooth arithmetical structure on
$CT(q, s)$ that is a coconut ancestor of $(d, r)$, that is, one obtained from $(d, r)$ by a
possibly empty sequence of smoothings, each performed at a vertex whose current $d$-label is $1$
and which is either a leaf or a path vertex other than the last path vertex (the one adjacent to
the leaves).

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Lemma 3.8.

articles.title: The all-ones structure on a single edge
articles.statement:
On the graph with two vertices joined by an edge,
the labelings $d = (1, 1)$ and $r = (1, 1)$ form an arithmetical structure.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.1 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Arithmetical structure
articles.statement:
An arithmetical structure on a graph $G$ with vertex set $V$ is a
pair of labelings $d, r : V \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $d(v) > 0$ and $r(v) > 0$ for every vertex
$v$, $d(v)\, r(v) = \sum_{w \sim v} r(w)$ for every vertex $v$, where the sum runs over the
neighbours $w$ of $v$, and the only natural number dividing every $r(v)$ is $1$. For a finite graph
with adjacency matrix $A$ the middle condition reads $(\operatorname{diag}(d) - A)\, r = 0$.

The neighbour sum is taken to be $0$ when $v$ has infinitely many neighbours, so no arithmetical
structure exists on a graph with a vertex of infinite degree.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.1 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Characterization of smooth coconut structures
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$ and let $(d, r)$ be an
arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ with path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$ and
leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_s$ adjacent to $v_p$. Then $(d, r)$ is smooth if and only if
$r(\ell_j) < r(v_p)$ for every $j$ and $r(v_1) < r(v_2) < \dots < r(v_p)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Smooth arithmetical structure on a coconut tree
articles.statement:
Let $CT(p, s)$ be the coconut tree with
path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$ and leaves $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_s$ adjacent to $v_p$. An
arithmetical structure $(d, r)$ on $CT(p, s)$ is smooth if $d(v_i) \ge 2$ for $1 \le i \le p - 1$
and $d(\ell_j) \ge 2$ for $1 \le j \le s$; there is no condition on $d(v_p)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.3 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Number of arithmetical structures on coconut trees
articles.statement:
For $p \ge 1$ and $s \ge 2$, the number
of arithmetical structures on the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ is

$$\sum_{j=0}^{s} \binom{s}{j} A(p + s - j, s - j),$$

where $A(x, y)$ is the coconut count term.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Number of arithmetical structures on coconut trees with two leaves
articles.statement:
For $p \ge 2$, the
number of arithmetical structures on the coconut tree $CT(p, 2)$ is

$$2 C_p - C_{p-1} + \sum_{i=3}^{p+2} B(p - 1, p + 2 - i)\, N(i - 2),$$

where $C_n$ is the $n$-th Catalan number, $B(n, k)$ is the ballot number and $N(q)$ is the number
of smooth arithmetical structures on $CT(q, 2)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Number of arithmetical structures on stars
articles.statement:
For $s \ge 2$, the number of arithmetical
structures on the star $CT(1, s)$, a centre joined to $s$ leaves, is

$$1 + \sum_{j=0}^{s-2} \binom{s}{j} N(s - j),$$

where $N(t)$ is the number of smooth arithmetical structures on the star $CT(1, t)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Counting coconut structures whose leaves cannot be smoothed
articles.statement:
For $p \ge 1$ and $s \ge 2$,
the number of arithmetical structures $(d, r)$ on the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ with $d(\ell_j) \ge 2$
at every leaf $\ell_j$ is

$$\sum_{i=1}^{p} B(p - 1, p - i)\, N(i),$$

where $B(n, k)$ is the ballot number and $N(i)$ is the number of smooth arithmetical structures on
$CT(i, s)$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Corollary 4.6.

articles.title: Arithmetical structures on a one-leaf coconut tree with a non-smoothable leaf
articles.statement:
For every
integer $p \ge 1$, the number of arithmetical structures $(d, r)$ on the coconut tree
$\mathrm{CT}(p, 1)$, which is the path on $p + 1$ vertices, whose leaf $\ell_1$ has
$d_{\ell_1} \ne 1$ (so that the leaf cannot be smoothed) is $C_p - C_{p-1}$, where $C_n$
denotes the $n$-th Catalan number.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Number of descendants of a smooth coconut structure
articles.statement:
Let $s \ge 2$ and $1 \le i \le p$,
and let $(d, r)$ be a smooth arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(i, s)$. Then
exactly $B(p - 1, p - i)$ arithmetical structures on $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$ are descendants of
$(d, r)$, where $B(n, k)$ is the ballot number.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 4.5.

articles.title: Smooth coconut structures with central label above one
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$ and let $(d, r)$ be
a smooth arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$, with central vertex $v_p$
and leaves $\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_s$. Then $d_{v_p} > 1$ if and only if
$r_{v_p} < \sum_{j=1}^{s} r_{\ell_j}$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Proposition 8.

articles.title: Leaves of a smooth coconut structure have label at least 2
articles.statement:
If $(d, r)$ is a smooth
arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$, then $d_{\ell_j} \ge 2$ for every
leaf $\ell_j$, $1 \le j \le s$.

## Sources

- Diaz-Lopez, Ha, Harris, Rogers, Koss and Smith, *Arithmetical Structures on Coconut Trees*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A82, Definition 2.3 (arXiv numbering).

articles.title: Cayley's formula
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the complete graph on $n$ vertices has
exactly $n^{n-2}$ spanning trees.

## Sources

- A. Cayley, "A theorem on trees", Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics 23 (1889), 376-378.

articles.title: Coxeter graph
articles.statement:
The Coxeter graph is the simple graph whose $28$ vertices are the pairs
$(i, j)$ with $i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and $j \in \mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}$, and whose edges are the
following: for each $i \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, the vertices $(i, j)$ and $(i, j')$ are adjacent when
$j - j' = i$ or $j' - j = i$ in $\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}$, and for each $j$ the vertex $(0, j)$ is
adjacent to $(1, j)$, $(2, j)$ and $(3, j)$. There are no other edges.

articles.title: Samal's theorem: infinite antichains in the cycle-continuous order exist
articles.statement:
There is a
sequence $G_0, G_1, G_2, \dots$ of pairwise distinct finite multigraphs, each with at least one
edge, such that for all $i \ne j$ there is no cycle-continuous map from the edges of $G_i$ to
the edges of $G_j$.

Samal (Theorem 1.3) proves this with an infinite set of cubic bridgeless graphs that are
pairwise incomparable under cycle-continuous maps, answering the DeVos-Nesetril-Raspaud
antichain question positively.

## Sources

- Robert Samal, Cycle-continuous mappings - order structure, Journal of Graph Theory 85 (2017) 56-73, arXiv:1212.6909, https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.6909.

articles.title: Infinite antichains in the cycle-continuous order
articles.statement:
There is a sequence
$G_0, G_1, G_2, \dots$ of pairwise distinct finite multigraphs, each with at least one edge,
such that for all $i \ne j$ there is no cycle-continuous map from the edges of $G_i$ to the
edges of $G_j$.

## Sources

- [OPG-323] (URL: http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/antichains_in_the_cycle_continuous_order).

articles.title: Binary cycle space
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a multigraph. A set $S$ of edges of $G$ is a binary cycle
when $S$ is finite and every vertex $v$ is an endpoint of an even number of edges of $S$, where
only edges with exactly one endpoint equal to $v$ are counted; loops are not counted, which
agrees modulo $2$ with counting each loop twice. The cycle space of $G$ is the set of all
binary cycles of $G$.

## Sources

- [OPG-323] (URL: http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/antichains_in_the_cycle_continuous_order).

articles.title: Multigraphs with loops and parallel edges
articles.statement:
A multigraph $G$ consists of a type $V$ of
vertices, a type $E$ of edges, and a map assigning to each edge an ordered pair of vertices,
its two endpoints. Distinct edges may have the same endpoints (parallel edges), and the two
endpoints of an edge may coincide (a loop). Neither $V$ nor $E$ is required to be finite.

## Sources

- [OPG-323] Antichains in the cycle continuous order (URL: http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/antichains_in_the_cycle_continuous_order).

articles.title: Cycle-continuous maps
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be multigraphs. A map $f$ from the edges of $G$
to the edges of $H$ is cycle-continuous when, for every binary cycle $C$ of $H$, the preimage
$f^{-1}(C)$ is a binary cycle of $G$.

## Sources

- [OPG-323] (URL: http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/antichains_in_the_cycle_continuous_order).

articles.title: Finite multigraphs with at least one edge
articles.statement:
A multigraph $G$ is finite and nontrivial
when its set of vertices and its set of edges are both finite and it has at least one edge.
These are the graphs on which the cycle-continuous order is considered.

## Sources

- [OPG-323] (URL: http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/antichains_in_the_cycle_continuous_order).

articles.title: Parameter bound $a \le k$ for Deza graphs
articles.statement:
If a finite simple graph $G$ is a Deza graph
with parameters $(n, k, b, a)$, then $a \le k$.

articles.title: Parameter bound $a < n$ for Deza graphs
articles.statement:
If a finite simple graph $G$ is a Deza graph
with parameters $(n, k, b, a)$, then $a < n$.

articles.title: Parameter bound $b < n$ for Deza graphs
articles.statement:
If a finite simple graph $G$ is a Deza graph
with parameters $(n, k, b, a)$, then $b < n$.

articles.title: Deza graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $n, k, b, a$ be
natural numbers. Then $G$ is a Deza graph with parameters $(n, k, b, a)$ when $a \le b \le k < n$,
$V$ has exactly $n$ elements, every vertex of $G$ has degree $k$, and any two distinct vertices of
$G$ have exactly $a$ or exactly $b$ common neighbours, whether or not they are adjacent.

## Sources

- Golubyatnikov, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13089v1, lines 163--164.

articles.title: Cayley digraph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a set with a binary operation written as multiplication,
and let $C \subseteq G$. The *Cayley digraph* $X(G, C)$ is the directed graph whose vertices
are the elements of $G$, with an arc $u \to v$ exactly when $v = uc$ for some $c \in C$.

Usually $G$ is a group and $C$ does not contain the identity, so that $X(G, C)$ has no loops;
neither condition is imposed here.

articles.title: Edge-transposition graph
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ be a set of permutations
of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, typically a set of transpositions in the symmetric group $S_n$. The
edge-transposition graph of $T$ is the simple graph with vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ in
which two distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent if and only if the transposition swapping $i$
and $j$ belongs to $T$.

articles.title: Frucht's theorem
articles.statement:
Every finite group is isomorphic to the automorphism group of a finite simple
graph.

## Sources

- R. Frucht, Compositio Math. 6 (1939), 239-250.

articles.title: Graph cover
articles.statement:
A finite graph $X$ *covers* a finite graph $Y$ if there is a surjective local
isomorphism from $X$ to $Y$.

articles.title: Folding of a graph homomorphism
articles.statement:
A homomorphism from X to Y is a *simple folding* if it has one fibre consisting of two vertices
at distance two, and all other fibres are singletons. A homomorphism is a *folding* if it is the
composition of a non-negative number of simple foldings.

articles.title: Core of a graph
articles.statement:
A finite graph $X$ is a *core* if every homomorphism from $X$ to itself
is a bijection. For finite graphs $X$ and $Y$, $Y$ is a *core of* $X$ if $Y$ is a core, there is a
homomorphism from $X$ to $Y$, and there is an injective homomorphism from $Y$ to $X$; that is, $Y$
is isomorphic to a subgraph of $X$.

articles.title: Local injection
articles.statement:
A homomorphism $f$ from a finite graph $X$ to a finite graph $Y$ is a
*local injection* if any two distinct vertices of $X$ with the same image under $f$ are at
distance at least $3$ in $X$.

Vertices in different components of $X$ count as being at infinite distance.

articles.title: Local isomorphism
articles.statement:
A homomorphism $f$ from a finite graph $X$ to a finite graph $Y$ is a
*local isomorphism* if for every vertex $x$ of $X$, $f$ maps the set of neighbours of $x$
bijectively onto the set of neighbours of $f(x)$.

articles.title: Retract
articles.statement:
Let $Y$ be a subgraph of a graph $X$. A *retraction* from $X$ to $Y$ is a
homomorphism $f$ from $X$ to $Y$, regarded as a graph in its own right, whose restriction to the
vertex set of $Y$ is the identity map. We say that $Y$ is a *retract* of $X$ if there is a
retraction from $X$ to $Y$.

articles.title: Vertices of the Grassmann graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$, the vertices of the
Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ are the $\ell$-dimensional linear subspaces of
$\mathbb{F}_2^k$.

articles.title: Grassmann graph over $\mathbb{F}_2$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$, the Grassmann
graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ has as vertices the $\ell$-dimensional linear subspaces of
$\mathbb{F}_2^k$, and two distinct such subspaces $L$ and $L'$ are adjacent when
$\dim(L \cap L') = \ell - 1$.

articles.title: Grassmann vertices between two subspaces
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$ and linear
subspaces $A$ and $B$ of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)[A, B]$ is the finite set of
vertices $L$ of the Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$, that is of $\ell$-dimensional
subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, with $A \subseteq L \subseteq B$. If $A \not\subseteq B$ the set
is empty.

This is the set $\mathrm{Gr}_{k,\ell}[A, B]$ on page 13 of Khot, Minzer and Safra, Pseudorandom
sets in Grassmann graph have near-perfect expansion.

articles.title: Non-expanding sets in the Grassmann graph (Khot–Minzer–Safra)
articles.statement:
For every real $\alpha$
with $0 < \alpha < 1$ there are a real $\varepsilon > 0$ and a natural number $r$ such that for
all sufficiently large natural numbers $\ell$ and, for each such $\ell$, all sufficiently large
natural numbers $k$, the following holds. For subspaces $A$ and $B$ of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, let
$\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)[A, B]$ be the set of vertices $L$ of the Grassmann graph
$\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ with $A \subseteq L \subseteq B$. Let $S$ be a nonempty set of at most
half of the vertices of $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ whose edge expansion in $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$
satisfies $\Phi(S) \le \alpha$. Then there are subspaces $A \subseteq B$ of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$
such that the dimension of $A$ plus the codimension $k - \dim B$ of $B$ is at most $r$ and
$|S \cap \mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)[A, B]| / |\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)[A, B]| \ge \varepsilon$.

## Sources

- S. Khot, D. Minzer, and M. Safra, `Pseudorandom sets in Grassmann graph have near-perfect expansion`, Annals of Math, 198 (1) 2023. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_pseudorandom_grassmann` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Edge expansion of a vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and
let $S \subseteq V$ be nonempty. Let $d$ be the degree in $G$ of a fixed vertex of $S$, chosen
once for each $S$. The expansion of $S$ is the rational number
$\Phi_G(S) = |E(S, V \setminus S)| / (d \cdot |S|)$, where $E(S, V \setminus S)$ is the set of
edges of $G$ with one endpoint in $S$ and the other in $V \setminus S$; it is $0$ when $d = 0$.

For a $d$-regular graph, $d$ is the common degree and this is Definition 1.8 of Khot, Minzer and
Safra, which also asks that $|S| \le |V|/2$; neither regularity nor that bound is assumed here.

articles.title: The 3-cycle Cayley graph of the alternating group is integral
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 3$, let $S$ be
the set of $3$-cycles $(1\,2\,k)$ with $3 \le k \le n$ in the alternating group $A_n$, and let
$R = S \cup S^{-1}$. Then the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(A_n, R)$, whose vertices are the elements
of $A_n$ with distinct $x$ and $y$ adjacent when $x^{-1} y \in R$ or $y^{-1} x \in R$, is
integral: every eigenvalue of its integer adjacency matrix (every complex root of the
characteristic polynomial of that matrix) is an integer.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.50 (D. V. Lytkina); resolution: (a) D. O. Revin, letter of 21 April 2018; A. Abdollahi, letter of 3 May 2018; (b) W. Guo, D. V. Lytkina, V. D. Mazurov and D. O. Revin, Integral Cayley graphs, Algebra Logic 58 (2019), no. 4, 297-305, doi:10.1007/s10469-019-09550-2, Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.50: (a) Yes, with a character-theoretic proof in the Archive (each eigenvalue is (1/χ(1)) ∑_{r ∈ R} χ(r), rational since characters take integer values on involutions); (b) Yes, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: The Kourovka 19.50(b) integrality claim
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 3$ let $S$ be the set of $3$-cycles
$(1\,2\,k)$ with $3 \le k \le n$ on the points $1, \dots, n$, and let $R = S \cup S^{-1}$, a subset
of the alternating group $A_n$. This is the proposition that for every $n \ge 3$ the Cayley graph
$\mathrm{Cay}(A_n, R)$ is integral. Here $\mathrm{Cay}(A_n, R)$ has vertex set $A_n$, distinct $x$
and $y$ being adjacent when $x^{-1} y \in R$ or $y^{-1} x \in R$, and a graph is integral when
every eigenvalue of its integer adjacency matrix (every complex root of the characteristic
polynomial of that matrix) is an integer.

articles.title: Integer matrix with integral spectrum
articles.statement:
A square integer matrix is integral: every complex root of its characteristic polynomial (every
eigenvalue) is an integer.

articles.title: Cayley graphs on normal sets of involutions are integral
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let
$R \subseteq G$ be a set of involutions ($r^2 = 1$ and $r \ne 1$ for every $r \in R$) that is
closed under conjugation ($g r g^{-1} \in R$ for all $r \in R$ and $g \in G$) and generates $G$.
Then the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(G, R)$, whose vertices are the elements of $G$ with distinct
$x$ and $y$ adjacent when $x^{-1} y \in R$ or $y^{-1} x \in R$, is integral: every eigenvalue of
its integer adjacency matrix (every complex root of the characteristic polynomial of that matrix)
is an integer.

The Kourovka Archive proof: every eigenvalue of $\mathrm{Cay}(G, R)$ has the form
$\frac{1}{\chi(1)} \sum_{r \in R} \chi(r)$ for an irreducible character $\chi$ of $G$; this number
is rational because characters take integer values on involutions, and it is an algebraic integer.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 19.50 (D. V. Lytkina); resolution: (a) D. O. Revin, letter of 21 April 2018; A. Abdollahi, letter of 3 May 2018; (b) W. Guo, D. V. Lytkina, V. D. Mazurov and D. O. Revin, Integral Cayley graphs, Algebra Logic 58 (2019), no. 4, 297-305, doi:10.1007/s10469-019-09550-2, Kourovka Archive, Problem 19.50: (a) Yes, with a character-theoretic proof in the Archive (each eigenvalue is (1/χ(1)) ∑_{r ∈ R} χ(r), rational since characters take integer values on involutions); (b) Yes, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v49.

articles.title: The Kourovka 19.50(a) integrality claim
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that for every finite
group $G$ and every subset $R \subseteq G$ such that every element of $R$ is an involution
($r^2 = 1$ and $r \ne 1$), $R$ is closed under conjugation ($g r g^{-1} \in R$ for all $r \in R$
and $g \in G$) and $R$ generates $G$, the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(G, R)$ is integral. Here
$\mathrm{Cay}(G, R)$ has vertex set $G$, distinct $x$ and $y$ being adjacent when $x^{-1} y \in R$
or $y^{-1} x \in R$, and a graph is integral when every eigenvalue of its integer adjacency matrix
(every complex root of the characteristic polynomial of that matrix) is an integer.

articles.title: The 3-cycles (1 2 k)
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the set of $3$-cycles $(1\,2\,k)$
with $3 \le k \le n$ in the symmetric group $S_n$. With the points numbered $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$,
these are the permutations $(0\,1\,k) = (0\,1)(1\,k)$ with $2 \le k < n$, products composed right
to left; the set is empty when $n < 3$.

articles.title: Moore graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $d$ be a natural
number. Then $G$ is a Moore graph of diameter $d$ when $G$ has diameter $d$ and girth $2d + 1$.

articles.title: Johnson graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Johnson graph $J(n, k)$ has as
vertices the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, and two vertices $s$ and $t$ are
adjacent when $|s \cap t| + 1 = k$, that is, when $s$ and $t$ share exactly $k - 1$ elements.

articles.title: Adjacency in the Johnson graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and $k$-element subsets
$s$ and $t$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, the vertices $s$ and $t$ of the Johnson graph $J(n, k)$
are adjacent if and only if $|s \cap t| + 1 = k$.

articles.title: Generalized Johnson graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $v$, $k$ and $i$, the generalized Johnson
graph $J(v,k,i)$ is the graph whose vertices are the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, v-1\}$,
in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if and only if their intersection has exactly $i$
elements.

The usual setting is $v \ge k \ge i$; the definition does not require it.

articles.title: Spanning tree
articles.statement:
A subgraph $T$ of a simple graph $G$ is a spanning tree of $G$ if it contains
every vertex of $G$ and, regarded as a graph on its own vertex set, it is a tree (connected and
acyclic).

articles.title: Matrix-tree theorem for principal minors of the Laplacian
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex set $V$, let $L = D - A$ be its Laplacian matrix over $\mathbb{Z}$, where $D$ is the
diagonal matrix of vertex degrees and $A$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$, and let $r \in V$. Then
the determinant of the submatrix of $L$ obtained by deleting the row and the column of $r$ equals
the number of spanning trees of $G$.

articles.title: Matrix-tree theorem for a chosen root
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$
and let $r \in V$. Then the determinant of the reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$, that is, the
integer Laplacian of $G$ with the row and the column of $r$ deleted, equals the number of spanning
trees of $G$.

No separate nonemptiness hypothesis on $V$ is needed, since $r$ is a vertex.

articles.title: Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite nonempty vertex set $V$
and let $r \in V$. Then the determinant of the reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$, that is, the
integer Laplacian of $G$ with the row and the column of $r$ deleted, equals the number of spanning
trees of $G$.

In particular, this determinant is $0$ when $G$ is disconnected.

## Sources

- G. Kirchhoff, "Über die Auflösung der Gleichungen, auf welche man bei der Untersuchung der linearen Verteilung galvanischer Ströme geführt wird", Annalen der Physik und Chemie 72 (1847), 497–508, DOI 10.1002/andp.18471481202

articles.title: The integer Laplacian is degree minus adjacency
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex
set, the integer Laplacian of $G$ equals $D - A$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix of vertex
degrees and $A$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$, both with integer entries.

articles.title: Integer Laplacian of a graph
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, the integer
Laplacian of $G$ is the $V \times V$ integer matrix $L$ with $L_{uu} = \deg u$ for every vertex
$u$, $L_{uv} = -1$ when $u \ne v$ are adjacent, and $L_{uv} = 0$ when $u \ne v$ are not adjacent.

articles.title: Spanning trees as trees on the whole vertex set
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex
set $V$, the number of spanning trees of $G$ equals the number of simple graphs $H$ on $V$ such
that every edge of $H$ is an edge of $G$ and $H$ is a tree.

articles.title: Number of spanning trees
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the number of
spanning trees of $G$ is the number of subgraphs of $G$ that are spanning trees, that is,
subgraphs that contain every vertex of $G$ and are trees.

articles.title: The reduced Laplacian is a principal submatrix
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex
set $V$ and let $L = D - A$ be its Laplacian matrix over $\mathbb{Z}$, where $D$ is the diagonal
matrix of vertex degrees and $A$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$. For every vertex $r \in V$, the
reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$ equals the submatrix of $L$ obtained by deleting the row and the
column of $r$.

articles.title: Reduced Laplacian
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ and a vertex
$r \in V$, the reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$ is the integer Laplacian of $G$ with the row and
the column of $r$ deleted, a matrix indexed by the vertices of $G$ other than $r$.

articles.title: Spanning trees as trees contained in the graph
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a vertex set $V$,
there is an equivalence between the spanning trees of $G$ (subgraphs of $G$ that contain every
vertex and are trees) and the simple graphs $H$ on $V$ that are trees with $H \le G$, that is,
every edge of $H$ is an edge of $G$. It sends a spanning tree to the graph on $V$ with the same
edges.

articles.title: Every graph has a large ε-light vertex set
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $c > 0$ such that for
every natural number $n$, every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and every
real number $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, there is a set $S$ of vertices with at least
$c \varepsilon n$ elements that is $\varepsilon$-light in $G$: the matrix $\varepsilon L - L_S$ is
positive semidefinite, where $L$ is the real Laplacian matrix of $G$ and $L_S$ is the real
Laplacian matrix of the graph on all $n$ vertices whose edges are the edges of $G$ with both
endpoints in $S$.

Appendix B.6 of the source proves this, with $c = 1/42$, as Lemma B.1 (stated for weighted graphs).

## Sources

- First Proof authors, arXiv:2602.05192v2, Appendix B.6 (Lemma B.1), https://arxiv.org/html/2602.05192v2.

articles.title: The large ε-light subset property
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a real constant $c > 0$
such that for every natural number $n$, every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and every real number $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, some set $S$
of vertices that is $\varepsilon$-light in $G$ has at least $c \varepsilon n$ elements.

articles.title: ε-light vertex sets
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let
$\varepsilon$ be a real number and let $S \subseteq V$. Let $L$ be the real Laplacian matrix of
$G$ and $L_S$ the real Laplacian matrix of the graph on $V$ whose edges are the edges of $G$ with
both endpoints in $S$. The set $S$ is $\varepsilon$-light in $G$ if $\varepsilon L - L_S$ is
positive semidefinite.

articles.title: Petersen graph
articles.statement:
The Petersen graph is the generalized Johnson graph $J(5,2,0)$: its
vertices are the $2$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$, and two of them are adjacent
exactly when they are disjoint.

articles.title: Two-edge paths close into triangles when μ = 0
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite strongly regular
graph with parameters $(n, k, \ell, \mu)$ where $\mu = 0$: $G$ has $n$ vertices, every vertex
has degree $k$, any two adjacent vertices have exactly $\ell$ common neighbors, and any two
distinct nonadjacent vertices have no common neighbor. If $u$, $v$, $w$ are vertices of $G$
such that $u$ is adjacent to $v$, $v$ is adjacent to $w$, and $u \neq w$, then $u$ is adjacent
to $w$.

articles.title: Non-principal eigenvalues of a strongly regular graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite strongly
regular graph with parameters $(n, k, \ell, \mu)$: $G$ has $n$ vertices, every vertex has degree
$k$, any two adjacent vertices have exactly $\ell$ common neighbors, and any two distinct
nonadjacent vertices have exactly $\mu$ common neighbors. Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of $G$
over $\mathbb{C}$. Then every eigenvalue $x \in \mathbb{C}$ of $A$ with $x \neq k$ satisfies
$x^2 = (\ell - \mu) x + (k - \mu)$.

articles.title: Connected strongly regular graphs with μ = 0 are complete
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite strongly
regular graph with parameters $(n, k, \ell, \mu)$ where $\mu = 0$: $G$ has $n$ vertices, every
vertex has degree $k$, any two adjacent vertices have exactly $\ell$ common neighbors, and any
two distinct nonadjacent vertices have no common neighbor. If $G$ is connected, then $G$ is
complete, that is, any two distinct vertices of $G$ are adjacent.

Proof: The $\mu = 0$ common-neighbor count makes every nontrivial two-edge walk a
triangle, so walk induction makes each component a clique. Connectedness then
gives completeness. Brouwer and Haemers, Section 9.1.4, state the component
fact: $\mu = 0$ makes the graph a disjoint union of complete graphs.

## Sources

- A. E. Brouwer and W. H. Haemers, Spectra of Graphs, Springer 2012, Ch. 9 (disconnected and complete strongly regular graphs); C. Godsil and G. Royle, Algebraic Graph Theory, GTM 207, Ch. 10.

articles.title: Non-principal eigenvalues of a connected non-complete strongly regular graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
finite strongly regular graph with parameters $(n, k, \ell, \mu)$: $G$ has $n$ vertices, every
vertex has degree $k$, any two adjacent vertices have exactly $\ell$ common neighbors, and any
two distinct nonadjacent vertices have exactly $\mu$ common neighbors. Suppose that $G$ is
connected and not complete, and let $A$ be its adjacency matrix over $\mathbb{C}$. Then every
eigenvalue $x \in \mathbb{C}$ of $A$ with $x \neq k$ satisfies $x^2 = (\ell - \mu) x + (k - \mu)$.

Proof: Apply the identity $A^2 = kI + \ell A + \mu \bar{A}$, where $I$ is the identity matrix
and $\bar{A}$ is the adjacency matrix of the complement of $G$, to an eigenvector $v$ for $x$;
regularity makes the coordinate sum of $v$ zero, so $\bar{A} v = -(1 + x) v$, and this gives
the quadratic. This is the proof of Theorem 9.1.2, (ii) ⇒ (iii), in Brouwer and Haemers,
Section 9.1.3.

## Sources

- A. E. Brouwer and W. H. Haemers, Spectra of Graphs, Springer 2012, Ch. 9, eigenvalues of strongly regular graphs; C. Godsil and G. Royle, Algebraic Graph Theory, GTM 207, Ch. 10 (eigenvalues of strongly regular graphs).

articles.title: Components of a strongly regular graph with μ = 0 are cliques
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite strongly
regular graph with parameters $(n, k, \ell, \mu)$ where $\mu = 0$: $G$ has $n$ vertices, every
vertex has degree $k$, any two adjacent vertices have exactly $\ell$ common neighbors, and any
two distinct nonadjacent vertices have no common neighbor. If $v$ and $w$ are vertices of $G$
joined by a walk, then $v = w$ or $v$ and $w$ are adjacent. Thus each connected component of
$G$ is a clique.

Without $\mu = 0$ this is false: two nonadjacent vertices of the 5-cycle, a strongly regular
graph with parameters $(5, 2, 0, 1)$, are joined by a walk but are neither equal nor adjacent.

Proof: Induct on a witnessing walk and close each two-edge segment using the
zero common-neighbor count. Brouwer and Haemers, Section 9.1.4, state the
result: $\mu = 0$ makes the graph a disjoint union of complete graphs.

## Sources

- A. E. Brouwer and W. H. Haemers, Spectra of Graphs, Springer 2012, Ch. 9 (a disconnected strongly regular graph is a disjoint union of complete graphs); C. Godsil and G. Royle, Algebraic Graph Theory, GTM 207, Ch. 10.

articles.title: Vertex-transitive graph
articles.statement:
A graph is vertex-transitive when its automorphism group acts transitively
on vertices.

articles.title: Hamidoune's reverse-connectivity conjecture fails for every $r \ge 3$
articles.statement:
For no natural
number $r \ge 3$ does the following hold: every digraph $D$ without loops or parallel arcs on a
finite nonempty vertex set, in which every vertex has at least $r$ out-neighbours and at least
$r$ in-neighbours, has an arc $(x, y)$ from $x$ to $y$ with $\kappa(y, x) \ge r$, that is, with
$r$ pairwise distinct directed paths from $y$ to $x$, no two of which share an internal vertex.
Here a directed path is a sequence of distinct vertices in which each vertex is joined to the
next by an arc, and its internal vertices are all its vertices except the first and the last.

Thomassen constructed, for every positive integer $r$, a digraph without digons with minimum
out-degree and minimum in-degree at least $r$ in which no arc $(x, y)$ has $\kappa(y, x) \ge 3$;
the report notes after Conjecture 6.21 that this is a counterexample for all $r \ge 3$.

## Sources

- B. D. Sullivan, A Summary of Problems and Results related to the Caccetta-Haggkvist Conjecture, arXiv:math/0605646, Conjecture 6.21; resolution: C. Thomassen, Even cycles in directed graphs, European J. Combin. 6 (1985) 85-89, as stated in the report's Theorem 5.2 (part ii) and the note after Conjecture 6.21, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0195-6698(85)80025-1.

articles.title: Hamidoune's reverse-connectivity conjecture for some $r \ge 3$
articles.statement:
The statement that there
is a natural number $r \ge 3$ such that every digraph $D$ without loops or parallel arcs on a
finite nonempty vertex set, in which every vertex has at least $r$ out-neighbours and at least
$r$ in-neighbours, has an arc $(x, y)$ from $x$ to $y$ with $\kappa(y, x) \ge r$, that is, with
$r$ pairwise distinct directed paths from $y$ to $x$, no two of which share an internal vertex.
Here a directed path is a sequence of distinct vertices in which each vertex is joined to the
next by an arc, and its internal vertices are all its vertices except the first and the last.

articles.title: Internally disjoint directed paths
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a digraph, $r$ a natural number and $y$, $x$
vertices of $D$. We write $\kappa(y, x) \ge r$ when there are $r$ pairwise distinct directed paths
in $D$ from $y$ to $x$, no two of which share an internal vertex. Here a directed path from $y$ to
$x$ is a sequence of distinct vertices starting at $y$ and ending at $x$ in which each vertex is
joined to the next by an arc of $D$, and its internal vertices are all its vertices except the
first and the last.

articles.title: Internal vertices of a path
articles.statement: The internal vertices of a path given as a vertex list (all but the first and the last).

articles.title: Directed paths
articles.statement:
A directed path in a digraph $D$ is a finite, possibly empty, sequence of
vertices of $D$ with no vertex repeated in which each vertex is joined to the next by an arc of
$D$.

articles.title: Dichromatically $k$-colourable graphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$ and
let $k$ be a natural number. Then $G$ is dichromatically $k$-colourable if for every orientation
$D$ of $G$ there is a map $c \colon V \to \{0, \dots, k - 1\}$, not required to be a proper
colouring, such that no closed directed walk of positive length in $D$ has all of its vertices of
the same colour under $c$.

Since every closed directed walk of positive length contains a directed cycle, this is the same as
asking for a colouring with no monochromatic directed cycle.

articles.title: The dichromatic number as a least natural number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph. If $G$ is
dichromatically $n$-colourable for some natural number $n$, then the dichromatic number of $G$
equals the least natural number $k$ such that $G$ is dichromatically $k$-colourable.

articles.title: Dichromatic number
Closed directed walks
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a binary relation on a set $V$, viewed as a digraph,
let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{n+1}$ be elements of $V$. The sequence
$(f_0, \dots, f_{n+1})$ is a closed directed walk of length $n + 1$ in $D$ if $f_0 = f_{n+1}$ and
$D(f_i, f_{i+1})$ holds for every $i$ with $0 \le i \le n$.

Vertices may repeat, so this is a closed walk of positive length rather than a directed cycle in
the strict sense.

articles.title: Orientations of a graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$. A binary relation
$D$ on $V$ is an orientation of $G$ if $D(u, v)$ holds only when $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$,
and for every pair of adjacent vertices $u$ and $v$ exactly one of $D(u, v)$ and $D(v, u)$
holds.

articles.title: Edgeless graphs are dichromatically $1$-colourable
articles.statement:
If a simple graph $G$ has no edges,
then $G$ is dichromatically $1$-colourable.

No orientation of $G$ has an arc, so there is no closed directed walk of positive length.

articles.title: The empty orientation of an edgeless graph
articles.statement:
If a simple graph $G$ has no edges, then the
empty relation on its vertex set, the digraph with no arcs, is an orientation of $G$.

articles.title: Extensionality for labeled directed graphs
articles.statement:
Two labeled directed graphs $G$ and $H$
with the same vertex set, edge set and label set are equal if they have the same source map,
the same target map and the same label map.

articles.title: Labeled directed graph
articles.statement:
A labeled directed graph with vertex set $V$, edge set $E$ and
label set $L$ consists of a source map $s : E \to V$, a target map $t : E \to V$ and a label
map $\ell : E \to L$; the edge $e$ goes from $s(e)$ to $t(e)$ and carries the label $\ell(e)$.
Loops and parallel edges are allowed.

articles.title: Label of an edge in a restriction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, $p$ a predicate
on its vertices, and $e$ an edge of $G$ whose source and target satisfy $p$, viewed as an edge of
the restriction of $G$ to $p$. The label of $e$ in the restriction is its label in $G$.

articles.title: Source of an edge in a restriction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, $p$ a predicate
on its vertices, and $e$ an edge of $G$ whose source and target satisfy $p$, viewed as an edge of
the restriction of $G$ to $p$. The source of $e$ in the restriction, viewed as a vertex of $G$,
is the source of $e$ in $G$.

articles.title: Target of an edge in a restriction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, $p$ a predicate
on its vertices, and $e$ an edge of $G$ whose source and target satisfy $p$, viewed as an edge of
the restriction of $G$ to $p$. The target of $e$ in the restriction, viewed as a vertex of $G$,
is the target of $e$ in $G$.

articles.title: Restriction of a labeled directed graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph with
vertex set $V$ and label set $L$, and let $p$ be a predicate on $V$. The restriction of $G$ to
$p$ is the labeled directed graph with label set $L$ whose vertices are the vertices $v$ of $G$
with $p(v)$, whose edges are the edges of $G$ whose source and target both satisfy $p$, and in
which each edge has the same source, target and label as in $G$.

articles.title: Jaeger's modular orientation conjecture is false
articles.statement:
There exist an integer $k \ge 1$ and a
finite multigraph (loops and parallel edges allowed) with at least two vertices, in which every
partition of the vertices into two nonempty sets is crossed by at least $4k$ edges, such that no
orientation of the edges makes the indegree minus the outdegree of every vertex divisible by
$2k + 1$.

Han, Li, Wu and Zhang (J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 131 (2018) 1-11) construct, for every $k \ge 3$,
a $4k$-edge-connected graph with no circular $(2+1/k)$-flow, equivalently no modulo $(2k+1)$
orientation; the cases $k = 1$ (Tutte's 3-flow conjecture) and $k = 2$ remain open.

## Sources

- Daniel W. Cranston and Jiaao Li, Circular flows in planar graphs, SIAM J. Discrete Math. (2020), arXiv:1812.09833, https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09833.

articles.title: Jaeger's modular orientation conjecture
articles.statement:
This is the statement that for every integer
$k \ge 1$, every finite multigraph (loops and parallel edges allowed) that has at least two
vertices, and in which every partition of the vertices into two nonempty sets is crossed by at
least $4k$ edges, admits an orientation of its edges in which, at every vertex, the indegree minus
the outdegree is divisible by $2k + 1$.

The parameter $k$ is positive, as in the source discussion of $(2 + 1/k)$-flows and its
specializations at $k = 1$ and $k = 2$.

articles.title: Edges crossing a cut
articles.statement:
Consider a multigraph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$ in which
each edge has a first and a second endpoint. For a set $S \subseteq V$, an edge crosses the cut at
$S$ when exactly one of its two endpoints lies in $S$.

articles.title: Size of a cut
articles.statement:
Consider a multigraph with finitely many edges in which each edge has a
first and a second endpoint. For a set $S$ of vertices, the size of the cut at $S$ is the number
of edges crossing it, that is, having exactly one endpoint in $S$. Distinct parallel edges are
counted separately.

articles.title: Indegree
articles.statement:
In a multigraph with finitely many edges and a chosen orientation, the
indegree of a vertex $v$ is the number of edges whose head is $v$, parallel edges counted
separately.

articles.title: 4k-edge-connected multigraphs
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a finite multigraph is
$4k$-edge-connected when it has at least two vertices and, for every set $S$ of vertices such that
both $S$ and its complement are nonempty, at least $4k$ edges cross the cut at $S$, that is, have
exactly one endpoint in $S$. Parallel edges are counted separately. For $k \ge 1$ the condition
implies that the multigraph is connected.

articles.title: Modular orientations
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, an orientation of a multigraph with
finitely many edges is a modulo $(2k+1)$ orientation when at every vertex the indegree minus the
outdegree is congruent to $0$ modulo $2k + 1$.

articles.title: Head of an oriented edge
articles.statement:
Each edge $e$ of the multigraph has a reference direction from
its first endpoint to its second endpoint, and an orientation chooses for each edge whether to
reverse it. The head of $e$ is its second endpoint if $e$ is not reversed and its first endpoint
if $e$ is reversed.

articles.title: Tail of an oriented edge
articles.statement:
Each edge $e$ of the multigraph has a reference direction from
its first endpoint to its second endpoint, and an orientation chooses for each edge whether to
reverse it. The tail of $e$ is its first endpoint if $e$ is not reversed and its second endpoint
if $e$ is reversed.

articles.title: Outdegree
articles.statement:
In a multigraph with finitely many edges and a chosen orientation, the
outdegree of a vertex $v$ is the number of edges whose tail is $v$, parallel edges counted
separately.

articles.title: Road coloring theorem
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite nonempty set and let $\to$ be a relation
on $V$, viewed as a directed graph on $V$ without parallel edges (loops allowed). Suppose that the
graph is strongly connected (for all $u, v \in V$ there is a directed walk, possibly of length $0$,
from $u$ to $v$), aperiodic (for every integer $d > 1$ there is a closed directed walk of positive
length not divisible by $d$), and of constant positive out-degree (there is $k > 0$ such that
every vertex has exactly $k$ out-neighbours). Then there exist a natural number $\ell$ and a map
$\delta : V \times \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \to V$ such that for every $v \in V$ the map
$c \mapsto \delta(v, c)$ is a bijection from $\{0, \dots, \ell - 1\}$ onto the out-neighbours of
$v$, together with a word $c_1 \cdots c_m$ over $\{0, \dots, \ell - 1\}$ and a vertex $r$ such
that following the labels $c_1, \dots, c_m$ in order from any vertex $v$ ends at $r$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_coloring_theorem

articles.title: Road coloring theorem for a finite vertex type
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite nonempty set and let
$\to$ be a relation on $V$, viewed as a directed graph on $V$ without parallel edges (loops
allowed). Suppose that the graph is strongly connected (for all $u, v \in V$ there is a directed
walk, possibly of length $0$, from $u$ to $v$), aperiodic (for every integer $d > 1$ there is a
closed directed walk of positive length not divisible by $d$), and of constant positive
out-degree (there is $k > 0$ such that every vertex has exactly $k$ out-neighbours). Then there
exist a natural number $\ell$ and a map $\delta : V \times \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \to V$ such that
for every $v \in V$ the map $c \mapsto \delta(v, c)$ is a bijection from $\{0, \dots, \ell - 1\}$
onto the out-neighbours of $v$, together with a word $c_1 \cdots c_m$ over $\{0, \dots, \ell - 1\}$
and a vertex $r$ such that following the labels $c_1, \dots, c_m$ in order from any vertex $v$
ends at $r$.

This form only assumes that $V$ is finite, as a property, rather than being given a finite set of
all its elements as data.

articles.title: Robbins' theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite nonempty vertex set $V$. Then $G$
is connected and, after deleting any single edge of $G$, every vertex is still reachable from
every vertex (that is, $G$ is 2-edge-connected) if and only if $G$ has a strongly connected
orientation: a relation $D$ on $V$ such that $D(u, v)$ holds only when $u$ and $v$ are
adjacent, for every edge $uv$ exactly one of $D(u, v)$ and $D(v, u)$ holds, and every vertex
$v$ can be reached from every vertex $u$ by a finite, possibly empty, sequence of $D$-steps.

## Sources

- H. E. Robbins, "A Theorem on Graphs, with an Application to a Problem of Traffic Control," American Mathematical Monthly 46 (1939), 281–283; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbins%27_theorem

articles.title: Robbins' theorem, allowing the empty graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite,
possibly empty, vertex set $V$. Then every vertex of $G$ is reachable from every vertex and,
after deleting any single edge of $G$, every vertex is still reachable from every vertex, if
and only if $G$ has a strongly connected orientation: a relation $D$ on $V$ such that $D(u, v)$
holds only when $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, for every edge $uv$ exactly one of $D(u, v)$ and
$D(v, u)$ holds, and every vertex $v$ can be reached from every vertex $u$ by a finite,
possibly empty, sequence of $D$-steps.

For nonempty $V$ the left-hand condition says that $G$ is 2-edge-connected; for empty $V$ both
sides hold.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbins%27_theorem

articles.title: Moon's count of circular triads
articles.statement:
In a tournament on $n$ players with scores
$s_1, \dots, s_n$, the number of circular triads is
$\binom{n}{3} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \binom{s_i}{2}$.

## Sources

- Ian R. Harris and Ryan P. A. McShane, "Counting Tournaments with a Specified Number of Circular Triads", Theorem 6.

articles.title: Exponential generating function of a shifted binomial sequence
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$
and $b$, let $g(n) = n! \binom{n-a+b}{b}$ for $n \ge a$ and $g(n) = 0$ for $n < a$, and let
$A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} g(n) x^n / n!$ be its exponential generating function, a formal power
series over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then $(1 - x)^{b+1} A(x) = x^a$; equivalently,
$A(x) = x^a (1 - x)^{-(b+1)}$.

## Sources

- Ian R. Harris and Ryan P. A. McShane, "Counting Tournaments with a Specified Number of Circular Triads", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Circular triad
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary relation on the players $1, \dots, n$, where
$T(i, j)$ means that $i$ beats $j$. A set $S$ of players is a circular triad of $T$ if $S$ has
exactly three elements and every $i \in S$ beats exactly one $j \in S$.

In a tournament this means that the three players form a directed $3$-cycle.

articles.title: Moon's reducibility criterion
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a tournament on $n$ players in which the score
$s_i$ of player $i$ satisfies $s_1 \le s_2 \le \dots \le s_n$. Then $T$ is reducible if and only
if $\sum_{i=1}^{k} s_i = \binom{k}{2}$ for some integer $k$ with $1 \le k < n$.

## Sources

- Ian R. Harris and Ryan P. A. McShane, "Counting Tournaments with a Specified Number of Circular Triads", Theorem 5.

articles.title: Reducible tournament
articles.statement:
A tournament is reducible if some nonempty proper
set of players loses all games against the complement.

articles.title: Tournament
articles.statement:
A tournament on the players $1, \dots, n$ is a binary relation $T$, where
$T(i, j)$ means that $i$ beats $j$, such that no player beats itself and for any two distinct
players $i$ and $j$ exactly one of $T(i, j)$ and $T(j, i)$ holds.

articles.title: Landau's theorem on score sequences
articles.statement:
Let $s_1 \le s_2 \le \dots \le s_n$ be a
nondecreasing sequence of natural numbers. There is a tournament on $n$ players in which player
$i$ has score $s_i$ for every $i$ if and only if $\sum_{i=1}^{k} s_i \ge \binom{k}{2}$ for every
$k$ with $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i = \binom{n}{2}$.

## Sources

- Ian R. Harris and Ryan P. A. McShane, "Counting Tournaments with a Specified Number of Circular Triads", Theorem 4.

articles.title: Score of a player
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary relation on the players $1, \dots, n$, where
$T(i, j)$ means that $i$ beats $j$. The score of a player $i$ is the number of players $j$ such
that $T(i, j)$ holds, that is, the number of players that $i$ beats.

In a tournament this is the outdegree of $i$.

articles.title: Containing $T^*$ as a subtournament
articles.statement:
**Containing $T^*$ as a subtournament.** A relation $T$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ contains $T^*$ when there is an injective map $f$ from the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, 5\}$ of $T^*$ to $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that for all vertices $i, j$ of $T^*$,
$i \to j$ in $T^*$ if and only if $T(f(i), f(j))$ holds.

articles.title: Tournaments
articles.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A relation $T$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a
tournament when $T(x, x)$ holds for no $x$ and, for all distinct $x$ and $y$, exactly one of
$T(x, y)$ and $T(y, x)$ holds.

articles.title: Transitivity on a vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $T$ be a relation on
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $S$ be a set of its elements. Then $T$ is transitive on $S$ when, for
all $x, y, z \in S$, $T(x, y)$ and $T(y, z)$ imply $T(x, z)$. For a tournament $T$ this says that
the subtournament of $T$ on $S$ is transitive.

articles.title: The backward arcs of $T^*$
articles.statement:
**The backward arcs of $T^*$.** The list of ordered pairs $(5, 0)$, $(5, 2)$, $(4, 1)$,
$(3, 0)$ of vertices in $\{0, \dots, 5\}$. These are the arcs of the six-vertex tournament $T^*$
that go from a larger to a smaller vertex: $6 \to 1$, $6 \to 3$, $5 \to 2$ and $4 \to 1$ in the
source's labelling $1, \dots, 6$, with every vertex lowered by one.

articles.title: Nguyen–Scott–Seymour: $T^*$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property
articles.statement:
**Nguyen–Scott–Seymour: $T^*$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property.** There is a real number
$\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every natural number $n$ and every tournament $T$ on the vertex
set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that does not contain $T^*$ as a subtournament, there is a set $S$ of
vertices on which $T$ is transitive with $|S| \ge n^{\varepsilon}$.

Resolved true: Nguyen, Scott and Seymour prove that every two-colourable tournament has the
Erdős–Hajnal property, "which completes the verification of the conjecture for six-vertex
tournaments"; Berger, Choromanski and Chudnovsky had proved it for every tournament on at most six
vertices except `T*` (the remark recorded with the problem), and `T*` is two-colourable (`{1, 2, 3}`
and `{4, 5, 6}` are transitive).

## Sources

- AimPL: Graph Ramsey Theory, Problem 1.12 [Maria Chudnovsky], http://aimpl.org/graphramsey/1/; resolution: T. Nguyen, A. Scott and P. Seymour, Induced subgraph density. VI. Bounded VC-dimension, Adv. Math. 482 (2025), 110601, arXiv:2312.15572, abstract and introduction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.15572.

articles.title: The Erdős–Hajnal problem for the tournament $T^*$
articles.statement:
**The Erdős–Hajnal problem for the tournament $T^*$.** There is a real number
$\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every natural number $n$ and every tournament $T$ on the vertex
set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that does not contain $T^*$ as a subtournament, there is a set $S$ of
vertices on which $T$ is transitive with $|S| \ge n^{\varepsilon}$.

This is Problem 1.12 of the AimPL problem list on graph Ramsey theory.

articles.title: The six-vertex tournament $T^*$
articles.statement:
**The six-vertex tournament $T^*$.** The tournament $T^*$ is the relation on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, 5\}$ with an arc $i \to j$ if and only if either $(i, j)$ is one of the backward
arcs $(5, 0)$, $(5, 2)$, $(4, 1)$, $(3, 0)$, or $i < j$ and $(j, i)$ is not a backward arc.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 1216 is false
articles.statement:
It is not the case that $f(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ for
every $n \ge 1$, where $f(n)$ is the largest $m$ such that every tournament on $n$ vertices
contains a transitive subtournament on $m$ vertices.

Reid and Parker proved $f(n) \ge \lfloor \log_2 n + 4 - \log_2 7 \rfloor$ for all $n \ge 14$; at
$n = 14$ this gives $f(14) \ge 5 > 4 = \lfloor \log_2 14 \rfloor + 1$, while Stearns' bound
$f(n) \ge \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ holds for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #1216, https://www.erdosproblems.com/1216 (status DISPROVED); resolution: K. B. Reid and E. T. Parker, Disproof of a conjecture of Erdős and Moser on tournaments, J. Combinatorial Theory 9 (1970), 225-238, erdosproblems.com/1216: f(n) ≥ ⌊log₂ n + 4 - log₂ 7⌋ for all n ≥ 14, so f(14) ≥ 5 > ⌊log₂ 14⌋ + 1.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 1216 (the Erdős–Moser formula)
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$,
$f(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$, where $f(n)$ is the largest $m$ such that every tournament
on $n$ vertices contains a transitive subtournament on $m$ vertices.

articles.title: Transitive subtournament number
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $f(n)$ is the largest $m$ such
that every tournament $T$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is transitive on some set of exactly $m$
vertices, that is, contains a transitive subtournament on $m$ vertices.

Such $m$ exist (for instance $m = 0$) and are at most $n$, so the largest one exists.

articles.title: Negation of the Erdős–Simonovits balanced subgraph claim
articles.statement:
The proposition that the
Erdős–Simonovits balanced subgraph claim fails, that is, that it is not the case that for all
reals $\varepsilon$ and $\alpha$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ and $0 < \alpha < 1$, for all
sufficiently large real $D$ and then all sufficiently large $n$, every simple graph $G$ on the
vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^{1+\alpha}$ edges has a (not necessarily
induced) subgraph $H$ with some number $m$ of vertices such that $H$ is $D$-balanced (its maximum
degree is at most $D$ times its minimum degree), $m > n^{1-\alpha}$, and $H$ has more than
$\varepsilon m^{1+\alpha}$ edges.

articles.title: Balanced graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and $D$ a real number. The graph $G$ is
$D$-balanced if its maximum degree $\Delta(G)$ is at most $D$ times its minimum degree
$\delta(G)$, that is, $\Delta(G) \le D \cdot \delta(G)$.

articles.title: The Erdős–Simonovits balanced subgraph claim is false
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for all reals
$\varepsilon$ and $\alpha$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ and $0 < \alpha < 1$, for all sufficiently
large real $D$ and then all sufficiently large $n$, every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^{1+\alpha}$ edges has a (not necessarily induced) subgraph
$H$ with some number $m$ of vertices such that $H$ is $D$-balanced (its maximum degree is at most
$D$ times its minimum degree), $m > n^{1-\alpha}$, and $H$ has more than $\varepsilon m^{1+\alpha}$
edges.

The disproof uses a bipartite witness: the requirement $m > n^{1-\alpha}$ is too strong, and the
correct order is $n^{\alpha}$ per Jun Gao and Jiang–Longbrake [JiLo25], per erdosproblems.com/1077.

## Sources

- External Lean disproof of Erdos Problem 1077, plby/lean-proofs, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/dfe2d78128b493c572cf525b1b8edf4897fb7664/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos1077.lean#L265.

articles.title: Erdős–Simonovits balanced subgraph claim
articles.statement:
