For all reals $\varepsilon$ and $\alpha$ with
$0 < \varepsilon < 1$ and $0 < \alpha < 1$, for all sufficiently large real $D$ and then all
sufficiently large $n$, every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more
than $n^{1+\alpha}$ edges has a (not necessarily induced) subgraph $H$ with some number $m$ of
vertices such that $H$ is $D$-balanced (its maximum degree is at most $D$ times its minimum
degree), $m > n^{1-\alpha}$, and $H$ has more than $\varepsilon m^{1+\alpha}$ edges.

This claim (Erdős Problem 1077) is false.

articles.title: Bounding the book number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and $b$ a natural number. If
every pair of adjacent vertices $u$, $v$ of $G$ has at most $b$ common neighbors, then the book
number of $G$ is at most $b$.

articles.title: Book number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. The book number of $G$ is the maximum,
over ordered pairs $(u, v)$ of adjacent vertices, of the number of common neighbors of $u$ and
$v$ (the number of triangles containing the edge $uv$); it is $0$ if $G$ has no edges.

articles.title: Edwards–Khadzhiivanov–Nikiforov theorem on edges in many triangles
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n$, every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with more than $n^2/4$ edges has an edge that lies in
at least $n/6$ triangles of $G$.

This was proved independently by Edwards and by Khadzhiivanov and Nikiforov, and answers Erdős
Problem 905 affirmatively.

## Sources

- External Lean proof of Erdős Problem 905, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos905.lean.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 905 on edges in many triangles
articles.statement:
The proposition asserts that for every
natural number $n$ and every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with more than $n^2/4$ edges, some
edge of $G$ lies in at least $n/6$ triangles of $G$.

articles.title: Common neighbors of an edge are bounded by the book number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple
graph. If $u$ and $v$ are adjacent vertices of $G$, then the number of common neighbors of $u$
and $v$ is at most the book number of $G$.

articles.title: Book lower bound for Erdős Problem 1034
articles.statement:
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the following
holds for all sufficiently large $n$: every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set $Y$ of
vertices, each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$, with
$|Y| \ge (1/6 - \varepsilon)n$.

articles.title: The Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture is false
articles.statement:
It is not true that for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, every simple graph on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set of more than
$(1/2 - \varepsilon)n$ vertices, each adjacent to two distinct vertices of $T$.

## Sources

- Ma and Tang (disproof with upper bound (2-√(5/2)+o(1))n; K₄-free sketch with (2√3-3+o(1))n), per erdosproblems.com/1034, https://www.erdosproblems.com/1034.

articles.title: Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture
articles.statement:
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the following holds
for all sufficiently large $n$: every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with
more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set $Y$ of vertices, each adjacent in $G$
to two distinct vertices of $T$, with $|Y| > (1/2 - \varepsilon)n$.

This claim (Erdős Problem 1034) was disproved by Ma and Tang.

articles.title: Negation of the Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture
articles.statement:
The proposition that the
Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture fails, that is, that it is not the case that for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set $Y$ of
vertices, each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$, with $|Y| > (1/2 - \varepsilon)n$.

articles.title: Vertices joined to two vertices of a set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex type $V$
and let $T$ and $Y$ be finite sets of vertices. The set $Y$ is joined to two vertices of $T$ in
$G$ if every vertex $y \in Y$ is adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices $u, v \in T$.

articles.title: $K_4$-free upper bound for Erdős Problem 1034
articles.statement:
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the
following holds for all sufficiently large $n$: there is a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no $K_4$ and has more than $n^2/4$ edges, such that for every
triangle $T$ of $G$, every set $Y$ of vertices each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of
$T$ satisfies $|Y| \le (2\sqrt{3} - 3 + \varepsilon)n$.

articles.title: Ma–Tang upper bound for Erdős Problem 1034
articles.statement:
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the following
holds for all sufficiently large $n$: there is a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges such that for every triangle $T$ of $G$, every
set $Y$ of vertices each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$ satisfies
$|Y| \le (2 - \sqrt{5/2} + \varepsilon)n$.

articles.title: Girth-five extremal number on fifty vertices
articles.statement:
The girth-five extremal number
$\mathrm{ex}(50; \{C_3, C_4\})$, the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $50$
vertices that contains no triangle and no four-cycle, equals $175$.

For graphs on $n$ vertices of girth at least $5$, the Hoffman–Singleton graph attains the
Moore-type bound $\frac{n}{2} \sqrt{n - 1}$ on the number of edges, with $n = 50$.

## Sources

- A. J. Hoffman and R. R. Singleton, *On Moore graphs with diameters 2 and 3*, IBM J. Res. Develop. 4 (1960), 497–504; OEIS A006856; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/ExGirthFive/README.md`.

articles.title: Girth-five extremal numbers up to twenty vertices
articles.statement:
For $n = 1, 2, \dots, 20$ the
girth-five extremal numbers $\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_3, C_4\})$, the largest numbers of edges of a
simple graph on $n$ vertices that contains no triangle and no four-cycle, are, in order,
$0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 18, 21, 23, 26, 28, 31, 34, 38, 41$.

## Sources

- D. K. Garnick, Y. H. H. Kwong, and F. Lazebnik, *Extremal graphs without three-cycles or four-cycles*, J. Graph Theory 17 (1993), 633–645 (`n ≤ 24`); OEIS A006856; listed in leansolving/SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/ExGirthFive/README.md`.

articles.title: Girth-five extremal number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_3, C_4\})$
is the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices whose girth is at least $5$,
that is, which contains no triangle and no four-cycle (OEIS A006856). An acyclic graph has
infinite girth, so the empty graph always qualifies.

articles.title: Extremal numbers of the four-cycle up to twenty vertices
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let
$\mathrm{ex}(n; C_4)$ be the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices that
contains no four-cycle $C_4$ as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph. For
$n = 1, 2, \dots, 20$ the values of $\mathrm{ex}(n; C_4)$ are, in order,
$0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 13, 16, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36, 39, 42, 46$.

## Sources

- C. R. J. Clapham, A. Flockhart, and J. Sheehan, *Graphs without four-cycles*, J. Graph Theory 13 (1989), 29–47 (`n ≤ 21`); OEIS A006855; listed in leansolving/SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/ExC4/README.md`.

articles.title: Füredi's theorem on four-cycle-free graphs
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let
$\mathrm{ex}(n; C_4)$ be the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices that
contains no four-cycle $C_4$ as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph. For every prime power
$q > 13$, $\mathrm{ex}(q^2 + q + 1; C_4) = q (q + 1)^2 / 2$; the division is exact because
$q (q + 1)$ is even.

The bound is attained by the polarity graph of the projective plane of order $q$.

## Sources

- Z. Füredi, *On the number of edges of quadrilateral-free graphs*, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 68 (1996), 1–6; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/ExC4/README.md`.

articles.title: The generalized Turán number is an upper bound
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and
$H$ be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. If $G$ is a simple graph on the vertex
set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$), then the
number of copies of $T$ in $G$ is at most the generalized Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$.

articles.title: The generalized Turán number is attained
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and $H$
be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. If some simple graph on the vertex set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ contains no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$), then some such graph
$G$ has exactly $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ copies of $T$, where $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is the
generalized Turán number.

articles.title: The generalized Turán number as a supremum
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and $H$
be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. Then the generalized Turán number
$\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is the supremum in $\mathbb{N}$, with the supremum of the empty family taken
to be $0$, of the number of copies of $T$ in $G$ over all simple graphs $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ that contain no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$).

articles.title: Upper bounds for the generalized Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $m$ be natural numbers and let
$T$ and $H$ be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. Then the generalized Turán
number $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is at most $m$ if and only if every simple graph on the vertex set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$) has at most $m$
copies of $T$.

articles.title: Generalized Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and $H$ be simple graphs,
where $T$ has finitely many vertices. A copy of a graph in a graph $G$ is a subgraph of $G$
isomorphic to it, and $G$ is $H$-free if it contains no copy of $H$. The generalized Turán number
$\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is the largest number of copies of $T$ in an $H$-free simple graph on the
vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, and is $0$ if there is no such graph.

The source considers graphs $T$ and $H$ without isolated vertices; the definition does not require
this.

articles.title: Saturation number is attained by a saturated graph
articles.statement:
Attainment: when a saturated graph exists, some saturated graph has exactly
`sat(n, H)` edges.

articles.title: Saturation via strict supergraphs
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is
$H$-saturated if and only if $G$ is $H$-free and every simple graph $G'$ on the same vertex set
with $G \subsetneq G'$ contains a copy of $H$.

articles.title: Saturation via missing edges
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is
$H$-saturated if and only if $G$ is $H$-free and, for all distinct vertices $s$ and $t$ of $G$
that are not adjacent in $G$, the graph $G + st$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $st$
contains a copy of $H$.

This is the usual missing-edge definition of $H$-saturation.

articles.title: Saturation of complete graphs
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph. The complete graph on any vertex
set is $H$-saturated if and only if it is $H$-free.

A complete graph has no missing edge, so only $H$-freeness matters. The vertex set of the complete
graph is independent of that of $H$, so this condition is not vacuous: $H$ need not embed in a
complete graph with fewer vertices.

articles.title: $H$-saturated graphs
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is $H$-saturated if $G$
is $H$-free (it contains no copy of $H$ as a subgraph) and is maximal with this property: every
$H$-free simple graph $G'$ on the same vertex set as $G$ with $G \subseteq G'$ equals $G$.

articles.title: Saturating non-edge
articles.statement:
Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs. A pair of vertices $x, y$ of $G$ is
an $F$-saturating non-edge of $G$ if $x \ne y$, $x$ and $y$ are not adjacent in $G$, and the graph
$G + xy$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $xy$ contains a copy of $F$ (a subgraph isomorphic
to $F$, not necessarily induced).

articles.title: A saturating non-edge of an $F$-free graph creates a copy of $F$
articles.statement:
Let $F$ and $G$ be simple
graphs, and let $xy$ be an $F$-saturating non-edge of $G$. If $G$ is $F$-free, that is, $G$
contains no copy of $F$, then the graph $G + xy$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $xy$
contains a copy of $F$, and $G$ does not.

articles.title: Number of saturating non-edges
articles.statement:
Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs such that $G$ has only
finitely many $F$-saturating non-edges. Then $f_F(G)$ is the number of $F$-saturating non-edges
of $G$, counted as unordered pairs $\{x, y\}$, that is, the number of edges of the graph of
$F$-saturating non-edges of $G$.

articles.title: Edge counts of saturated graphs
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph and $n$ a natural number.
The set of saturated edge counts of $H$ on $n$ vertices is the set of natural numbers $m$ such
that some $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ has exactly $m$
edges.

articles.title: The saturation number is zero when no saturated graph exists
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph,
$n$ a natural number, and $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ the saturation number of $H$ on $n$
vertices. If the set of saturated edge counts of $H$ on $n$ vertices is empty, that is, no
$H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ exists, then
$\operatorname{sat}(n, H) = 0$.

articles.title: Saturated graphs bound the saturation number
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph, $n$ a natural
number, and $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ the saturation number of $H$ on $n$ vertices. Every
$H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ has at least
$\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ edges.

articles.title: Saturation number
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph and $n$ a natural number. The saturation
number $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ is the minimum number of edges of an $H$-saturated simple graph
on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, and is $0$ when no such graph exists.

articles.title: Graph of saturating non-edges
articles.statement:
Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs. The graph of $F$-saturating
non-edges of $G$ is the simple graph on the vertices of $G$ whose edges are exactly the
$F$-saturating non-edges of $G$.

articles.title: Kővári–Sós–Turán bound
articles.statement:
Let $m, n, s, t$ be natural numbers with $s \ge 1$ and
$1 \le t \le n$. Let $z(m, n; s, t)$ be the Zarankiewicz number, the largest number of edges in a
bipartite graph with parts of sizes $m$ and $n$ that contains no copy of the complete bipartite
graph $K_{s,t}$. Then

$$z(m, n; s, t) \le (s - 1)^{1/t} (n - t + 1) m^{1 - 1/t} + (t - 1) m.$$

Proof: Double-count common right neighborhoods, apply the power-mean inequality, and take a real
$t$-th root, following Kővári–Sós–Turán (1954) and Jukna, Theorem 2.10.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarankiewicz_problem.

articles.title: Monomial graphs of girth eight
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $e$ a natural number, $q = p^e$, and
$\mathbb{F}$ a field with $q$ elements, and suppose that either $p \ge 5$ and $e = 2^a 3^b$ for
some natural numbers $a, b$, or $3 \le q \le 10^{10}$. For natural numbers $m_2, n_2, m_3, n_3$,
let $G$ be the bipartite graph with two copies of $\mathbb{F}^3$ as its parts, in which
$(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ in the first part is adjacent to $(y_1, y_2, y_3)$ in the second part exactly
when $x_2 + y_2 = x_1^{m_2} y_1^{n_2}$ and $x_3 + y_3 = x_1^{m_3} y_1^{n_3}$, and let $\Gamma_3$
be the graph defined in the same way by $x_2 + y_2 = x_1 y_1$ and $x_3 + y_3 = x_1 y_1^2$. If
the girth of $G$ is at least $8$, then $G$ is isomorphic to $\Gamma_3$ and the girth of $G$ is
exactly $8$.

## Sources

- V. Dmytrenko, F. Lazebnik, and J. Williford, "On monomial graphs of girth eight", Finite Fields Appl. 13 (2007), 828–842, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Pentagon bound for triangle-free graphs (five-cycle case of Erdős Problem 24)
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$, every graph on $5n$ vertices with no three pairwise adjacent vertices has at
most $n^5$ subgraphs isomorphic to the $5$-cycle $C_5$.

## Sources

- Erdős Problems, Problem 24 (records the Grzesik and Hatami–Hladký–Králʼ–Norine–Razborov resolution), https://www.erdosproblems.com/24; Andrzej Grzesik, On the maximum number of five-cycles in a triangle-free graph, arXiv:1102.0962v3, https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.0962v3; Hamed Hatami, Jan Hladky, Daniel Kral, Serguei Norine, and Alexander Razborov, On the number of pentagons in triangle-free graphs, arXiv:1102.1634v4, https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.1634v4.

articles.title: Pentagons in triangle-free graphs (Erdős Problem 24)
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, every
graph on $5n$ vertices with no three pairwise adjacent vertices has at most $n^5$ subgraphs
isomorphic to the $5$-cycle $C_5$.

articles.title: The Conlon–Lee subdivision conjecture holds
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $F$ and a natural number
$n$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n, F)$ be the maximum number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices
that contains no copy of $F$ (not necessarily induced), or $0$ if there is no such graph. For a
simple graph $H$ and a natural number $k \ge 2$, let $H^{k-1}$ be the graph obtained from $H$ by
replacing each edge with a path of length $k$ through $k - 1$ new vertices (internally disjoint
for different edges). Then for every even natural number $k \ge 2$, every natural number $m$ and
every simple graph $H$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, there are real numbers
$\delta > 0$ and $C$ such that $\mathrm{ex}(n, H^{k-1}) \le C \cdot n^{1 + 1/k - \delta}$ for
every natural number $n$.

This was proved by Janzer (Bull. London Math. Soc. 53 (2021) 108–118, Theorem 1.7).

## Sources

- O. Janzer, The extremal number of longer subdivisions, Bull. London Math. Soc. 53 (2021) 108-118, arXiv:1905.08001, https://doi.org/10.1112/blms.12404.

articles.title: The Conlon–Lee subdivision conjecture
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $H$ and a natural number $k$,
write $H^{k-1}$ for the $(k-1)$-subdivision of $H$, and for a simple graph $F$ and a natural
number $n$ write $\mathrm{ex}(n, F)$ for the extremal number of $F$ on $n$ vertices. The
conjecture is the statement that for every even natural number $k \ge 2$, every natural number
$m$ and every simple graph $H$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, there are real numbers
$\delta > 0$ and $C$ such that $\mathrm{ex}(n, H^{k-1}) \le C \cdot n^{1 + 1/k - \delta}$ for
every natural number $n$. In other words, $\mathrm{ex}(n, H^{k-1}) = O(n^{1 + 1/k - \delta})$
for some $\delta > 0$.

articles.title: Containing a copy of a graph
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ contains a copy of a simple graph $F$ if
there is an injective map $f$ from the vertices of $F$ to the vertices of $G$ such that $f(u)$ and
$f(v)$ are adjacent in $G$ whenever $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $F$; the copy need not be induced.

articles.title: Counterexample to the Erdős–Simonovits degeneracy conjecture
articles.statement:
It is not true that for
every finite simple graph $H$ and every natural number $r \ge 1$ such that $H$ is bipartite and
$r$-degenerate (every nonempty set of vertices contains a vertex with at most $r$ neighbours in
that set), the extremal number $\mathrm{ex}(n; H)$ (the largest number of edges of a simple
graph on $n$ vertices containing no copy of $H$) is $O(n^{2 - 1/r})$ as $n \to \infty$.

An internal OpenAI model constructed a connected bipartite $2$-degenerate graph $H$ with
$\mathrm{ex}(n; H) \ge c n^{3/2 + \varepsilon}$ for all large $n$, for some constants $c > 0$ and
$\varepsilon > 0$; erdosproblems.com/146 records the conjecture as disproved.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problem #146, erdosproblems.com (live page, LaTeX source and forum threads read 2026-10-22), https://www.erdosproblems.com/146; OpenAI, Ten proofs (section disproving the Erdős degeneracy conjecture), 2026, https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/ten-proofs-oai.pdf.

articles.title: Erdős–Simonovits degeneracy conjecture (Erdős Problem 146)
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every finite simple graph $H$ and every natural number $r \ge 1$, if $H$ is bipartite and
$r$-degenerate (every nonempty set of vertices contains a vertex with at most $r$ neighbours in
that set), then $\mathrm{ex}(n; H) = O(n^{2 - 1/r})$ as $n \to \infty$, where
$\mathrm{ex}(n; H)$ is the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices containing
no copy of $H$.

articles.title: The extremal number of a graph
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $F$, the
extremal number $\mathrm{ex}(n, F)$ is the maximum number of edges of a simple graph on the vertex
set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ that contains no copy of $F$. It is $0$ when every simple graph on these
$n$ vertices contains a copy of $F$.

articles.title: The $(k-1)$-subdivision of a graph
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $H$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ and a natural number $k \ge 2$, the $(k-1)$-subdivision $H^{k-1}$ is the
graph obtained from $H$ by replacing each edge $ij$ with $i < j$ by a path
$i, (ij, 0), (ij, 1), \dots, (ij, k - 2), j$ of length $k$ through $k - 1$ new vertices, the paths
of different edges sharing no new vertices. For $k \le 1$ there are no new vertices and the
resulting graph has no edges.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 574 is false
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for every natural number $k \ge 2$ the
ratio $\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_{2k-1}, C_{2k}\}) / (n/2)^{1 + 1/k}$ tends to $1$ as $n \to \infty$.
Here $\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_{2k-1}, C_{2k}\})$ is the extremal number: the supremum of the numbers
of edges of simple graphs on $n$ vertices that contain no copy of the cycle graph $C_{2k-1}$ and
no copy of the cycle graph $C_{2k}$.

Lazebnik, Ustimenko and Woldar (Discrete Math. 1999), per Füredi–Simonovits
(arXiv:1306.5167, Construction 4.28), blow up one side of Benson's girth-12 bipartite graph to
get bipartite $C_{10}$-free graphs (hence also $C_9$-free) with
$4(n/5)^{6/5} > 0.5798\, n^{6/5}$ edges for infinitely many $n$, refuting the case $k = 5$.

## Sources

- Zoltán Füredi and Miklós Simonovits, The history of degenerate (bipartite) extremal graph problems, in Erdős Centennial, Bolyai Soc. Math. Stud. 25 (2013), arXiv:1306.5167, https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.5167.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 574
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural number $k \ge 2$ the ratio
$\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_{2k-1}, C_{2k}\}) / (n/2)^{1 + 1/k}$ tends to $1$ as $n \to \infty$, that is,
$\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_{2k-1}, C_{2k}\}) = (1 + o(1)) (n/2)^{1 + 1/k}$. Here
$\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_{2k-1}, C_{2k}\})$ is the extremal number: the supremum of the numbers of
edges of simple graphs on $n$ vertices that contain no copy of the cycle graph $C_{2k-1}$ and no
copy of the cycle graph $C_{2k}$.

articles.title: Extremal number for cycles of lengths $2k-1$ and $2k$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and
$n$, $\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_{2k-1}, C_{2k}\})$ is the supremum of the numbers of edges of the simple
graphs on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that contain no copy of the cycle graph $C_{2k-1}$
and no copy of the cycle graph $C_{2k}$, where the supremum of the empty set is $0$. Here $2k-1$
is computed in the natural numbers, so it is $0$ when $k = 0$.

articles.title: Graphs without cycles of lengths $2k-1$ and $2k$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a simple
graph $G$ is free of the cycle lengths $2k-1$ and $2k$ when it contains no copy of the cycle
graph $C_{2k-1}$ and no copy of the cycle graph $C_{2k}$, where a copy is an injective graph
homomorphism, that is, a subgraph that need not be induced.

Here $C_m$ is the cycle graph on $m$ vertices, which has no edges for $m \le 1$ and is a single
edge for $m = 2$, and $2k-1$ is computed in the natural numbers, so it is $0$ when $k = 0$.

articles.title: Attainment of the hypercube Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, $H$ a simple
graph, $Q_n$ the $n$-dimensional hypercube, and $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$ the hypercube Turán number.
If $Q_n$ has at least one subgraph (not necessarily spanning) that contains no copy of $H$, then
some subgraph $S$ of $Q_n$ contains no copy of $H$ and has exactly $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$ edges.

articles.title: Adjacency in the hypercube
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and all vertices $x, y$ of the
$n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$ (functions from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the Booleans), $x$ and
$y$ are adjacent in $Q_n$ if and only if there is exactly one coordinate $i$ with
$x_i \ne y_i$.

articles.title: An edge of the one-dimensional hypercube
articles.statement:
In the $1$-dimensional hypercube $Q_1$, the
constant vertex $\mathrm{true}$ and the constant vertex $\mathrm{false}$ are adjacent.

articles.title: Subgraphs of the hypercube have at most as many edges
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
every subgraph of the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$ has at most as many edges as $Q_n$.

articles.title: The zero-dimensional hypercube has no edges
articles.statement:
The edge set of the $0$-dimensional
hypercube $Q_0$ is empty.

articles.title: No two vertices of the zero-dimensional hypercube are adjacent
articles.statement:
For all vertices $x, y$
of the $0$-dimensional hypercube $Q_0$, $x$ and $y$ are not adjacent in $Q_0$.

Any two vertices agree on all (zero) coordinates.

articles.title: Hypercube graph
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$ is the
simple graph whose vertices are the functions from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the Booleans
$\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$, with an edge between two vertices exactly when they differ
in exactly one coordinate.

articles.title: Four-cycle-free subgraphs of the hypercubes of dimensions one to six
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $n$, let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube, let $C_4$ be the cycle on four vertices,
and let $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, C_4)$ be the largest number of edges of a subgraph of $Q_n$ that
contains no copy of $C_4$. Then for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ the value of $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, C_4)$
is $1$, $3$, $9$, $24$, $56$ and $132$ respectively.

## Sources

- OEIS A245762; `ex(Q₆, C₄) = 132` is H. Harborth and H. Nienborg, *Maximum number of edges in squarefree subgraphs of the n-cube*, Bull. Inst. Combin. Appl. 12 (1994), 55–60; listed in leansolving/SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/HypercubeC4/README.md`.

articles.title: Upper bound for the hypercube Turán number
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every
simple graph $H$, writing $Q_n$ for the $n$-dimensional hypercube, the hypercube Turán number
$\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$ is at most the number of edges of $Q_n$.

articles.title: Upper bound for four-cycle-free subgraphs of the seven-dimensional hypercube
articles.statement:
Let $Q_7$
be the $7$-dimensional hypercube and $C_4$ the cycle on four vertices. The largest number
$\mathrm{ex}(Q_7, C_4)$ of edges of a subgraph of $Q_7$ that contains no copy of $C_4$ is at
most $308$.

The bound comes from averaging over the fourteen facets of $Q_7$: each is a copy of $Q_6$ and
each edge lies in six of them, so $\mathrm{ex}(Q_7, C_4) \le 14 \cdot \mathrm{ex}(Q_6, C_4) / 6 =
14 \cdot 132 / 6 = 308$.

## Sources

- the averaging bound applied to `ex(Q₆, C₄) = 132` (Harborth and Nienborg 1994), as stated in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/HypercubeC4/README.md`.

articles.title: The hypercube Turán number in dimension zero
articles.statement:
For every simple graph $H$, writing $Q_0$
for the $0$-dimensional hypercube, the hypercube Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(Q_0, H)$ is $0$.

articles.title: Hypercube Turán number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $H$, let $Q_n$ be the
$n$-dimensional hypercube. The hypercube Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$ is the largest number
of edges of a subgraph (not necessarily spanning) of $Q_n$ that contains no copy of $H$, that is,
no subgraph isomorphic to $H$; it is $0$ when no such subgraph exists.

articles.title: Lower bound for four-cycle-free subgraphs of the eight-dimensional hypercube
articles.statement:
Let $Q_8$
be the $8$-dimensional hypercube and $C_4$ the cycle on four vertices. The largest number
$\mathrm{ex}(Q_8, C_4)$ of edges of a subgraph of $Q_8$ that contains no copy of $C_4$ is at
least $682$.

The bound is witnessed by an explicit construction.

## Sources

- M. Minamoto, *C₄-free subgraphs of the hypercubes Q₆, Q₇, and Q₈*, arXiv:2603.29127v5 (2026), which improves the bound `680` of its earlier versions; SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/HypercubeC4/README.md` and OEIS A245762 still list `680`.

articles.title: Lower bound for four-cycle-free subgraphs of the seven-dimensional hypercube
articles.statement:
Let $Q_7$
be the $7$-dimensional hypercube and $C_4$ the cycle on four vertices. The largest number
$\mathrm{ex}(Q_7, C_4)$ of edges of a subgraph of $Q_7$ that contains no copy of $C_4$ is at
least $304$.

The bound is witnessed by an explicit construction.

## Sources

- M. Minamoto, *C₄-free subgraphs of the hypercubes Q₆, Q₇, and Q₈*, arXiv:2603.29127 (2026); listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/HypercubeC4/README.md`.

articles.title: The hypercube Turán number bounds every free subgraph
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and
every simple graph $H$, let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube and let $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$
be the hypercube Turán number of $H$ in $Q_n$. If $S$ is a subgraph of $Q_n$ that contains no
copy of $H$, then $S$ has at most $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$ edges.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 426 is false (Bradač–Christoph)
articles.statement:
For a graph $H$ on a finite vertex set, let
$u(H)$ be the number of spanning subgraphs of $H$ that are isomorphic to no other spanning
subgraph of $H$ (its unique subgraphs). There is no real constant $c > 0$ such that for infinitely
many $n$ some graph $H$ on $n$ vertices has $u(H) \ge c \cdot 2^{\binom{n}{2}} / n!$.

## Sources

- Bradač and Christoph [BrCh24] (f(n) = o(2^C(n,2)/n!)), per erdosproblems.com/426, https://www.erdosproblems.com/426.

articles.title: Many unique subgraphs (Erdős Problem 426)
articles.statement:
For a graph $H$ on a finite vertex set, let
$u(H)$ be the number of spanning subgraphs of $H$ that are isomorphic to no other spanning
subgraph of $H$ (its unique subgraphs). The statement is that there is a real constant $c > 0$
such that for infinitely many $n$ some graph $H$ on $n$ vertices has
$u(H) \ge c \cdot 2^{\binom{n}{2}} / n!$.

articles.title: Negation of the Erdős Problem 426 statement
articles.statement:
For a graph $H$ on a finite vertex set, let
$u(H)$ be the number of spanning subgraphs of $H$ that are isomorphic to no other spanning
subgraph of $H$. This is the proposition that there is no real constant $c > 0$ such that for
infinitely many $n$ some graph $H$ on $n$ vertices has $u(H) \ge c \cdot 2^{\binom{n}{2}} / n!$.

articles.title: Unique subgraph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs on the same vertex set $V$. Then $G$ is a
unique subgraph of $H$ if exactly one subgraph of $H$ is isomorphic to $G$. Here a subgraph of
$H$ means a spanning subgraph: a graph on $V$ all of whose edges are edges of $H$ (not
necessarily induced).

articles.title: Number of unique subgraphs
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a graph on a finite vertex set $V$. The number of
unique subgraphs of $H$ is the number of spanning subgraphs $G$ of $H$ (graphs on $V$ all of
whose edges are edges of $H$) that are unique subgraphs of $H$, that is, isomorphic to no other
spanning subgraph of $H$.

Equivalently, it is the number of isomorphism classes of graphs on $V$ that occur exactly once
as a spanning subgraph of $H$: sending each such $G$ to its isomorphism class is a bijection onto
these classes. In particular, isomorphic copies do not inflate the count: if two distinct
spanning subgraphs of $H$ are isomorphic, neither is a unique subgraph of $H$, so neither is
counted.

articles.title: Brooks' theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite connected simple graph and let $\Delta$ be its maximum
degree: every vertex of $G$ has degree at most $\Delta$ and some vertex has degree exactly $\Delta$.
If $G$ is not complete and is not isomorphic to a cycle graph on an odd number of vertices, then $G$
has a proper vertex coloring with $\Delta$ colors.

## Sources

- R. L. Brooks, On colouring the nodes of a network, Proc. Camb. Philos. Soc. 37 (1941), DOI 10.1017/S030500410002168X.

articles.title: Injective colorings are centered
articles.statement:
Every injective proper vertex coloring of a simple graph
is centered: any vertex of a set whose induced subgraph is connected is a center of that set.

articles.title: Centered coloring
articles.statement:
A proper vertex coloring $\varphi$ of a simple graph $G$ is centered
if, for every set $s$ of vertices of $G$ whose induced subgraph is connected, some vertex is a
$\varphi$-center of $s$.

Quantifying over vertex sets whose induced subgraph is connected suffices: adding all induced
edges on the same vertices keeps a connected subgraph connected, and whether a color occurs
exactly once depends only on the vertex set together with the coloring.

articles.title: Centers via unique existence
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a proper vertex coloring of a simple graph
$G$, let $s$ be a set of vertices of $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex of $G$. Then $v$ is a
$\varphi$-center of $s$ if and only if $v \in s$ and there is exactly one vertex $u \in s$ with
$\varphi(u) = \varphi(v)$.

articles.title: A vertex is a center of its singleton
articles.statement:
For every proper vertex coloring $\varphi$ of a
simple graph $G$ and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ is a $\varphi$-center of $\{v\}$.

articles.title: Center of a vertex set under a coloring
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a proper vertex coloring of a
simple graph $G$, let $s$ be a set of vertices of $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex of $G$. Then $v$ is
a $\varphi$-center of $s$ if $v \in s$ and no other vertex of $s$ has the color $\varphi(v)$.

articles.title: The identity coloring is centered
articles.statement:
For every simple graph $G$ with vertex set $V$, the
proper vertex coloring of $G$ by $V$ that gives each vertex itself as its color is centered.

articles.title: No finite $(0,2)$-graph has chromatic number three
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and
every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every two distinct vertices
have either zero or two common neighbors, the chromatic number of $G$ is not $3$. In particular,
the three-chromatic $(0,2)$-graph conjecture is false.

Williamson proves the stronger statement that every finite three-colourable $(0,2)$-graph is
bipartite (Theorem 2 of the source below).

## Sources

- Christopher Williamson, Finite Three-Colourable (0,2)-Graphs Are Bipartite, arXiv preprint (2026), arXiv:2607.10125, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10125.

articles.title: The three-chromatic $(0,2)$-graph conjecture
articles.statement:
It asserts that there are a natural number
$n$ and a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every two distinct
vertices have either zero or two common neighbors, such that the chromatic number of $G$ is $3$.

articles.title: $(0,2)$-graphs
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a $(0,2)$-graph when every two distinct vertices of $G$ have either
exactly zero or exactly two common neighbors.

articles.title: Induced wheels
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ has an induced wheel if there are a natural
number $\ell \ge 4$, distinct vertices $r_0, \dots, r_{\ell-1}$ of $G$ (the rim) and a vertex
$h$ of $G$ (the hub) with $h \ne r_i$ for every $i$, such that for all $i, j < \ell$ the
vertices $r_i$ and $r_j$ are adjacent in $G$ exactly when $i - j \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{\ell}$,
and $h$ is adjacent to $r_i$, $r_j$ and $r_k$ for some pairwise distinct $i, j, k < \ell$.
The hub may have further neighbours on the rim.

## Sources

- James Davies, *Triangle-free graphs with large chromatic number and no induced wheel*, arXiv:2104.05907v3, page 1, defining paragraph, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.05907v3.

articles.title: Davies's theorem on triangle-free wheel-free graphs
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $k$
there are a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$
such that $G$ contains no triangle, $G$ is wheel-free (it has no induced wheel) and the
chromatic number of $G$ is at least $k$.

## Sources

- James Davies, arXiv:2104.05907v3, Corollary 2, page 1, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.05907v3.

articles.title: Triangle-free wheel-free graphs of large chromatic number (proposition)
articles.statement:
This is the
proposition that for every positive integer $k$ there are a natural number $n$ and a simple
graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that $G$ contains no triangle, $G$ is
wheel-free (it has no induced wheel) and the chromatic number of $G$ is at least $k$.

Since $G$ is finite, its chromatic number is finite.

## Sources

- Davies, arXiv:2104.05907v3, Corollary 2, page 1; the finite constructions are given on pages 5 and 6, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.05907v3.

articles.title: Wheel-free graphs
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ is wheel-free if it has no induced wheel, that
is, no induced cycle of length at least four together with a vertex outside the cycle that is
adjacent to at least three vertices of the cycle.

## Sources

- James Davies, arXiv:2104.05907v3, page 1, wheel definition, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.05907v3.

articles.title: Anti-Ramsey number
articles.statement:
For a graph $H$ on a finite vertex type and a natural number $n$, the
anti-Ramsey number $\mathrm{AR}(n, H)$ is the largest $k$ for which there is a coloring of the edges
of the complete graph $K_n$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with colors $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, every color
used, that contains no rainbow copy of $H$. Here a copy of $H$ is an injective homomorphism from
$H$ to $K_n$, and it is rainbow when distinct edges of $H$ are sent to edges of distinct colors.
If no such $k$ exists, $\mathrm{AR}(n, H) = 0$.

articles.title: CDS-colorable graphs
articles.statement:
A graph $G$ on a finite vertex set is CDS-colorable if it has a
proper coloring $C$ with colors in $\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the number
of vertices whose color under $C$ is less than $k$ equals the maximum size of a union of $k$
independent sets of $G$.

articles.title: Chromatic cardinal of a graph
articles.statement:
The chromatic cardinal is the minimal number of colors need to color it. In contrast to
`chromaticNumber`, which assigns `⊤ : ℕ∞` to all non-finitely colorable graphs, this definition
returns a `Cardinal` and can therefore distinguish between different infinite chromatic numbers.

articles.title: Cochromatic number as a minimum
articles.statement:
If a graph $G$ is cocolorable with $n$ colors for some
natural number $n$, then the cochromatic number of $G$ equals the least natural number $m$ such
that $G$ is cocolorable with $m$ colors.

articles.title: Cochromatic number of a finite graph
articles.statement:
For every graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the
cochromatic number of $G$, converted from $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ by sending
$\infty$ to $0$, equals the least natural number $m$ such that $G$ is cocolorable with $m$
colors.

articles.title: Cochromatic number
articles.statement:
The cochromatic number of a graph $G$, an element of
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, is the least natural number $n$ such that $G$ is cocolorable with
$n$ colors, that is, the least number of colors in a coloring of the vertices of $G$ in which
each color class induces either an independent set or a complete graph. It is $\infty$ exactly
when $G$ is not cocolorable with any finite number of colors.

articles.title: Colorable graphs are cocolorable
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, if a graph $G$ has a
proper coloring with $n$ colors, then $G$ is cocolorable with $n$ colors.

Each color class of a proper coloring induces an independent set.

articles.title: Finite graphs are cocolorable
articles.statement:
Every graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is cocolorable
with $|V|$ colors.

Giving every vertex its own color is a proper coloring.

articles.title: Cocolorable graphs
articles.statement:
A graph $G$ is cocolorable with $n$ colors if there is a map from its
vertices to the colors $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that each color class induces either an
independent set or a complete graph in $G$.

articles.title: Largest union of independent sets
articles.statement:
For a graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and a
natural number $k$, this is the maximum number of vertices in a union of $k$ (possibly empty,
possibly overlapping) independent sets of $G$.

articles.title: Critical edge
articles.statement:
For a graph $G$ and an unordered pair $e$ of vertices, $e$ is a critical
edge of $G$ if removing $e$ from the edge set of $G$ strictly lowers the chromatic number of $G$,
taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.

Only edges of $G$ can be critical.

articles.title: Critical edge sets
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph and $S$ a set of unordered pairs of its
vertices. Then $S$ is critical for $G$ if deleting the edges of $G$ that lie in $S$ strictly
lowers the chromatic number, as an element of $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.

articles.title: Critical vertices of a subgraph
articles.statement:
Let $G'$ be a subgraph of a graph $G$. A vertex $v$ is
critical for $G'$ if $\{v\}$ is a critical vertex set of $G'$, that is, deleting $v$ from $G'$
strictly lowers the chromatic number of $G'$, viewed as a graph on its own vertex set, with
chromatic numbers taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.

articles.title: Critical vertex sets of a subgraph
articles.statement:
Let $G'$ be a subgraph of a graph $G$. A set $S$ of
vertices is critical for $G'$ if deleting the vertices in $S$ from $G'$ strictly lowers the
chromatic number of $G'$, viewed as a graph on its own vertex set, with chromatic numbers taken
in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.

articles.title: Vertex-critical graphs
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. A graph $G$ is $k$-critical (or
vertex-critical) if its chromatic number equals $k$ and every vertex $v$ of $G$ is critical,
that is, deleting $v$ from $G$ strictly lowers the chromatic number.

articles.title: Rainbow homomorphisms
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a graph homomorphism from $H$ to $G$ and let $c$ be a
labeling of the edges of $G$ by elements of a type $K$. Then $f$ is rainbow for $c$ if distinct
edges of $H$ are mapped to edges of $G$ with distinct labels, that is, the labeling
$e \mapsto c(f(e))$ of the edges of $H$ is injective.

articles.title: Odd cycle lengths and infinite chromatic number (Erdős Problem 57)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on
an arbitrary vertex set that has no proper colouring with finitely many colours. Then the family
$(1/\ell)$, indexed by the odd cycle lengths $\ell$ of $G$ (the odd numbers $\ell$ such that $G$
contains a cycle of length $\ell$), is not summable; that is, $\sum_\ell 1/\ell = \infty$.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 63
articles.statement:
The proposition that every simple graph $G$ with infinite
chromatic number has cycles of length $2^n$ for infinitely many $n$: for every natural number
$N$ there is some $n \ge N$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $2^n$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 63 (Liu–Montgomery)
articles.statement:
Every simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number has
cycles of length $2^n$ for infinitely many $n$: for every natural number $N$ there is some
$n \ge N$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $2^n$.

## Sources

- Liu–Montgomery [LiMo20], per erdosproblems.com/63, https://www.erdosproblems.com/63.

articles.title: Resolution of the Erdős–Hajnal odd cycle problem (Liu–Montgomery)
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on
an arbitrary vertex set that has no proper colouring with finitely many colours. Then the family
$(1/\ell)$, indexed by the odd cycle lengths $\ell$ of $G$ (the odd numbers $\ell$ such that $G$
contains a cycle of length $\ell$), is not summable; that is, $\sum_\ell 1/\ell = \infty$.

## Sources

- Hong Liu and Richard Montgomery, A solution to Erdős and Hajnal's odd cycle problem, arXiv:2010.15802 (J. Amer. Math. Soc., doi:10.1090/jams/1018), https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15802.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 751 is false
articles.statement:
It is not the case that both of the following hold:
(i) for every natural number $k$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ in
which any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$; (ii) for all natural numbers
$k$ and $g$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ and girth at least $g$ in which
any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$.

## Sources

- J. A. Bondy and A. Vince, Cycles in a graph whose lengths differ by one or two, Journal of Graph Theory 27 (1998), 11-15, https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0118(199801)27:1%3C11::AID-JGT3%3E3.0.CO;2-J; Jun Gao, Qingyi Huo, Chun-Hung Liu, and Jie Ma, A unified proof of conjectures on cycle lengths in graphs, arXiv:1904.08126v3, https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.08126v3.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 751
articles.statement:
The statement that both of the following hold:
(i) for every natural number $k$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ in
which any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$; (ii) for all natural numbers
$k$ and $g$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ and girth at least $g$ in which
any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$.

articles.title: Chromatic number of a degenerate graph
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is a
$k$-degenerate simple graph on a finite vertex set, then the chromatic number of $G$ is at
most $k + 1$.

articles.title: $k$-degenerate graphs are $(k + 1)$-colorable
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. Every
$k$-degenerate simple graph on a finite vertex set is $(k + 1)$-colorable.

## Sources

- Diestel, §5.1–5.2.

articles.title: Coloring a $k$-degenerate vertex set with $k + 1$ colors
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph
on a finite vertex set $V$, let $s \subseteq V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is
$k$-degenerate on $s$, then there is a map $f : V \to \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$ such that
$f(a) \ne f(b)$ for all adjacent vertices $a, b \in s$.

The proof removes a vertex of small degree and gives it a color absent from its
neighborhood.

articles.title: Degenerate graphs have degeneracy orderings
articles.statement:
If $G$ is a $k$-degenerate simple
graph on a finite vertex set $V$, then $G$ has a degeneracy ordering with bound $k$:
an injective map $e : V \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every vertex $v$ has at most $k$
neighbors $w$ with $e(v) < e(w)$.

articles.title: Degeneracy orderings of a vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex set $V$ and let $s \subseteq V$. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $s$, then there is
a map $e : V \to \mathbb{N}$, injective on $s$, such that every $v \in s$ has at most
$k$ neighbors $w \in s$ with $e(v) < e(w)$.

The proof removes a vertex of small degree in $s$ and labels it $0$.

articles.title: A degenerate vertex set has a vertex of small degree
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph
on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $s \subseteq V$ be nonempty. If $G$ is
$k$-degenerate on $s$, then some vertex $v \in s$ has at most $k$ neighbors in $s$.

articles.title: Degeneracy ordering
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and
let $k$ be a natural number. A map $e : V \to \mathbb{N}$ is a degeneracy ordering of
$G$ with bound $k$ if $e$ is injective and every vertex $v$ has at most $k$ neighbors
$w$ with $e(v) < e(w)$.

articles.title: The edgeless graph is degenerate
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the edgeless
graph on a finite vertex set is $k$-degenerate.

articles.title: A degenerate graph is degenerate on every vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex type $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate, then $G$ is
$k$-degenerate on every subset $U \subseteq V$.

articles.title: Degeneracy on a vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type $V$, let
$U \subseteq V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. Then $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $U$ if every
nonempty subset $W \subseteq U$ contains a vertex $v$ with at most $k$ neighbors in $W$.

articles.title: Degenerate graph
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex type $V$ is $k$-degenerate, for a
natural number $k$, if it is $k$-degenerate on the full vertex set $V$: every nonempty set $W$ of
vertices contains a vertex with at most $k$ neighbors in $W$.

articles.title: Degeneracy is monotone in the bound
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex set. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate and $k \le l$, then $G$ is $l$-degenerate.

articles.title: Degeneracy on a vertex set is monotone in the degree bound
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on
a finite vertex type $V$, let $U \subseteq V$, and let $k \le l$ be natural numbers. If $G$ is
$k$-degenerate on $U$, then $G$ is $l$-degenerate on $U$.

articles.title: Bounded maximum degree implies degeneracy
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex set. If every vertex of $G$ has degree at most $k$, then $G$ is
$k$-degenerate.

articles.title: Degeneracy on a vertex set passes to subsets
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex type $V$, let $T \subseteq U \subseteq V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is
$k$-degenerate on $U$, then $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $T$.

articles.title: Proper colorings of unordered pairs restrict to proper edge colorings
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
simple graph on $V$ and let $c$ assign a color in $K$ to every unordered pair of elements of $V$.
If $c$ is a proper coloring of unordered pairs for $G$, then the edge labeling of $G$ that gives
each edge $e$ the color $c(e)$ is a proper edge coloring of $G$.

articles.title: Proper edge coloring
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on $V$. An edge labeling $C$ of $G$ with
colors in $K$ is a proper edge coloring when any two distinct edges of $G$ that share a vertex
receive different colors: whenever a vertex $v$ is adjacent to $w_1$ and to $w_2$ with
$w_1 \ne w_2$, the edges $v w_1$ and $v w_2$ have different colors under $C$.

articles.title: Proper coloring of unordered pairs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on $V$. A map $c$ that
assigns a color in $K$ to every unordered pair of elements of $V$ is a proper coloring of
unordered pairs for $G$ when, for all vertices $x, y, z$ such that $x$ is adjacent to both $y$ and
$z$ and $y \ne z$, the pairs $\{x, y\}$ and $\{x, z\}$ receive different colors under $c$.

Only pairs that are edges of $G$ are constrained, so the same map $c$ can be compared across
different graphs on $V$.

articles.title: König's edge coloring theorem for bounded-degree bipartite multigraphs
articles.statement:
König's line coloring, bounded-degree multigraph case: a bipartite
multigraph of maximum degree at most `d` is `d`-edge-colorable. The proof
pads both sides with dummy edges to reach the regular case. Shared API also
used by the multigraph Galvin development.

articles.title: König's edge coloring theorem for regular bipartite multigraphs
articles.statement:
König's line coloring, regular multigraph case: a `d`-regular bipartite
multigraph (given by endpoint projections) is `d`-edge-colorable. The proof
extracts a perfect matching by Hall's theorem and inducts. Shared API also
used by the multigraph Galvin development.

articles.title: König's line coloring theorem
articles.statement:
Every finite bipartite simple graph $G$ has a proper edge
coloring with $\Delta(G)$ colors, where $\Delta(G)$ is the maximum degree of $G$.

Since every proper edge coloring of $G$ needs at least $\Delta(G)$ colors, the edge chromatic
number of $G$ equals $\Delta(G)$.

## Sources

- D. Konig, Theorie der endlichen und unendlichen Graphen, Akademische Verlagsgesellschaft (1936).

articles.title: Proper colorings of unordered pairs pass to subgraphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs
on $V$ such that every edge of $H$ is an edge of $G$. If a map $c$ from unordered pairs of
elements of $V$ to $K$ is a proper coloring of unordered pairs for $G$, then it is also a proper
coloring of unordered pairs for $H$.

articles.title: Vizing's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $\Delta$ be its
maximum degree. Then $G$ has a proper edge coloring with $\Delta + 1$ colors: there is an
assignment of colors from $\{0, 1, \dots, \Delta\}$ to the edges of $G$ such that any two
distinct edges sharing a vertex receive different colors.

## Sources

- V. G. Vizing, Diskret. Analiz 3 (1964), 25-30.

articles.title: Erdős's theorem on graphs of high girth and high chromatic number
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$k$ and $g$ with $g \ge 3$, there is a finite simple graph $G$ that has a cycle, whose girth
(the length of a shortest cycle) is at least $g$, and whose chromatic number is at least $k$.

In particular, there are finite graphs of arbitrarily high girth and chromatic number.

## Sources

- P. Erdős, Graph theory and probability, Canad. J. Math. 11 (1959), 34–38, DOI 10.4153/CJM-1959-003-9.

articles.title: Four color theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ that has neither
$K_5$ nor $K_{3,3}$ as a minor, and let $\ell$ assign a natural number $\ell(u, v)$ to every
ordered pair of vertices $u, v$ such that $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ if and only if
$u \ne v$ and $\ell(u, v) > 0$. Then $G$ has a proper vertex coloring with four colors.

Here the vertices stand for the regions of a map and $\ell(u, v)$ for the length of their common
boundary, so regions that meet only at a corner are not adjacent. Without the minor condition the
conclusion fails: $K_5$ needs five colors.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_color_theorem.

articles.title: Graphs with a $K_5$ minor
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ has $K_5$ as a minor if there are five
nonempty, pairwise disjoint sets of vertices $S_1, \dots, S_5$ such that any two vertices in the
same set are joined by a walk in $G$ all of whose vertices lie in that set, and for all distinct
$i, j$ some vertex of $S_i$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $S_j$.

Together with $K_{3,3}$, this is one of the two forbidden minors for planarity (Wagner,
Kuratowski).

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_color_theorem.

articles.title: Graphs with a $K_{3,3}$ minor
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ has $K_{3,3}$ as a minor if there are
six nonempty, pairwise disjoint sets of vertices $L_1, L_2, L_3, R_1, R_2, R_3$ such that any two
vertices in the same set are joined by a walk in $G$ all of whose vertices lie in that set, and
for all $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ some vertex of $L_i$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $R_j$.

Together with $K_5$, this is one of the two forbidden minors for planarity (Wagner, Kuratowski).

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_color_theorem.

articles.title: Planarity by forbidden minors
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ is called planar here if it has neither
$K_5$ nor $K_{3,3}$ as a minor.

Without this condition the four color theorem fails: $K_5$ is not 4-colorable.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_color_theorem.

articles.title: Fractional chromatic number
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a graph with finite vertex set $V(X)$. A
*fractional colouring* of $X$ assigns to each set $S$ of vertices of $X$ a real weight
$f(S) \ge 0$, with $f(S) = 0$ unless $S$ is independent, such that $\sum_{S \ni x} f(S) \ge 1$
for every vertex $x$ of $X$, the sum running over all sets of vertices containing $x$. The
*weight* of $f$ is the sum of $f(S)$ over all sets $S$ of vertices of $X$. The *fractional
chromatic number* $\chi^*(X)$ of $X$ is the infimum of the weights of all fractional colourings
of $X$.

Since $f$ vanishes off the independent sets, a fractional colouring is the same as a nonnegative
function on the independent sets of $X$, and both sums run over independent sets only.

articles.title: Fractional clique number
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a graph with finite vertex set $V(X)$. A
*fractional clique* of $X$ is a function $f \colon V(X) \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(v) \ge 0$ for
every vertex $v$, such that $\sum_{v \in S} f(v) \le 1$ for every independent set $S$ of $X$. The
*weight* of $f$ is $\sum_{v \in V(X)} f(v)$. The *fractional clique number* $\omega^*(X)$ of $X$
is the supremum of the weights of all fractional cliques of $X$.

articles.title: Regular fractional colouring
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite simple graph. A fractional colouring
of $X$ assigns to each set $S$ of vertices of $X$ a real weight $f(S) \ge 0$, with $f(S) = 0$
unless $S$ is independent, such that $\sum_{S \ni x} f(S) \ge 1$ for every vertex $x$, the sum
running over all sets of vertices containing $x$. The fractional colouring $f$ is *regular* if
$\sum_{S \ni x} f(S) = 1$ for every vertex $x$ of $X$. Since $f$ vanishes off the independent
sets, this is the sum of $f$ over the independent sets of $X$ containing $x$.

articles.title: Hajnal–Szemerédi theorem in clique-factor and equitable-colouring form
articles.statement:
For all integers
$r \ge 2$ and $m \ge 1$ and every finite simple graph $G$ with exactly $rm$ vertices, (a) if every
vertex of $G$ has degree at least $m(r - 1)$, then $G$ contains $m$ pairwise disjoint cliques of
$r$ vertices each, and (b) if every vertex of $G$ has degree at most $m - 1$, then $G$ has a
proper colouring with $m$ colours in which every colour class has exactly $r$ vertices.

This resolves Erdős Problem 914 affirmatively: part (a) was proved by Corrádi and Hajnal for
$r = 3$ and by Hajnal and Szemerédi for all $r$, and part (b) is its equitable-colouring
reformulation, obtained by applying (a) to the complement of $G$.

## Sources

- A. Hajnal and E. Szemerédi, Proof of a conjecture of P. Erdős (1970), 601–623, https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet-getitem?mr=297607; External Lean proof of Erdős Problem 914, plby/lean-proofs, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos914.lean.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 914 on clique factors and equitable colourings
articles.statement:
The proposition asserts
that for all integers $r \ge 2$ and $m \ge 1$ and every finite simple graph $G$ with exactly $rm$
vertices, (a) if every vertex of $G$ has degree at least $m(r - 1)$, then $G$ contains $m$
pairwise disjoint cliques of $r$ vertices each, and (b) if every vertex of $G$ has degree at most
$m - 1$, then $G$ has a proper colouring with $m$ colours in which every colour class has exactly
$r$ vertices.

articles.title: Equitable coloring with more colors than the maximum degree
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex set with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$, and let $k$ be a natural number with
$\Delta(G) < k$. Then $G$ has a proper coloring with the $k$ colors $0, 1, \dots, k-1$ that is
equitable: for any two colors $i$ and $j$, the number of vertices of color $i$ is at most one more
than the number of vertices of color $j$.

articles.title: Hajnal–Szemerédi theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set with maximum degree
$\Delta(G)$, and let $k$ be a natural number with $\Delta(G) < k$. Then $G$ has a proper coloring
with the $k$ colors $0, 1, \dots, k-1$ that is equitable: for any two colors $i$ and $j$, the
number of vertices of color $i$ is at most one more than the number of vertices of color $j$.

## Sources

- A. Hajnal and E. Szemerédi, "Proof of a conjecture of P. Erdős", Combinatorial Theory and Its Applications II, Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai 4 (1970), 601-623.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 750 is true
articles.statement:
The following three statements hold. (i) For every function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with $f(m) \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ there is a
simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number such that for every $m > 0$, every set $S$ of
exactly $m$ vertices of $G$ contains an independent set $I$ of $G$ with $|I| \ge m/2 - f(m)$.
(ii) For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number
such that for every $m > 0$, every set of exactly $m$ vertices of $G$ contains an independent
set of $G$ with at least $m/2 - \varepsilon m$ elements. (iii) For every real $c > 1/4$ there
is a simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number such that for every $m > 0$, every set of
exactly $m$ vertices of $G$ contains an independent set of $G$ with at least $m/2 - cm$
elements.

## Sources

- plby/lean-proofs, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos750.lean#L41.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 750
articles.statement:
The statement that the following three assertions all hold.
(i) For every function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with $f(m) \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ there is a
simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number such that for every $m > 0$, every set $S$ of
exactly $m$ vertices of $G$ contains an independent set $I$ of $G$ with $|I| \ge m/2 - f(m)$.
(ii) For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number
such that for every $m > 0$, every set of exactly $m$ vertices of $G$ contains an independent
set of $G$ with at least $m/2 - \varepsilon m$ elements. (iii) For every real $c > 1/4$ there
is a simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number such that for every $m > 0$, every set of
exactly $m$ vertices of $G$ contains an independent set of $G$ with at least $m/2 - cm$
elements.

articles.title: Adjacency in the Kneser graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and $k$-element subsets
$x$ and $y$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ of the Kneser graph $K(n, k)$
are adjacent if and only if $x$ and $y$ are disjoint and $x \ne y$.

articles.title: Kneser graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $v$ and $k$, the Kneser graph $K_{v:k}$ has as vertices
the $k$-element subsets of the $v$-element set $\{0, 1, \dots, v-1\}$, with two distinct vertices
adjacent when they are disjoint.

By definition, $K_{v:k}$ is the generalized Johnson graph $J(v, k, 0)$.

articles.title: Kneser–Lovász theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $0 < k$ and $2k \le n$. The
Kneser graph $K(n, k)$, whose vertices are the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ and
in which two such subsets are adjacent when they are disjoint and distinct, has chromatic number
$n - 2k + 2$.

## Sources

- L. Lovasz, JCT A 25 (1978), 319-324, DOI 10.1016/0097-3165(78)90022-5.

articles.title: List-colorable graphs are colorable
articles.statement:
If a simple graph $G$ is $q$-list-colorable, then $G$
is $q$-colorable, that is, it has a proper coloring with $q$ colors.

articles.title: Iradmusa's partial list colouring conjecture
articles.statement:
For every finite graph $G$ with choice
number $\chi_\ell$ and all natural numbers $r$, $s$ with $1 \le r \le s \le \chi_\ell$, one has
$\lambda_r / r \ge \lambda_s / s$, where $\lambda_t$ is the minimum, over all assignments of
lists of exactly $t$ colours to the vertices, of the largest number of vertices of $G$ that can
be properly coloured from their lists.

articles.title: The partial list colouring conjecture is false
articles.statement:
There exist a finite graph $G$ with choice
number $\chi_\ell$ and natural numbers $r$, $s$ with $1 \le r \le s \le \chi_\ell$ such that
$\lambda_r / r < \lambda_s / s$, where $\lambda_t$ is the minimum, over all assignments of lists
of exactly $t$ colours to the vertices, of the largest number of vertices of $G$ that can be
properly coloured from their lists. So Iradmusa's partial list colouring conjecture fails.

Noel's counterexample (Theorem 1.1) is a 14-vertex graph (four triangles plus two terminals)
with choice number 3 and a 2-list assignment colouring at most 9 vertices, so
$\lambda_2 / 2 \le 9/2 < 14/3 = \lambda_3 / 3$.

## Sources

- Jonathan A. Noel, The Partial List Colouring Conjecture is False, arXiv preprint (2026), arXiv:2609.23291, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23291.

articles.title: The partial list coloring conjecture is false
articles.statement:
There exist a finite simple graph $G$ on
$n$ vertices whose choice number $q$ is positive, a natural number $t \le q$, and an assignment
to each vertex $v$ of a list $L(v)$ of exactly $t$ colors, such that every set $S$ of vertices
of $G$ whose induced subgraph has a proper coloring giving each vertex a color from its list
satisfies $q|S| < tn$.

Noel (arXiv:2609.23291, Sep 2026) gives a $14$-vertex graph with choice number $3$ and an
assignment of lists of exactly $2$ colors from which at most $9 < 28/3$ vertices can be properly
colored, so the conjectured bound $|S| \ge tn/q$ fails at $q = 3$, $t = 2$.

## Sources

- Jonathan A. Noel, The Partial List Colouring Conjecture is False, arXiv preprint (2026), arXiv:2609.23291, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23291.

articles.title: Albertson–Grossman–Haas partial list coloring conjecture
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph
on $n$ vertices whose choice number $q$ is positive, let $t \le q$ be a natural number, and assign
to each vertex $v$ a list $L(v)$ of exactly $t$ colors. Then there is a set $S$ of vertices of $G$
that is partially list-colorable from $L$ (the subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$ has a proper
coloring giving each vertex a color from its list) and satisfies $tn \le q|S|$, that is,
$|S| \ge tn/q$.

articles.title: Choice number
articles.statement:
A natural number $q$ is the choice number of a simple graph $G$ if $G$ is
$q$-list-colorable but is not $r$-list-colorable for any $r < q$.

articles.title: List colorability
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ is $q$-list-colorable if, for every set of colors and
every assignment of a finite list $L(v)$ of at least $q$ colors to each vertex $v$, there is a
proper coloring $c$ of $G$ with $c(v) \in L(v)$ for every vertex $v$.

articles.title: Proper list colouring of a vertex subset
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on a finite vertex set $V$,
let $L$ assign to each vertex $v$ a finite list $L(v)$ of colours (natural numbers), and let
$S \subseteq V$. A map $f : V \to \mathbb{N}$ is a proper $L$-colouring of $S$ when
$f(v) \in L(v)$ for every $v \in S$ and $f(v) \ne f(w)$ for all adjacent $v, w \in S$.

articles.title: Partial list colorability
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and assign to each vertex $v$ a finite
list $L(v)$ of colors. A finite set $S$ of vertices is partially list-colorable from $L$ when the
subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$ has a proper coloring $c$ with $c(v) \in L(v)$ for every
$v \in S$. No colors are assigned to vertices outside $S$.

articles.title: Maximum number of list-colourable vertices
articles.statement:
For a graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and an
assignment $L$ of a finite list $L(v)$ of natural-number colours to each vertex $v$, $\lambda_L$
is the largest $k$ such that some set of $k$ vertices of $G$ has a proper $L$-colouring.

articles.title: The partial list colouring number $\lambda_t$
articles.statement:
For a graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and
a natural number $t$, $\lambda_t$ is the minimum of $\lambda_L$ over all assignments $L$ of a
list $L(v)$ of exactly $t$ natural-number colours to each vertex $v$, where $\lambda_L$ is the
largest $k$ such that some set of $k$ vertices of $G$ has a proper $L$-colouring.

articles.title: Monotonicity of list colorability
articles.statement:
If a simple graph $G$ is $q$-list-colorable and
$q \le r$, then $G$ is $r$-list-colorable.

articles.title: Davies' odd distance theorem
articles.statement:
The odd distance graph on the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$,
in which two points are adjacent when their distance is an odd integer, has infinite chromatic
number: it has no proper colouring with finitely many colours.

Davies proves (Theorem 1) that every finite colouring of the plane has a monochromatic pair of
points at odd integer distance.

## Sources

- James Davies, Odd distances in colourings of the plane, Geometric and Functional Analysis 34 (2024) 19-31, arXiv:2209.15598, https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15598.

articles.title: Infinite chromatic number of the odd distance graph
articles.statement:
The proposition that the odd distance
graph on $\mathbb{R}^2$ has infinite chromatic number, that is, has no proper colouring with
finitely many colours.

articles.title: Odd distance graph
articles.statement:
The odd distance graph is the simple graph on the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ in which two points $x$ and $y$ are adjacent when their Euclidean distance is an
odd integer.

articles.title: Perfect graphs have an NP description
articles.statement:
The perfect-graph decision problem, which accepts
exactly the bitstrings that decode to a valid adjacency-matrix instance whose graph is perfect,
lies in the complexity class NP.

Chudnovsky, Cornuéjols, Liu, Seymour and Vušković recognize Berge graphs in polynomial time,
and the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem identifies Berge graphs with perfect graphs; hence
perfect-graph recognition is in P, and so in NP.

## Sources

- Maria Chudnovsky, Gerard Cornuejols, Xinming Liu, Paul Seymour, Kristina Vuskovic, Recognizing Berge graphs, Combinatorica 25 (2005), 143-186, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00493-005-0012-8; Maria Chudnovsky, Neil Robertson, Paul Seymour, Robin Thomas, The strong perfect graph theorem, Annals of Mathematics 164 (2006), 51-229, https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2006.164.51.

articles.title: Edmonds's question: an NP description of perfect graphs
articles.statement:
The perfect-graph decision
problem, which accepts exactly the bitstrings that decode to a valid adjacency-matrix instance
whose graph is perfect, lies in the complexity class NP: there are a polynomial $p$ with
natural-number coefficients and a polynomial-time verifier $R$ on pairs of bitstrings such that a
bitstring $x$ is accepted if and only if $R$ accepts $(x, w)$ for some bitstring $w$ of length at
most $p(|x|)$.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0270] Source item 4, notes[269], Section A.4, Contributor Jack Edmonds.

articles.title: Perfect graph
articles.statement:
A finite simple graph $G$ is perfect if, for every set $S$ of its
vertices, the induced subgraph $G[S]$ has chromatic number equal to its clique number, the
largest size of a clique in $G[S]$.

articles.title: Weak perfect graph theorem
articles.statement:
A finite simple graph $G$ is perfect if and only if its
complement $\overline{G}$ is perfect.

articles.title: Lovász's weak perfect graph theorem
articles.statement:
A finite simple graph $G$ is perfect if and only if
its complement $\overline{G}$ is perfect.

## Sources

- L. Lovasz, "Normal hypergraphs and the perfect graph conjecture", Discrete Math. 2 (1972), 253-267, DOI 10.1016/0012-365X(72)90006-4.

articles.title: Gasparian's condition (P)
articles.statement:
A finite simple graph $G$ satisfies condition (P) if, for
every set $S$ of its vertices, the induced subgraph $G[S]$, with independence number
$\alpha(G[S])$ and clique number $\omega(G[S])$, satisfies
$|S| \le \alpha(G[S]) \cdot \omega(G[S])$.

articles.title: Adjacency-matrix graph instance
articles.statement:
An instance consists of a natural number $n$ and a
Boolean $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with rows and columns indexed by $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read as the
adjacency matrix of a graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$. The matrix is arbitrary; symmetry
and the absence of loops are imposed separately by the validity condition.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0270] Source item 4, notes[269], Section A.4.

articles.title: The perfect-graph decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem on bitstrings that accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the bitstring encoding of adjacency-matrix
instances, to a valid instance whose graph is perfect. Bitstrings that do not decode to an
instance, or decode to an invalid one, are rejected.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0270] Source item 4, notes[269], Section A.4.

articles.title: Perfect graphs satisfy condition (P)
articles.statement:
Every finite perfect graph $G$ satisfies
Gasparian's condition (P): for every set $S$ of its vertices, the induced subgraph $G[S]$,
with independence number $\alpha(G[S])$ and clique number $\omega(G[S])$, satisfies
$|S| \le \alpha(G[S]) \cdot \omega(G[S])$.

Indeed, $G[S]$ has a coloring with $\omega(G[S])$ colors, and each color class is an
independent set, so it has at most $\alpha(G[S])$ vertices.

articles.title: Graph of a valid instance
articles.statement:
A valid instance with $n$ vertices and adjacency matrix $A$
determines the simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which vertices $x$ and $y$
are adjacent exactly when $A_{xy}$ is true.

articles.title: Valid adjacency-matrix instance
articles.statement:
An instance with $n$ vertices and adjacency matrix $A$ is
valid when $A$ is symmetric, that is, $A_{yx}$ is true whenever $A_{xy}$ is true, and has no
loops, that is, $A_{xx}$ is false for every vertex $x$.

articles.title: The Petersen coloring conjecture is false
articles.statement:
There are a finite vertex type $V$ and a
simple graph $G$ on $V$ in which every vertex has exactly three neighbors and no edge is a bridge,
such that $G$ has no Petersen coloring: no map $f$ from unordered pairs of vertices of $G$ to
unordered pairs of vertices of the Petersen graph $P$ sends every edge of $G$ to an edge of $P$
and, for every vertex $v$ of $G$, maps the edges of $G$ at $v$ bijectively onto the edges of $P$
at some vertex $w$ of $P$.

Putman (arXiv:2608.10012, Aug 2026) gave 112-vertex counterexamples with SAT/DRAT certificates,
and Goedgebeur, Jooken, Macajova, Mattiolo, Mazzuoccolo and Ulyanov (arXiv:2608.10028,
Theorem 6) prove two simple bridgeless cubic 52-vertex graphs have no Petersen colouring.

## Sources

- Jan Goedgebeur, Jorik Jooken, Edita Macajova, Davide Mattiolo, Giuseppe Mazzuoccolo and Nikolay Ulyanov, Disproving the Petersen Coloring Conjecture: Theoretical Analysis and an Infinite Family of Counterexamples, arXiv preprint (2026), arXiv:2608.10028, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10028; Bryce Putman, A 112-Vertex Counterexample to the Petersen Coloring Conjecture, arXiv preprint (2026), arXiv:2608.10012, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10012.

articles.title: Petersen coloring conjecture
articles.statement:
For every finite vertex type $V$ and every simple graph $G$
on $V$, if every vertex of $G$ has exactly three neighbors and $G$ is bridgeless, then $G$ admits
a Petersen coloring.

articles.title: Petersen coloring
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex type $V$ and let $P$ be the
Petersen graph. A map $f$ from unordered pairs of vertices of $G$ to unordered pairs of vertices
of $P$ is a Petersen coloring of $G$ when $f$ sends every edge of $G$ to an edge of $P$ and, for
every vertex $v$ of $G$, there is a vertex $w$ of $P$ such that $f$ maps the set of edges of $G$
incident to $v$ bijectively onto the set of edges of $P$ incident to $w$.

articles.title: Edges of the Petersen graph
articles.statement:
The edge set of the Petersen graph on
$\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z} \times \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$ consists of the unordered
pairs $\{(i, \mathrm{false}), (i + 1, \mathrm{false})\}$ (the outer 5-cycle),
$\{(i, \mathrm{false}), (i, \mathrm{true})\}$ (the spokes) and
$\{(i, \mathrm{true}), (i + 2, \mathrm{true})\}$ (the inner 5-star), for
$i \in \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Petersen graph
articles.statement:
The Petersen graph is the simple graph on
$\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z} \times \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$ whose edges are the outer
5-cycle edges $\{(i, \mathrm{false}), (i + 1, \mathrm{false})\}$, the spokes
$\{(i, \mathrm{false}), (i, \mathrm{true})\}$ and the inner 5-star edges
$\{(i, \mathrm{true}), (i + 2, \mathrm{true})\}$ for $i \in \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Vertices of the Petersen graph
articles.statement:
The vertex set of the Petersen graph is
$\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z} \times \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$; the vertices
$(i, \mathrm{false})$ with $i \in \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ form the outer 5-cycle and the vertices
$(i, \mathrm{true})$ form the inner 5-star.

articles.title: Alon–Krivelevich–Sudakov theorem on subgraphs of large cochromatic number
articles.statement:
There is a real
number $c > 0$ such that for every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set with chromatic number
$m$ there are a subgraph $H$ of $G$ and a natural number $k$ with $k \ge c\,m / \log m$ such that
the cochromatic number of $H$ is at least $k$. Moreover, there is a real number $c > 0$ with the
same property for the bound $k \ge c\sqrt{m / \log m}$.

Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm, with the conventions $\log 0 = 0$ and $x / 0 = 0$, so both
bounds are $0$ when $m \le 1$. This answers Erdős Problem 760 affirmatively.

## Sources

- plby/lean-proofs (following Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov, Subgraphs with a large cochromatic number, 1997), https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos760.lean#L1306.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 760: subgraphs of large cochromatic number
articles.statement:
The proposition asserts two
statements. First, there is a real number $c > 0$ such that for every simple graph $G$ on a finite
vertex set with chromatic number $m$ there are a subgraph $H$ of $G$ and a natural number $k$ with
$k \ge c\,m / \log m$ such that the cochromatic number of $H$ is at least $k$. Second, there is a
real number $c > 0$ with the same property for the bound $k \ge c\sqrt{m / \log m}$.

Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm, with the conventions $\log 0 = 0$ and $x / 0 = 0$, so both
bounds are $0$ when $m \le 1$. The second statement is the Erdős–Gimbel form.

articles.title: Rödl's theorem on triangle-free subgraphs
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ there is a natural
number $k$ such that every simple graph $G$, on any vertex set, whose chromatic number is at least
$k$ has a triangle-free subgraph $H$ on the same vertex set whose chromatic number is at least
$n$. Chromatic numbers may be infinite.

This answers Erdős Problem 923 affirmatively; it was proved by Rödl.

## Sources

- Vojtěch Rödl, On the chromatic number of subgraphs of a given graph, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 64 (1977), 370–371, https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9939-1977-0469806-4.
