articles.title: Erdős Problem 923 on triangle-free subgraphs of large chromatic number
articles.statement:
The proposition
asserts that for every natural number $n$ there is a natural number $k$ such that every simple
graph $G$, on any vertex set, whose chromatic number is at least $k$ has a triangle-free subgraph
$H$ on the same vertex set whose chromatic number is at least $n$. Chromatic numbers may be
infinite.

articles.title: Five color theorem
articles.statement:
Every straight-line planar simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set
has a proper vertex coloring with five colors.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_color_theorem.

articles.title: Mycielski's theorem
articles.statement:
Write $\chi(G)$ for the chromatic number of a simple graph $G$. For
every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set there is a simple graph $H$ on a finite vertex set
with strictly more vertices than $G$ that contains a subgraph isomorphic to $G$, such that $H$ is
triangle-free whenever $G$ is, and such that $\chi(H) = \chi(G) + 1$ whenever $\chi(G)$ is
finite. Moreover, for every natural number $k$ there is a triangle-free simple graph $H$ on a
finite vertex set with $\chi(H) \ge k$.

The explicit Mycielski construction is abstracted here to the existence of such a graph $H$.

## Sources

- J. Mycielski, "Sur le coloriage des graphes" (1955), https://doi.org/10.4064/cm-3-2-161-162 (statement ID `mycielski-theorem-s1`).

articles.title: External neighbours have a neighbour in the set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex
set $V$ and let $A \subseteq V$. If $v$ is an external neighbour of $A$ in $G$, then $v$ is
adjacent in $G$ to some vertex $a \in A$.

articles.title: The external neighbourhood is disjoint from the set
articles.statement:
For every simple graph $G$ on a
vertex set $V$ and every set $A \subseteq V$, the external neighbourhood of $A$ in $G$ is
disjoint from $A$.

articles.title: External neighbourhood
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a vertex set $V$ and a set
$A \subseteq V$, the external neighbourhood of $A$ in $G$ is the set of vertices $v \notin A$
that are adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $A$.

articles.title: C-expander
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ with $n$ vertices, and
let $C$ be a real number. Then $G$ is a $C$-expander if $C > 0$, every set $A \subseteq V$
with $|A| < n/(2C)$ has an external neighbourhood in $G$ with at least $C|A|$ vertices, and
for any two disjoint sets $A, B \subseteq V$ with $|A| \ge n/(2C)$ and $|B| \ge n/(2C)$ some
vertex of $A$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $B$.

## Sources

- Krivelevich, Lew and Michaeli, *Rigidity of expanders and pseudorandom graphs*, Definition 1.

articles.title: Uniform vertex expander
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let
$h$ be a real number. Then $G$ is a uniform vertex expander with parameter $h$ if $h > 0$ and
every set $S \subseteq V$ with $|S| \le |V|/2$ has an external neighbourhood in $G$ with at
least $h|S|$ vertices.

articles.title: Large disjoint sets in a C-expander span an edge
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex set $V$ with $n$ vertices, let $C$ be a real number, and suppose $G$ is a $C$-expander.
If $A, B \subseteq V$ are disjoint sets with $|A| \ge n/(2C)$ and $|B| \ge n/(2C)$, then some
vertex $a \in A$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex $b \in B$.

articles.title: Membership in the external neighbourhood
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set
$V$, let $A \subseteq V$ and let $v \in V$. Then $v$ lies in the external neighbourhood of $A$
in $G$ if and only if $v \notin A$ and $v$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex $a \in A$.

articles.title: The parameter of a uniform vertex expander is positive
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex set $V$ and let $h$ be a real number. If $G$ is a uniform vertex expander with
parameter $h$, then $h > 0$.

articles.title: The parameter of a C-expander is positive
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex
set $V$ and let $C$ be a real number. If $G$ is a $C$-expander, then $C > 0$.

articles.title: Small sets expand in a uniform vertex expander
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex set $V$ and let $h$ be a real number. If $G$ is a uniform vertex expander with parameter
$h$ and $S \subseteq V$ satisfies $|S| \le |V|/2$, then the external neighbourhood of $S$ in
$G$ has at least $h|S|$ vertices.

articles.title: Small sets expand in a $C$-expander
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a real number and let $G$ be a
$C$-expander on a finite vertex set $V$. Then every set $A \subseteq V$ with $|A| < |V|/(2C)$ has
at least $C|A|$ external neighbours, that is, at least $C|A|$ vertices outside $A$ are adjacent to
some vertex of $A$.

articles.title: Adjacency through an edge set
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$ be maps,
viewed as an undirected multigraph on $V$ in which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints
$\mathrm{end}_1(e)$ and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. For a finite set $F \subseteq E$, vertices
$u, v \in V$ are adjacent using $F$ when some $e \in F$ has $\mathrm{end}_1(e) = u$ and
$\mathrm{end}_2(e) = v$, or $\mathrm{end}_1(e) = v$ and $\mathrm{end}_2(e) = u$.

articles.title: Cut of a vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite set and $\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$
be maps, viewed as an undirected multigraph on $V$ in which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints
$\mathrm{end}_1(e)$ and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. For a finite set $X \subseteq V$, the cut of $X$ is
the set of edges $e \in E$ such that exactly one of $\mathrm{end}_1(e)$ and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$
lies in $X$. Loops never cross a cut.

articles.title: Degree counts incident edges in a loopless edge set
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$ be maps, viewed as an undirected multigraph on $V$ in
which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints $\mathrm{end}_1(e)$ and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. Let
$F \subseteq E$ be a finite set of edges with no loops, that is,
$\mathrm{end}_1(e) \ne \mathrm{end}_2(e)$ for every $e \in F$. Then for every vertex $v \in V$,
the degree of $v$ in $F$ equals the number of edges of $F$ incident to $v$.

articles.title: Degree within an edge set
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$ be maps, viewed
as an undirected multigraph on $V$ in which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints $\mathrm{end}_1(e)$
and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. For a finite set $F \subseteq E$ and a vertex $v \in V$, the degree of
$v$ in $F$ is the number of $e \in F$ with $\mathrm{end}_1(e) = v$ plus the number of $e \in F$
with $\mathrm{end}_2(e) = v$. Each endpoint incidence counts once, so a loop at $v$ contributes
two.

articles.title: Edges incident to a vertex
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$ be maps, viewed
as an undirected multigraph on $V$ in which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints $\mathrm{end}_1(e)$
and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. For a vertex $v \in V$ and a finite set $F \subseteq E$, the edges of
$F$ incident to $v$ form the finite set of all $e \in F$ with $\mathrm{end}_1(e) = v$ or
$\mathrm{end}_2(e) = v$. An edge appears once even when it is a loop.

articles.title: Circuits in an edge set
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$ be maps, viewed
as an undirected multigraph on $V$ in which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints $\mathrm{end}_1(e)$
and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. A finite set $F \subseteq E$ is a circuit when $F$ is nonempty, $F$ is
connected on its support, and every vertex in the support of $F$ has degree exactly $2$ in $F$,
where degree counts endpoint incidences, so that a loop contributes two.

This includes a loop as a $1$-circuit and two parallel edges between distinct vertices as a
$2$-circuit.

articles.title: Edge sets connected on their support
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$ be
maps, viewed as an undirected multigraph on $V$ in which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints
$\mathrm{end}_1(e)$ and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. A finite set $F \subseteq E$ is connected on its
support when for all vertices $u$ and $v$ in the support of $F$ there are vertices
$u = w_0, w_1, \dots, w_k = v$, with $k \ge 0$, such that $w_{i-1}$ and $w_i$ are adjacent
using $F$ for each $1 \le i \le k$.

articles.title: Support of an edge set
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{end}_1, \mathrm{end}_2 : E \to V$ be maps, viewed as
an undirected multigraph on $V$ in which each edge $e \in E$ has endpoints $\mathrm{end}_1(e)$
and $\mathrm{end}_2(e)$. The support of a finite set $F \subseteq E$ is the set of vertices
$v \in V$ such that $\mathrm{end}_1(e) = v$ or $\mathrm{end}_2(e) = v$ for some $e \in F$.

articles.title: Base point of the exterior of a box
articles.statement: The site `(R + 1, …, R + 1)`, a fixed base point of the exterior of `box d R`.

articles.title: Size of the vertex boundary of the box $(-n, n)^d$
articles.statement: The number of sites in the vertex boundary of `[-n, n]^d`.

articles.title: Box $(-n, n)^d$ as a finite set of sites
articles.statement: The box `[-n, n]^d` as a finite set of sites.

articles.title: Number of nearest-neighbour pairs inside the box $(-n, n)^d$
articles.statement: The number of ordered nearest-neighbour pairs inside `[-n, n]^d`.

articles.title: Nearest-neighbour pairs inside the box $(-n, n)^d$
articles.statement: The ordered pairs of nearest-neighbour sites that both lie in `[-n, n]^d`.

articles.title: Box sites with a forward neighbour in the box
articles.statement: Sites of `[-n, n]^d` whose successor in the first coordinate direction is still in the box.

articles.title: Vertex boundary of the box $(-n, n)^d$ as a finite set
articles.statement: The vertex boundary of `[-n, n]^d` as a finite set of sites.

articles.title: Box $(-n, n)^d$ in the hypercubic lattice
articles.statement: The box `[-n, n]^d` of sites whose coordinates all have absolute value at most `n`.

articles.title: Nearest neighbours of a lattice site
articles.statement: The finite set of the `2d` nearest neighbours of `x`.

articles.title: Neighbour of a site in a coordinate direction
articles.statement: The neighbour of `x` in direction `j`, positive if the flag is `true` and negative otherwise.

articles.title: Edge boundary of a set of sites
articles.statement:
The edge boundary of a set `S` of sites: ordered nearest-neighbour pairs with exactly one
endpoint in `S`.

articles.title: Exterior of a box in $\mathbb{Z}^d$
articles.statement:
The exterior of the box `[-R, R]^d`: sites with some coordinate of absolute value greater than
`R`.

articles.title: Every finite set of sites lies in a box
articles.statement: Every finite set of sites lies in some box `box d R`.

articles.title: Square lattice is connected
articles.statement: The square lattice `ℤ²` is connected.

articles.title: Hypercubic lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$
articles.statement:
The hypercubic lattice `ℤ^d`: the simple graph on `Site d` whose edges join
nearest
neighbours.

articles.title: $\ell^1$ distance on $\mathbb{Z}^d$
articles.statement: The `ℓ¹` (graph) distance `∑ i, |x i - y i|` between two sites.

articles.title: Nearest neighbours in $\mathbb{Z}^d$
articles.statement: Two sites are nearest neighbours when their `ℓ¹` distance `∑ i, |x i - y i|` equals one.

articles.title: First index where a walk reaches a coordinate value
articles.statement: The first index at which the walk `w` has `k`-th coordinate equal to `r`.

articles.title: Increasing one coordinate stays in the same component
articles.statement: In `ℤ²`, increasing one coordinate by `n` stays in the same component.

articles.title: Changing one coordinate stays in the same component
articles.statement: In `ℤ²`, changing one coordinate stays in the same component.

articles.title: Setting a set of coordinates of a lattice site
articles.statement: The site obtained from `p` by setting every coordinate in `T` to `v`.

articles.title: Shift of a site along a coordinate
articles.statement: The site obtained from `x` by adding `s` to its `j`-th coordinate.

articles.title: Site of the hypercubic lattice
articles.statement: A site of the `d`-dimensional hypercubic lattice `ℤ^d`, encoded as an integer vector.

articles.title: Complement of a finite set in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ has one infinite component
articles.statement:
For `d ≥ 2`, the complement of a finite set of sites of `ℤ^d` has exactly one infinite connected
component.

articles.title: Inner vertex boundary of a box
articles.statement: The inner vertex boundary of `box d n`: sites of `box d n` that are not in `box d (n - 1)`.

articles.title: Graphs that are line graphs
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex type is a line graph if
there are a natural number $k$ and a simple graph $H$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ such
that $G$ is isomorphic to the line graph $L(H)$. Here $L(H)$ has the edges of $H$ as its vertices,
and two distinct edges of $H$ are adjacent in $L(H)$ when they share an endpoint.

articles.title: Lexicographic product of graphs
articles.statement:
Given simple graphs $X$ and $Y$, the *lexicographic
product* $X[Y]$ of $X$ and $Y$ is the simple graph with vertex set $V(X) \times V(Y)$ in which
two vertices $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ are adjacent exactly when $x_1$ and $x_2$ are
adjacent in $X$, or $x_1 = x_2$ and $y_1$ and $y_2$ are adjacent in $Y$.

articles.title: Adjacency in the simplex graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph. Two simplex vertices $s$ and
$t$ of $G$ are adjacent in the simplex graph of $G$ if and only if their symmetric difference
$s \triangle t$ has exactly one element.

articles.title: The empty clique is adjacent to every singleton
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph. For every
vertex $v$ of $G$, the empty simplex vertex of $G$ and the singleton simplex vertex of $v$ are
adjacent in the simplex graph of $G$.

articles.title: Empty simplex vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph. The empty simplex vertex of $G$ is
the empty set of vertices, which is a clique of $G$.

articles.title: Simplex graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph. The simplex graph of $G$ is the simple graph
whose vertices are the simplex vertices of $G$ (the finite cliques of $G$), in which two cliques
$s$ and $t$ are adjacent exactly when their symmetric difference $s \triangle t$ has exactly one
element.

The vertex type of $G$ is not required to be finite.

articles.title: Simplex vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex type $V$. A simplex vertex
of $G$ is a finite set $s$ of vertices that is a clique of $G$, meaning that any two distinct
elements of $s$ are adjacent in $G$.

articles.title: Singleton simplex vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph. For a vertex $v$ of $G$, the
singleton simplex vertex of $v$ is the one-element set containing $v$, which is a clique of
$G$.

articles.title: Chromatic profile count
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $k$ be
a natural number and let $m : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \mathbb{N}$. The chromatic profile count of
$G$ at $k$ and $m$ is the number of proper colorings $c : V \to \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ of $G$ such
that for every color $i$, exactly $m(i)$ vertices $v$ satisfy $c(v) = i$.

These counts are the coefficients of the chromatic symmetric function.

articles.title: Isomorphic graphs have the same chromatic symmetric function
articles.statement:
If $G$ and $H$ are
isomorphic simple graphs on finite vertex sets, then $G$ and $H$ have the same chromatic
symmetric function.

The proof transports colorings and their color classes along the isomorphism.

articles.title: Reflexivity of having the same chromatic symmetric function
articles.statement:
Every simple graph on a
finite vertex set has the same chromatic symmetric function as itself.

articles.title: Graphs with the same chromatic symmetric function
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on
finite vertex sets. We say that $G$ and $H$ have the same chromatic symmetric function when, for
every natural number $k$ and every $m : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \mathbb{N}$, the chromatic profile
count of $G$ at $k$ and $m$ equals that of $H$: both graphs have equally many proper colorings
with colors $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ in which each color $i$ is used on exactly $m(i)$ vertices.

This is equality of chromatic symmetric functions, expressed through their coefficients.

articles.title: Symmetry of having the same chromatic symmetric function
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be simple
graphs on finite vertex sets. If $G$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $H$, then $H$
has the same chromatic symmetric function as $G$.

articles.title: Transitivity of having the same chromatic symmetric function
articles.statement:
Let $G$, $H$ and $K$ be
simple graphs on finite vertex sets. If $G$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $H$, and
$H$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $K$, then $G$ has the same chromatic symmetric
function as $K$.

articles.title: Incident-edge sum
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $q$ be a
natural number and let $\ell$ be a bijection from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}$.
The incident-edge sum at a vertex $v$ is $\sum_{e \ni v} (\ell(e) + 1)$, the sum over the edges
$e$ of $G$ that contain $v$; in other words, the edges carry the labels $1, \dots, q$.

articles.title: Value of the induced residue
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite nonempty vertex set
$V$, let $q$ be a natural number and let $\ell$ be a bijection from the edge set of $G$ to
$\{0, \dots, q-1\}$. For every vertex $v$, the induced residue of $v$ with respect to $\ell$, read
as a natural number, equals the incident-edge sum at $v$ with respect to $\ell$ modulo $|V|$.

articles.title: Induced vertex residue
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $q$ be
a natural number and let $\ell$ be a bijection from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$.
The induced residue of a vertex $v$ is the incident-edge sum at $v$ (with edge labels
$\ell(e) + 1$) reduced modulo $|V|$, viewed as an element of $\{0, \dots, |V| - 1\}$. When
$|V| = 0$ there are no vertices, so there is nothing to define.

articles.title: Edge-graceful graphs via a vertex bijection
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$
is edge-graceful if and only if there are a natural number $q$, a bijection $\ell$ from the edge
set of $G$ to $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ and a bijection $\lambda$ from $V$ to $\{0, \dots, |V| - 1\}$ such
that for every vertex $v$, $\lambda(v)$ is the induced residue of $v$ with respect to $\ell$ and,
if $V$ is nonempty, $\lambda(v)$ equals the incident-edge sum at $v$ with respect to $\ell$ modulo
$|V|$.

articles.title: Edge-graceful graph
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is edge-graceful when
there are a natural number $q$ and a bijection $\ell$ from the edge set of $G$ to
$\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ such that the induced residue map, sending each vertex $v$ to the sum of
$\ell(e) + 1$ over the edges $e$ containing $v$ taken modulo $|V|$, is a bijection from $V$ to
$\{0, \dots, |V| - 1\}$.

articles.title: Erdős–Gallai theorem
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set and $d \colon V \to \mathbb{N}$. There is a
simple graph on $V$ in which every vertex $v$ has degree $d(v)$ if and only if the sum
$\sum_{v \in V} d(v)$ is even and, for every subset $S \subseteq V$,

$$\sum_{v \in S} d(v) \le |S|(|S| - 1) + \sum_{v \in V \setminus S} \min(d(v), |S|).$$

## Sources

- P. Erdős and T. Gallai, Graphs with prescribed degrees of vertices, Matematikai Lapok 11 (1960), 264-274.

articles.title: Induced forests are no larger than the induced forest number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph
on a finite vertex set $V$. For every set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced
on $S$ is acyclic, $|S|$ is at most the induced forest number of $G$.

articles.title: The induced forest number is attained
articles.statement:
For every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set
$V$, there is a set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced on $S$ is acyclic and
$|S|$ equals the induced forest number of $G$.

articles.title: The induced forest number is at most the number of vertices
articles.statement:
For every simple graph $G$
on a finite vertex set $V$, the induced forest number of $G$ is at most $|V|$.

articles.title: Induced forest number
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, the induced
forest number $a(G)$ is the maximum number of vertices of an induced forest in $G$, that is, the
maximum cardinality of a set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced on $S$ is
acyclic.

## Sources

- H. Jung, A 15/31 Counterexample Family to the Albertson--Berman Conjecture, arXiv:2608.17350v1, the definition of $a(G)$.

articles.title: Arboricity colorings
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and $k$ a natural number. A labeling of the
edges of $G$ with labels in $\{0, 1, \dots, k - 1\}$ is an arboricity coloring when, for each
label $i$, the graph on the vertices of $G$ whose edges are the edges of $G$ labeled $i$ is
acyclic, that is, a forest.

articles.title: Nash–Williams arboricity theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let
$k$ be a natural number. Then $G$ has an arboricity coloring with $k$ labels, that is, its edges
can be labeled with $k$ labels so that the edges of each label form a forest, if and only if for
every nonempty set $U \subseteq V$, the number of edges of $G$ with both endpoints in $U$ is at
most $k(|U| - 1)$.

## Sources

- C. St. J. A. Nash-Williams, J. London Math. Soc. 39 (1964), DOI 10.1112/jlms/s1-39.1.12.

articles.title: Cyclic labels do not exceed the number of vertices
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n > 0$ and
$s$ and every position $i \in \{0, \dots, 2n-1\}$, the cyclic label of $i$ with offset $s$ is at
most $2n$.

articles.title: Range of the cyclic labels
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n > 0$ and $s$ and every position
$i \in \{0, \dots, 2n-1\}$, the cyclic label $c$ of $i$ with offset $s$ satisfies
$1 \le c \le 2n$.

articles.title: Cyclic labels are positive
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $s$ and every position
$i \in \{0, \dots, 2n-1\}$, the cyclic label of $i$ with offset $s$ is at least $1$.

articles.title: The cyclic label of the first position with offset zero
articles.statement:
Let $n > 0$ be a natural number
and number the vertices of the ladder $P_n \times P_2$ along its perimeter by $0, 1, \dots, 2n - 1$,
with $v_k$ at position $k - 1$ and $u_k$ at position $2n - k$ for $1 \le k \le n$. Then the cyclic
label with offset $0$ of the position $0$ (the vertex $v_1$) is $1$.

articles.title: Cyclic labeling of the ladder perimeter
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $s$ be natural numbers. Number the
vertices of the ladder $P_n \times P_2$ along its perimeter by $0, 1, \dots, 2n - 1$, with $v_k$ at
position $k - 1$ and $u_k$ at position $2n - k$ for $1 \le k \le n$. The cyclic label with offset
$s$ of the position $i \in \{0, \dots, 2n - 1\}$ is $((i + s) \bmod 2n) + 1$.

Following Mbirika et al., JIS Vol. 19, the ladder has horizontal adjacency within each row and
vertical adjacency between $v_k$ and $u_k$.

articles.title: Consecutive cyclic prime labeling of the ladder
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $s$ be natural numbers.
Number the vertices of the ladder $P_n \times P_2$ along its perimeter by $0, 1, \dots, 2n - 1$,
with $v_k$ at position $k - 1$ and $u_k$ at position $2n - k$ for $1 \le k \le n$. The offset $s$
gives a consecutive cyclic prime labeling of the ladder when $n > 0$ and, for all positions
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, 2n - 1\}$ that are adjacent in the ladder graph, the cyclic labels of $i$
and $j$ with offset $s$ are relatively prime.

The cyclic labels place $1, \dots, 2n$ consecutively along the perimeter order: if $1$ is on $v_k$
the order runs $v_k, \dots, v_n, u_n, \dots, u_1, v_1, \dots, v_{k - 1}$ (and analogously from
$u_k$).

articles.title: Adjacency in the ladder graph
articles.statement:
Number the vertices of the ladder $P_n \times P_2$ along
its perimeter by $0, 1, \dots, 2n-1$, with $v_k$ at position $k - 1$ and $u_k$ at position
$2n - k$ for $1 \le k \le n$. Two positions $i, j \in \{0, \dots, 2n-1\}$ are adjacent when
$j \equiv i + 1 \pmod{2n}$ or $i \equiv j + 1 \pmod{2n}$ (neighbours along the perimeter
cycle), or when $i + j = 2n - 1$ (the rung joining $v_k$ and $u_k$).

The two end rungs $v_1 u_1$ and $v_n u_n$ are also perimeter edges.

articles.title: Baumert et al. lower bound for the capacity of the 7-cycle
articles.statement:
The Shannon capacity of the
$7$-cycle is at least $343^{1/5}$, as an inequality in $[0, \infty]$.

## Sources

- Baumert--McEliece--Rodemich--Rumsey--Stanley--Taylor (1971), exact rate row.

is a finite set of words of length $174$ over $\mathbb{Z}/11\mathbb{Z}$ that is an independent

articles.title: Iterated squaring of BPZ profiles
articles.statement:
Write $\star$ for the BPZ profile product. For a
natural number $k$ and a BPZ profile $p$, the $k$-fold iterated square $S_k(p)$ is defined by
$S_0(p) = p$ and $S_{k+1}(p) = S_k(p \star p)$; that is, $S_k(p)$ is obtained from $p$ by
squaring $k$ times under $\star$.

articles.title: BPZ profiles
articles.statement:
A BPZ profile is an arbitrary quadruple of integers, called its code,
pairs, auxiliary and neutral coordinates: the four integer coordinates propagated by the
valid-tuple product of Buys, Polak and Zuiddam. No validity condition is imposed on the
quadruple.

## Sources

articles.title: Finitely many cycle codes of each length
articles.statement:
For every nonzero natural number $q$ and every
natural number $n$, there are only finitely many cycle codes of length $n$ modulo $q$.

articles.title: Code rates are at most the cycle capacity
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q$, every positive
integer $n$ and every cycle code $A$ of length $n$ modulo $q$, the rate of $A$ is at most the
Shannon capacity of the $q$-cycle.

articles.title: Rate of a cycle code
articles.statement:
For a natural number $q$, a positive integer $n$ and a cycle code
$A$ of length $n$ modulo $q$, the rate of $A$ is $|A|^{1/n}$, the $n$-th root of the number of
codewords of $A$, taken in the extended nonnegative reals $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Cycle codes
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $q$ and $n$, a cycle code of length $n$ modulo $q$ is a
finite set of words of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ that is an independent code for
the $q$-cycle.

articles.title: Codes give lower bounds on the cycle capacity
articles.statement:
Let $q$, $n$ and $M$ be natural numbers
with $n \ge 1$. If some finite set of words of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ is an
independent code for the $q$-cycle and has exactly $M$ elements, then $M^{1/n}$ is at most the
Shannon capacity of the $q$-cycle, as an inequality in $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Gao's code of dimension 200 for the 7-cycle
articles.statement:
Let $M_{40}$ be Gao's printed dimension-200
cardinality, a natural number with 103 decimal digits. There is a finite set $A$ of words of
length $200$ over $\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}$ that is an independent code for the $7$-cycle and has
exactly $M_{40}$ elements.

## Sources

- Gao, arXiv:2607.27869, exact dimension-200 construction.

articles.title: Gao's lower bound for the capacity of the 7-cycle
articles.statement:
Let $M_{40}$ be Gao's printed
dimension-200 cardinality, a natural number with 103 decimal digits. The Shannon capacity of the
$7$-cycle is at least $M_{40}^{1/200}$, as an inequality in $[0, \infty]$.

## Sources

- Gao, arXiv:2607.27869, exact dimension-200 root rate.

articles.title: Gao's code size in dimension 200
articles.statement:

$4085567963379990282748597333793399773399910167372462

articles.title: Shannon capacity of a graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let
$\theta$ be a real number. For $k \ge 1$ let $G^{\boxtimes k}$ be the $k$-th strong power of $G$
and $\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})$ its independence number. The graph $G$ has Shannon capacity $\theta$
when $\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k} \to \theta$ as $k \to \infty$.

articles.title: Independent codes for the modular cycle
articles.statement:
Let $q$ and $n$ be natural numbers. A finite set
$A$ of words of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ is an independent code for the $q$-cycle
when every difference $x = a_1 - a_2$ with $a_1, a_2 \in A$ whose coordinates all lie in
$\{-1, 0, 1\}$ is the zero word. For $q \ge 3$ this says exactly that $A$ is an independent set
in the $n$-th strong power of the cycle graph $C_q$.

The source uses odd $q \ge 7$; the definition is stated for every $q$.

articles.title: Itty–Rosin–Carstensen–Reichman code of dimension 10 for the 7-cycle

$7$-cycle and has exactly $134753$ elements.

articles.title: Itty–Rosin–Carstensen–Reichman lower bound for the capacity of the 7-cycle
articles.statement:

articles.title: Lovász's upper bound for the capacity of the 7-cycle
articles.statement:

$7$-cycle is at most $\frac{7 \cos(\pi/7)}{1 + \cos(\pi/7)}$, as an inequality in $[0, \infty]$.

## Sources

articles.title: Lovász's theta value for the 7-cycle

Approximate decimal displays of this number in the source are not asserted as equalities.

articles.title: Positive block lengths
articles.statement:
The type of positive integers, that is, of natural numbers $n$
with $1 \le n$, used as the block lengths of codes.

articles.title: Shannon's upper bound for the capacity of the 7-cycle
articles.statement:

$7$-cycle is at most $7/2$.

articles.title: Shannon capacity of the modular cycle
articles.statement:
For a natural number $q$, the Shannon capacity of
the $q$-cycle is the supremum, in $[0, \infty]$, of the rates $|A|^{1/n}$ over all positive
integers $n$ and all cycle codes $A$ of length $n$ modulo $q$.

articles.title: Lovász's theorem: the Shannon capacity of the pentagon
articles.statement:
The cycle graph $C_5$ on five
vertices has Shannon capacity $\sqrt{5}$: writing $\alpha(C_5^{\boxtimes k})$ for the independence
number of the $k$-th strong power of $C_5$, we have $\alpha(C_5^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k} \to \sqrt{5}$
as $k \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §238. Problem `shannon_capacity_pentagon` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Product of BPZ profiles
articles.statement:
For $i = 1, 2$ let $p_i = (c_i, \pi_i, a_i, z_i)$ be a BPZ
profile, with integer code, pairs, auxiliary and neutral coordinates. The product $p_1 \star p_2$
is the BPZ profile with code coordinate $(c_1 - \pi_1)(c_2 - \pi_2) + a_1 \pi_2 + \pi_1 a_2$,
pairs coordinate $z_1 \pi_2 + \pi_1 z_2$, auxiliary coordinate $a_1 a_2$ and neutral coordinate
$z_1 z_2 + (a_1 - z_1)(a_2 - z_2)$.

The product is arithmetic on the four coordinates only; it does not supply an independent set.

## Sources

- BPZ, arXiv:2607.29681, the profile product.

articles.title: Strong power of a graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph with vertex set $V$ and let $k$ be a
natural number. The $k$-th strong power $G^{\boxtimes k}$ is the simple graph whose vertices are
the words $x = (x_1, \dots, x_k) \in V^k$ of length $k$, in which two words $x$ and $y$ are
adjacent (confusable) when $x \neq y$ and for every $i$ either $x_i = y_i$ or $x_i$ and $y_i$ are
adjacent in $G$.

articles.title: Tandon's dimension-500 code for the 7-cycle
articles.statement:
Let $M^*$ be Tandon's dimension-500 code
size. There is an independent code for the $7$-cycle consisting of words of length $500$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}$ with exactly $M^*$ codewords.

## Sources

- Tandon, arXiv:2608.30273, exact dimension-500 construction.

articles.title: Tandon's lower bound for the capacity of the 7-cycle
articles.statement:

dimension-500 code size. The Shannon capacity of the $7$-cycle is at least $(M^*)^{1/500}$.

## Sources

articles.title: Tandon's dimension-500 code size
Vesel–Žerovnik lower bound for the capacity of the 7-cycle
articles.statement:
The Shannon capacity of the
$7$-cycle is at least $108^{1/4}$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 136: the $(4, 5)$-colouring number of $K_n$ is asymptotically $5n/6$
articles.statement:
Let
$f(n)$ be the least number of colours in a $(4, 5)$-colouring of $K_n$, that is, a symmetric
colouring of the pairs of vertices of $K_n$ in which the six edges of every $K_4$ receive at
least five distinct colours. Then $f(n)/n \to 5/6$ as $n \to \infty$.

Erdős and Gyárfás proved $f(n) > 5(n - 1)/6$, and Bennett, Cushman, Dudek and Prałat constructed
$(4, 5)$-colourings of $K_n$ with $5n/6 + o(n)$ colours (Joos and Mubayi gave a shorter proof).

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #136, https://www.erdosproblems.com/136 (status SOLVED); resolution: P. Bennett, R. Cushman, A. Dudek and P. Prałat, The Erdős-Gyárfás function f(n, 4, 5) = 5n/6 + o(n) - so Gyárfás was right, arXiv:2207.02920 (2022); F. Joos and D. Mubayi, Ramsey theory constructions from hypergraph matchings, arXiv:2208.12563 (2022), abstract: (4, 5)-colourings of K_n with 5n/6 + o(n) colours; with the Erdős-Gyárfás lower bound f(n) > 5(n - 1)/6 this gives f(n) ~ 5n/6 (erdosproblems.com/136), https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02920.

articles.title: The asymptotic of the $(4, 5)$-colouring number (Erdős Problem 136)
articles.statement:
Let $f(n)$ be the
least number of colours in a $(4, 5)$-colouring of $K_n$. This is the proposition that $f(n)/n$
tends to $5/6$ as $n \to \infty$; equivalently, $f(n) = (5/6 + o(1))\, n$.

articles.title: The $(4, 5)$-colouring number $f(n)$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $f(n)$ is the least
natural number $k$ such that $K_n$ has a $(4, 5)$-colouring with $k$ colours; such a $k$
always exists.

articles.title: $(4, 5)$-colourings of $K_n$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the complete graph $K_n$ on
the vertices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ has a $(4, 5)$-colouring with $k$ colours if there is a map $c$
assigning to every ordered pair $(x, y)$ of vertices one of $k$ colours, with $c(x, y) = c(y, x)$
for all $x, y$, such that for any four distinct vertices the six edges between them receive at
least five distinct colours.

articles.title: The Ramsey property for cliques
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $s$, $t$ and $N$, the classical
Ramsey property for $(s, t)$ holds at $N$ when every simple graph $G$ on $N$ vertices contains the
complete graph $K_s$ as a subgraph, or its complement $\overline{G}$ contains $K_t$ as a subgraph.

Thus the graph and its complement encode the two colors of a complete graph.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 800 on linear Ramsey numbers
articles.statement:
The proposition asserts that there is a real
number $C > 0$ such that for every natural number $n$ and every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices
in which no two adjacent vertices both have degree at least $3$, the diagonal Ramsey number
$R(G, G)$ is at most $Cn$.

articles.title: Alon's theorem on linear Ramsey numbers
articles.statement:
There is a real number $C > 0$ such that for every
natural number $n$ and every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices in which no two adjacent vertices
both have degree at least $3$, the diagonal Ramsey number $R(G, G)$ is at most $Cn$.

This answers Erdős Problem 800 affirmatively.

## Sources

- Noga Alon, Subdivided graphs have linear Ramsey numbers, Journal of Graph Theory 18 (1994), 343–347, https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.3190180406.

articles.title: Resolution of Erdős Problem 570
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k \ge 3$ there is an $M$ such that
for every $m \ge M$ and every finite simple graph $H$ with exactly $m$ edges and no isolated
vertices, the Ramsey number $R(C_k, H)$ of the cycle $C_k$ on $k$ vertices and $H$ is at most
$2m + \lfloor (k-1)/2 \rfloor$.

## Sources

- S. Cambie, A. Freschi, P. Morawski, K. Petrova, A. Pokrovskiy, Ramsey number of a cycle versus a graph of a given size, arXiv:2601.10238 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10238.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 570 (cycle versus graph Ramsey bound)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural
number $k \ge 3$ there is an $M$ such that for every $m \ge M$ and every finite simple graph $H$
with exactly $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, the Ramsey number $R(C_k, H)$ of the cycle $C_k$
on $k$ vertices and $H$ is at most $2m + \lfloor (k-1)/2 \rfloor$.

articles.title: Diagonal Ramsey number of a graph
articles.statement:
For a finite simple graph $G$, the diagonal Ramsey
number of $G$ is $R(G, G)$: the least $n$ such that for every simple graph $C$ on $n$ vertices,
$C$ or its complement contains a copy of $G$ as a subgraph, and $0$ if there is no such $n$.

articles.title: The pair Ramsey number as an infimum
articles.statement:
For finite simple graphs $G$ and $H$, the Ramsey
number $R(G, H)$ equals the infimum in $\mathbb{N}$ (where the empty set has infimum $0$) of the
set of $n$ such that every simple graph $C$ on $n$ vertices contains a copy of $G$ as a subgraph
or has a complement containing a copy of $H$ as a subgraph.

articles.title: Ramsey number of a pair of graphs
articles.statement:
For finite simple graphs $G$ and $H$, the Ramsey number
$R(G, H)$ is the least $n$ such that every simple graph $C$ on $n$ vertices contains a copy of $G$
as a subgraph or has a complement containing a copy of $H$ as a subgraph, and $0$ if there is no
such $n$.

articles.title: Classical Ramsey numbers as an infimum
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $s$ and $t$, the Ramsey
number $R(s, t)$ equals the infimum in $\mathbb{N}$ (where the empty set has infimum $0$) of the
set of $N$ such that every simple graph on $N$ vertices contains the complete graph $K_s$ as a
subgraph or has a complement containing $K_t$ as a subgraph.

articles.title: Classical Ramsey numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $s$ and $t$, the Ramsey number $R(s, t)$ is
the least $N$ such that every simple graph on $N$ vertices contains the complete graph $K_s$ as a
subgraph or has a complement containing $K_t$ as a subgraph, and $0$ if there is no such $N$.

Such an $N$ always exists by the finite Ramsey theorem.

articles.title: Ramsey size linear graphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. For a finite simple graph
$H$, write $R(G, H)$ for the least $m$ such that every simple graph on $m$ vertices contains a
copy of $G$ or has a complement containing a copy of $H$ ($0$ if there is no such $m$), and write
$e(H)$ for the number of edges of $H$. Then $G$ is Ramsey size linear if there is a real constant
$c > 0$ such that for every $n$ and every simple graph $H$ on $n$ vertices with no isolated
vertices, $R(G, H) \le c \cdot e(H)$.

articles.title: No superlinear threshold for triangle-good graphs (Erdős Problem 1182)
articles.statement:
It is not true
that for every real number $C$, for all sufficiently large natural numbers $n$, every connected
graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with at most $Cn$ edges has
$R(K_3, G) = 2n - 1$. Equivalently, there is a real number $C$ such that for infinitely many $n$
some connected graph $G$ on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with at most $Cn$ edges has
$R(K_3, G) \ne 2n - 1$. Here $R(K_3, G)$ is the Ramsey number of the pair: the least $N$ such
that every graph on $N$ vertices contains a triangle or has a complement containing a copy of
$G$, and $0$ if there is no such $N$.

Brandt proved $F(n) \le 84n$, where $F(n)$ is the largest $m$ such that every connected graph on
$n$ vertices with at most $m$ edges has $R(K_3, G) = 2n - 1$. So for all large $n$ some connected
graph on $n$ vertices with at most $84n + 1$ edges has $R(K_3, G) \ne 2n - 1$, and the statement
fails for $C = 85$. Brandt's 1996 preprint is unrefereed; erdosproblems.com/1182 accepts it.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #1182, https://www.erdosproblems.com/1182 (status OPEN); resolution: S. Brandt, Expanding graphs and Ramsey numbers, preprint, Serie A Mathematik, Freie Universität Berlin, 1996 (unrefereed; accepted on erdosproblems.com/1182), F(n) ≤ 84n, as recorded on erdosproblems.com/1182: 'The upper bound was improved to F(n) ≤ 84n by Brandt ... (This resolves the final question in the negative.)', https://ftp.math.fu-berlin.de/pub/math/publ/pre/1996/pr-a-96-24.ps.

articles.title: Superlinear threshold for triangle-good graphs (Erdős Problem 1182)
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every real number $C$, for all sufficiently large natural numbers $n$, every connected graph $G$ on
the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with at most $Cn$ edges has $R(K_3, G) = 2n - 1$. Here
$R(K_3, G)$ is the Ramsey number of the pair: the least $N$ such that every graph on $N$ vertices
contains a triangle or has a complement containing a copy of $G$.

This is the last question of Erdős Problem 1182, whether $F(n) / n \to \infty$, where $F(n)$ is the
largest $m$ such that every connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with at most $m$ edges has
$R(K_3, G) = 2n - 1$; since this property is downward closed in $m$, the two forms agree.

articles.title: Monochromatic clique packings
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and view a simple
graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ as a two-colouring of the edges of the
complete graph $K_n$: the edges of $G$ are red and the edges of its complement $G^c$ are blue.
A finite family $P$ of sets of vertices is a monochromatic $k$-clique packing for $G$ when the
sets in $P$ are pairwise disjoint and each of them is a $k$-clique of $G$ or a $k$-clique of
$G^c$, that is, a set of exactly $k$ vertices spanning a monochromatic copy of $K_k$.

articles.title: Burr–Erdős–Spencer leftover value
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, let $r = R(k, k - 1)$
be the classical two-colour Ramsey number. The leftover value is
$r - 1 + \big((n + 1 - r) \bmod k\big)$, where subtraction is truncated at $0$ (in particular
$n + 1 - r$ is read as $0$ when $n + 1 \le r$) and $a \bmod 0 = a$.

For $k \ge 2$ and large $n$, Burr, Erdős and Spencer showed that this is the least number of
vertices that vertex-disjoint monochromatic copies of $K_k$ can be guaranteed to leave uncovered
in every two-colouring of the edges of $K_n$.

articles.title: Burr–Erdős–Spencer theorem on monochromatic clique packings
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$k \ge 2$ there is $n_0$ such that for every $n \ge n_0$ the following holds. Let
$r = R(k, k - 1)$ be the classical two-colour Ramsey number and let
$L = r - 1 + \big((n + 1 - r) \bmod k\big)$, where $n + 1 - r$ is read as $0$ if it is negative.
View a simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices as a two-colouring of the edges of $K_n$, with the edges
of $G$ red and those of its complement $G^c$ blue. Then every such colouring admits a finite
family of pairwise disjoint sets of vertices, each a $k$-clique of $G$ or of $G^c$, that leaves at
most $L$ vertices uncovered; and some colouring admits no such family leaving fewer than $L$
vertices uncovered.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #1015, https://www.erdosproblems.com/1015 (status SOLVED); resolution: S. A. Burr, P. Erdős and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey theorems for multiple copies of graphs, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 209 (1975), 87-99, §5, Theorem 6: if k is given, then for sufficiently large n, f(n, k) = r(k, k - 1) - 1 + rem(n - r(k, k - 1) + 1, k), where f(n, k) is the minimal integer such that any two-coloring of K_n admits vertex-disjoint monochromatic K_k with at most f(n, k) points left over; erdosproblems.com/1015 lists the problem as solved citing this paper, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1975-35.pdf.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 1015 in the Burr–Erdős–Spencer form
articles.statement:
This is the statement that for every
natural number $k \ge 2$ there is $n_0$ such that for every $n \ge n_0$ the following holds. Let
$r = R(k, k - 1)$ be the classical two-colour Ramsey number and let
$L = r - 1 + \big((n + 1 - r) \bmod k\big)$, where $n + 1 - r$ is read as $0$ if it is negative.
View a simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices as a two-colouring of the edges of $K_n$, with the edges
of $G$ red and those of its complement $G^c$ blue. Then every such colouring admits a
monochromatic $k$-clique packing, that is, a finite family of pairwise disjoint sets of vertices,
each a $k$-clique of $G$ or of $G^c$, leaving at most $L$ vertices uncovered; and some colouring
admits no such packing leaving fewer than $L$ vertices uncovered. In other words, for these $n$
the least number $f(n, k)$ such that every two-colouring of $K_n$ admits such a packing leaving at
most $f(n, k)$ vertices uncovered equals $L$.

articles.title: The order-robust ordered Ramsey conjecture holds
articles.statement:
There are a real number $c > 0$ and a
natural number $N_0$ such that for every $n \ge N_0$ there is a $100$-regular simple graph $H$ on
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that $r_<(H, \lt _H) \ge n^{1+c}$ for every strict total order $\lt _H$ on
its vertices. Here $r_<(H, \lt _H)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges
of the complete graph on $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ with its natural order contains a monochromatic
copy of $H$ (not necessarily induced) under an injective map sending $\lt _H$ into the natural
order, and $0$ if there is no such $N$.

Balko, Jelínek and Valtr prove that for every $d \ge 3$ almost every $d$-regular $n$-vertex
graph has ordered Ramsey number at least $n^{3/2-1/d}/(4 \log n \log \log n)$ under every vertex
ordering; for $d = 100$ this exceeds $n^{1+c}$ for any $c < 49/100$ and all large $n$.

## Sources

- M. Balko, V. Jelínek and P. Valtr, On ordered Ramsey numbers of bounded-degree graphs, arXiv:1606.05628, https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.05628.

articles.title: Order-robust ordered Ramsey conjecture for 100-regular graphs
articles.statement:
There are a real number
$c > 0$ and a natural number $N_0$ such that for every $n \ge N_0$ there is a $100$-regular simple
graph $H$ on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that $r_<(H, \lt _H) \ge n^{1+c}$ for every strict total
order $\lt _H$ on its vertices, where $r_<(H, \lt _H)$ is the ordered Ramsey number of $H$ with the
order $\lt _H$.

This is the AIM question asking whether such a $c$ exists, stated as a claim.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0079] Order-robust ordered Ramsey numbers of regular graphs (aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[78], Source item 32, Section: Ordered Ramsey numbers, Workshop: Graph Ramsey theory, https://www.overleaf.com/read/mnvcscjjysvg).

articles.title: Blue ordered copy
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with a strict total
order $\lt _H$ on its vertices, and let $G$ be a simple graph on $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$, the red
graph. Then $G$ admits a blue ordered copy of $(H, \lt _H)$ when there is an ordered embedding $f$
of $(\{0, \dots, n - 1\}, \lt _H)$ into $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ such that $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are not
adjacent in $G$ whenever $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $H$. Since $f$ is injective, these pairs are
edges of the blue graph, the complement of $G$. The copy need not be induced.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0079] Order-robust ordered Ramsey numbers of regular graphs (aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[78], Source item 32, Section: Ordered Ramsey numbers, Workshop: Graph Ramsey theory, https://www.overleaf.com/read/mnvcscjjysvg).

articles.title: Red ordered copy
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with a strict total
order $\lt _H$ on its vertices, and let $G$ be a simple graph on $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$, the red
graph. Then $G$ contains a red ordered copy of $(H, \lt _H)$ when there is an ordered embedding $f$
of $(\{0, \dots, n - 1\}, \lt _H)$ into $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ such that $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are
adjacent in $G$ whenever $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $H$. The copy need not be induced.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0079] Order-robust ordered Ramsey numbers of regular graphs (aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[78], Source item 32, Section: Ordered Ramsey numbers, Workshop: Graph Ramsey theory, https://www.overleaf.com/read/mnvcscjjysvg).

articles.title: Ordered embedding
articles.statement:
Let $\lt _H$ be a strict total order on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$. A map
$f \colon \{0, \dots, n - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ is an ordered embedding when it is
injective and $a \lt _H b$ implies $f(a) < f(b)$ for all $a$ and $b$, where $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$
carries its natural order.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0079] Order-robust ordered Ramsey numbers of regular graphs (aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[78], Source item 32, Section: Ordered Ramsey numbers, Workshop: Graph Ramsey theory, https://www.overleaf.com/read/mnvcscjjysvg).

articles.title: Ordered Ramsey number
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $H$ on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with a strict total
order $\lt _H$ on its vertices, the ordered Ramsey number $r_<(H, \lt _H)$ is the least natural number
$N$ with the ordered Ramsey property for $(H, \lt _H)$, that is, such that every red/blue colouring
of the edges of the complete graph on $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ with its natural order contains a
monochromatic ordered copy of $(H, \lt _H)$. It is $0$ if no such $N$ exists.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0079] Order-robust ordered Ramsey numbers of regular graphs (aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[78], Source item 32, Section: Ordered Ramsey numbers, Workshop: Graph Ramsey theory, https://www.overleaf.com/read/mnvcscjjysvg).

articles.title: Ordered Ramsey property
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with a strict
total order $\lt _H$ on its vertices. A natural number $N$ has the ordered Ramsey property for
$(H, \lt _H)$ when every simple graph $G$ on $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ contains a red ordered copy of
$(H, \lt _H)$ or admits a blue ordered copy of $(H, \lt _H)$. Equivalently, every red/blue colouring of
the edges of the complete graph on $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ with its natural order, with red edges
those of $G$, contains a monochromatic ordered copy of $(H, \lt _H)$.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0079] Order-robust ordered Ramsey numbers of regular graphs (aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[78], Source item 32, Section: Ordered Ramsey numbers, Workshop: Graph Ramsey theory, https://www.overleaf.com/read/mnvcscjjysvg).

articles.title: Rödl's question on Ramsey graphs that are locally trees of triangles
articles.statement:
This is the
statement that for every natural number $\ell$ there is a finite graph $G$ with at least $\ell$
vertices such that $G \to_2 K_3$ (every colouring of the edges of $G$ with two colours contains
a monochromatic triangle) and $G$ is locally a tree of triangles on $\ell$ vertices: for every
set $S$ of exactly $\ell$ vertices of $G$, some tree of triangles on the vertex set of $G$
contains every edge of $G$ with both endpoints in $S$.

Posed as an open question, it has been answered in the affirmative.

## Sources

- AIM-COMBINATORICS-0056, aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[55]: for every `ℓ`, does there exist a graph `G →₂ K₃` which on every `ℓ` vertices induces a subgraph of a tree of triangles.

articles.title: Ramsey graphs for the triangle that are locally trees of triangles
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$\ell$ there is a finite graph $G$ with at least $\ell$ vertices such that $G \to_2 K_3$, that is,
every colouring of the edges of $G$ with two colours contains a monochromatic triangle, and such
that for every set $S$ of exactly $\ell$ vertices of $G$, some tree of triangles on the vertex set
of $G$ contains every edge of $G$ with both endpoints in $S$.

This follows from Reiher and Rödl's girth Ramsey theorem (Theorem 1.6 with $F = K_3$, $r = 2$,
$n = \ell$), which gives a graph $H$ with $H \to_2 K_3$ in which every set of at most $\ell$
vertices induces a partial $K_3$-forest; such graphs have treewidth at most $2$, hence lie in
trees of triangles ($2$-trees).

## Sources

- C. Reiher and V. Rödl, The girth Ramsey theorem, arXiv:2308.15589, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.15589.

articles.title: Minimum degree of minimal Ramsey graphs for the triangle (Guo–Warnke)
articles.statement:
Let $s_r(K_3)$ be
the least minimum degree of a graph that is $r$-Ramsey-minimal for the triangle, with
$s_r(K_3) = 0$ if there is no such graph, as defined for the conjecture. Then
$s_r(K_3) = \Theta(r^2 \log r)$ as the natural number $r$ tends to infinity, where $\log$ is the
natural logarithm: there are constants $c, C > 0$ such that
$c \, r^2 \log r \le s_r(K_3) \le C \, r^2 \log r$ for all sufficiently large $r$.

Resolved true: Guo and Warnke (Packing nearly optimal Ramsey R(3,t) graphs, arXiv:1711.05877)
prove this, confirming the conjecture of Fox, Grinshpun, Liebenau, Person and Szabó.

## Sources

- H. Guo and L. Warnke, Packing nearly optimal Ramsey R(3,t) graphs, arXiv:1711.05877, https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05877.

articles.title: Minimum-degree conjecture for minimal Ramsey graphs of the triangle
articles.statement:
The statement that
$s_r(K_3) = \Theta(r^2 \log r)$ as the natural number $r$ tends to infinity, where $s_r(K_3)$ is
the least minimum degree of a graph that is $r$-Ramsey-minimal for the triangle ($0$ if there is
none) and $\log$ is the natural logarithm: there are constants $c, C > 0$ such that
$c \, r^2 \log r \le s_r(K_3) \le C \, r^2 \log r$ for all sufficiently large $r$.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0060], `aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[59]`, Source item 13, Section Ramsey minimal graphs, Workshop Graph Ramsey theory, Canonical tag conjecture.

articles.title: Minimum degree of a finite graph
articles.statement:
A graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ has
minimum degree $d$ when every vertex of $G$ has at least $d$ neighbours and some vertex of $G$ has
exactly $d$ neighbours; in particular $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0060], `aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[59]`, Source item 13, Section Ramsey minimal graphs, Workshop Graph Ramsey theory.

articles.title: Graphs that are locally trees of triangles
articles.statement:
A graph $G$ on a vertex set $V$ is locally a
tree of triangles on $\ell$ vertices if for every set $S$ of exactly $\ell$ vertices there is a
tree of triangles on $V$ that contains every edge of $G$ with both endpoints in $S$.

## Sources

- AIM-COMBINATORICS-0056, aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[55]: on every `ℓ` vertices `G` induces a subgraph of a tree of triangles.

articles.title: Ramsey-minimal graphs for the triangle
articles.statement:
A graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$
is $r$-Ramsey-minimal for the triangle when $G$ is $r$-Ramsey for the triangle, no proper spanning
subgraph of $G$ (a graph on the same vertices whose edges are edges of $G$, missing at least one
of them) is $r$-Ramsey for the triangle, and for every vertex $x$ it is false that every symmetric
colouring of the ordered pairs of vertices with $r$ colours admits a triangle of $G$ avoiding $x$
whose three edges have the same colour.

Given the first two conditions, the last one says exactly that $G$ has no isolated vertices.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0060], `aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[59]`, Source item 13, Section Ramsey minimal graphs, Workshop Graph Ramsey theory.

articles.title: Ramsey property for the triangle after deleting a vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on the vertex
set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, $r$ a natural number and $x$ a vertex. The property holds when every
colouring $c$ of the ordered pairs of vertices with $r$ colours that is symmetric
($c(a, b) = c(b, a)$) admits three distinct vertices $u, v, w$, all different from $x$, that form a
triangle in $G$ with $c(u, v) = c(v, w) = c(w, u)$.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0060], `aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[59]`, Source item 13, Section Ramsey minimal graphs, Workshop Graph Ramsey theory.

articles.title: Ramsey graphs for the triangle
articles.statement:
A graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ is
$r$-Ramsey for the triangle when every colouring $c$ of the ordered pairs of vertices with $r$
colours that is symmetric ($c(a, b) = c(b, a)$) admits three distinct vertices $u, v, w$ that form
a triangle in $G$ with $c(u, v) = c(v, w) = c(w, u)$.

For $r \ge 1$ this says that every colouring of the edges of $G$ with $r$ colours has a
monochromatic triangle.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0060], `aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[59]`, Source item 13, Section Ramsey minimal graphs, Workshop Graph Ramsey theory.

articles.title: Trees of triangles
articles.statement:
The trees of triangles on a vertex set $V$ are the graphs on $V$
built recursively as follows. A graph whose edges are exactly the three edges of a triangle on
distinct vertices $a, b, c$ is a tree of triangles. If $H_0$ is a tree of triangles, $xy$ is an
edge of $H_0$, and $z$ is a vertex different from $x$ and $y$ with no neighbours in $H_0$, then
the graph obtained from $H_0$ by joining $z$ to $x$ and to $y$ is a tree of triangles.

## Sources

- AIM-COMBINATORICS-0056, aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[55]: any graph built recursively by starting with a triangle, and then adding two edges at a time that forms a single new triangle with an existing edge.

articles.title: Graphs that arrow the triangle
articles.statement:
A graph $G$ arrows the triangle in two colours, written
$G \to_2 K_3$, if every colouring of the edges of $G$ with two colours contains a monochromatic
triangle: three distinct pairwise adjacent vertices whose three edges all have the same colour.

## Sources

- AIM-COMBINATORICS-0056, aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[55]: `G` with `2` colors arrows `K₃`, i.e. every 2-coloring of the edges of `G` contains a monochromatic triangle.

articles.title: Least minimum degree of Ramsey-minimal graphs for the triangle
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$,
$s_r(K_3)$ is the least natural number $d$ such that, for some $n$, some graph on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ is $r$-Ramsey-minimal for the triangle and has minimum degree $d$; if no
such graph exists, $s_r(K_3) = 0$.

## Sources

- [AIM-COMBINATORICS-0060], `aim-combinatorics-notes.json notes[59]`, Source item 13, Section Ramsey minimal graphs, Workshop Graph Ramsey theory, Conjecture `$s_r(3) = \Theta(r^2 \log r)$`.

articles.title: Ramsey–Turán problem for $K_4$ (Erdős Problem 22)
articles.statement:
For a graph $G$ write $\alpha(G)$ for
its independence number and $e(G)$ for its number of edges, and call $G$ $K_4$-free if it has no
four pairwise adjacent vertices. The statement is the conjunction of the following four
assertions.

(i) For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, there is a $K_4$-free graph
$G$ on $n$ vertices with $\alpha(G) \le \varepsilon n$ and $e(G) \ge n^2/8$.

(ii) (Szemerédi's upper bound.) For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such
that, for all sufficiently large $n$, every $K_4$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with
$\alpha(G) \le \delta n$ satisfies $e(G) \le (1/8 + \varepsilon) n^2$.

(iii) (Bollobás–Erdős lower bound.) For all real $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\delta > 0$ and all
sufficiently large $n$, there is a $K_4$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with
$\alpha(G) \le \delta n$ and $e(G) \ge (1/8 - \varepsilon) n^2$.

(iv) (Fox–Loh–Zhao quantitative form.) There is a real $C > 0$ such that, for all sufficiently
large $n$, there is a $K_4$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $e(G) \ge n^2/8$ and
$\alpha(G) \le C n (\log \log n)^{3/2} / (\log n)^{1/2}$.

articles.title: Resolution of Erdős Problem 22 (Fox–Loh–Zhao)
articles.statement:
For a graph $G$ write $\alpha(G)$ for its
independence number and $e(G)$ for its number of edges, and call $G$ $K_4$-free if it has no four
pairwise adjacent vertices. All four of the following assertions hold.

(i) For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, there is a $K_4$-free graph
$G$ on $n$ vertices with $\alpha(G) \le \varepsilon n$ and $e(G) \ge n^2/8$.

(ii) (Szemerédi's upper bound.) For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such
that, for all sufficiently large $n$, every $K_4$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with
$\alpha(G) \le \delta n$ satisfies $e(G) \le (1/8 + \varepsilon) n^2$.

(iii) (Bollobás–Erdős lower bound.) For all real $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\delta > 0$ and all
sufficiently large $n$, there is a $K_4$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with
$\alpha(G) \le \delta n$ and $e(G) \ge (1/8 - \varepsilon) n^2$.

(iv) (Fox–Loh–Zhao quantitative form.) There is a real $C > 0$ such that, for all sufficiently
large $n$, there is a $K_4$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $e(G) \ge n^2/8$ and
$\alpha(G) \le C n (\log \log n)^{3/2} / (\log n)^{1/2}$.

## Sources

- Jacob Fox, Po-Shen Loh, and Yufei Zhao, The critical window for the classical Ramsey-Turán problem, Combinatorica 35 (2015), 435–476.

articles.title: EP-533 is false: dense $K_5$-free graphs without linear triangle-free sets
articles.statement:
There is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that for every real $c > 0$ there are infinitely many $n$ for which some
$K_5$-free simple graph on $n$ vertices has at least $\delta n^2$ edges and yet has no
triangle-free set of at least $c n$ vertices (a set of vertices no three of which are pairwise
adjacent). In other words, the EP-533 conjecture fails.

Balogh and Lenz (2011) first gave $K_5$-free graphs of positive density with no linear
triangle-free set; Liu, Reiher, Sharifzadeh and Staden (Theorem 1.1 with $p = 3$, $\ell = 1$)
give $K_5$-free graphs on $2n$ vertices with $(1/3 - o(1))n^2$ edges whose largest
triangle-free set has $o(n)$ vertices, refuting $\delta = 1/24$.

## Sources

- Hong Liu, Christian Reiher, Maryam Sharifzadeh and Katherine Staden, Geometric constructions for Ramsey–Turán theory, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), arXiv:2103.10423, https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.10423.

articles.title: EP-533: linear triangle-free sets in dense $K_5$-free graphs
articles.statement:
The conjecture states that
for every real $\delta > 0$ there is a real $c > 0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$,
every $K_5$-free simple graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\delta n^2$ edges has a
triangle-free set of at least $c n$ vertices (a set of vertices no three of which are pairwise
adjacent).

articles.title: The empty graph meets the Ramsey–Turán edge bound for $K_4$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$
and every real $\varepsilon > 0$, the empty graph on $n$ vertices has no four pairwise adjacent
vertices, and its number of edges (namely $0$) is at most $(1/8 + \varepsilon) n^2$.

articles.title: Exoo's lower bound for $R(3, 10)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(3, 10)$ is at
least $40$.

## Sources

- G. Exoo, *On two classical Ramsey numbers of the form R(3,n)*, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 2 (1989), 488–490; Radziszowski, DS1; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey3/README.md`.

articles.title: Exoo's lower bound for $R(5, 5)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(5, 5)$ is at
least $43$.

Thus some simple graph on $42$ vertices contains no $K_5$ and no independent set of size $5$.

## Sources

- G. Exoo, *A lower bound for R(5,5)*, J. Graph Theory 13 (1989), 97–98; Radziszowski, DS1; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey/README.md`.

articles.title: The Angeltveit–McKay upper bound for $R(5, 5)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number
$R(5, 5)$ is at most $46$.

## Sources

- V. Angeltveit and B. D. McKay, *R(5,5) ≤ 46*, arXiv:2409.15709 (2024); listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey/README.md`.

articles.title: The value of $R(4, 4)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(4, 4)$ equals $18$.

## Sources

- R. E. Greenwood and A. M. Gleason, *Combinatorial relations and chromatic graphs*, Canad. J. Math. 7 (1955), 1–7; S. P. Radziszowski, *Small Ramsey Numbers*, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS1; listed in leansolving/SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey/README.md`.

articles.title: The value of $R(3, 8)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(3, 8)$ equals $28$.

## Sources

- C. Grinstead and S. Roberts, *On the Ramsey numbers R(3,8) and R(3,9)*, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 33 (1982), 27–51 (lower bound); B. D. McKay and Zhang Ke Min, *The value of the Ramsey number R(3,8)*, J. Graph Theory 16 (1992), 99–105 (upper bound); Radziszowski, DS1; OEIS A000791; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey3/README.md`.

articles.title: The value of $R(3, 5)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(3, 5)$ equals $14$.

## Sources

- Greenwood and Gleason (1955), op. cit.; Radziszowski, DS1; OEIS A000791; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey3/README.md`.

articles.title: The value of $R(3, 9)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(3, 9)$ equals $36$.

## Sources

- Kalbfleisch (1966), op. cit. (lower bound); Grinstead and Roberts (1982), op. cit. (upper bound); Radziszowski, DS1; OEIS A000791; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey3/README.md`.

articles.title: The value of $R(3, 7)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(3, 7)$ equals $23$.

## Sources

- J. G. Kalbfleisch, *Chromatic graphs and Ramsey's theorem*, Ph.D. thesis, University of Waterloo (1966) (lower bound); J. E. Graver and J. Yackel, *Some graph theoretic results associated with Ramsey's theorem*, J. Combin. Theory 4 (1968), 125–175 (upper bound); Radziszowski, DS1; OEIS A000791; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey3/README.md`.

articles.title: The value of $R(3, 6)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(3, 6)$ equals $18$.

## Sources

- G. Kéry, *On a theorem of Ramsey*, Mat. Lapok 15 (1964), 204–224 (upper bound), with the lower bound from Kalbfleisch (1966); Radziszowski, DS1; OEIS A000791; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey3/README.md`.

articles.title: Angeltveit's upper bound for $R(3, 10)$
articles.statement:
The classical Ramsey number $R(3, 10)$
is at most $41$.

## Sources

- V. Angeltveit, *R(3,10) ≤ 41*, arXiv:2401.00392 (2024); Radziszowski, DS1; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Ramsey3/README.md`.

articles.title: Caro–Wei bound for the independence number
articles.statement:
For every finite simple graph $G$, the
independence number of $G$ is at least $\sum_{v} \frac{1}{\deg(v) + 1}$, the sum running over all
vertices $v$ of $G$.

articles.title: Caro–Wei bound
articles.statement:
Every finite graph has an independent set of size at
least the sum over its vertices of the reciprocal of one more than the
degree.

articles.title: Dominating sets are at least as large as the domination number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph
on a finite vertex set. If $S$ is a dominating set of $G$, then the domination number of $G$ is at
most the number of elements of $S$.

articles.title: Domination number
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the domination number of
$G$ is the least number of elements of a dominating set of $G$.

articles.title: A minimum dominating set exists
articles.statement:
Every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set has a
dominating set whose number of elements equals the domination number of $G$.

articles.title: A minimum independent dominating set exists
articles.statement:
Every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set
has an independent dominating set whose number of elements equals the independent domination
number of $G$.

articles.title: Existence of independent dominating sets
articles.statement:
Every finite graph has an independent dominating
set.

articles.title: Independent dominating sets are at least as large as the independent domination number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set. If $S$ is an independent dominating set of $G$,
then the independent domination number of $G$ is at most the number of elements of $S$.

articles.title: Independent domination number
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the
independent domination number of $G$ is the least number of elements of an independent dominating
set of $G$.

articles.title: Dominating set
articles.statement:
A set $S$ of vertices of a simple graph $G$ dominates $G$ when every vertex
of $G$ lies in $S$ or is adjacent to some vertex of $S$.

articles.title: Independent dominating set
articles.statement:
A set $S$ of vertices of a simple graph $G$ is an independent
dominating set of $G$ when no two vertices of $S$ are adjacent and $S$ dominates $G$.

articles.title: Recursion for rook placements covering all rows and columns
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$n, m \ge 1$ and $k$, let $E_{a,b}(k)$ denote the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the
$a \times b$ board that contain a cell in every row and a cell in every column. Then

$$E_{n,m}(k) = \binom{nm}{k} -
\sum_{(r,c) \ne (0,0)} \binom{n}{r} \binom{m}{c} E_{n-r,m-c}(k),$$

where the sum runs over all pairs $(r, c) \ne (0, 0)$ with $0 \le r \le n$ and $0 \le c \le m$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, "Domination Polynomial of the Rook Graph", Theorem 2 (`thm:E-recursion`).

articles.title: Rook placements covering all rows and columns
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $m$ and $k$,
$E_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that contain a
cell in every row and a cell in every column (Mertens' $E_{n,m}(k)$).

articles.title: Dominating rook placements at high density
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n, m \ge 1$ and $k$ with
$k > nm - n - m - \min(n, m) + 2$, let $d_{n,m}(k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of cells
of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board. Then

$$d_{n,m}(k) = \binom{nm}{k} - nm \binom{(n-1)(m-1)}{k}.$$

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, "Domination Polynomial of the Rook Graph", Corollary 3 (`cor:high-density`).

articles.title: Dominating rook placements via covering placements
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n, m \ge 1$ and
$k$, let $d_{n,m}(k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that
are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board, and let $E_{a,b}(k)$ be the number of
$k$-element sets of cells of the $a \times b$ board that contain a cell in every row and a cell
in every column. Then

$$d_{n,m}(k) = \binom{nm}{k} -
\sum_{r=1}^{n} \sum_{c=1}^{m} \binom{n}{r} \binom{m}{c} E_{n-r,m-c}(k).$$

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, "Domination Polynomial of the Rook Graph", Theorem 1 (`thm:R-E`).

articles.title: Dominating rook placements
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $m$ and $k$, $d_{n,m}(k)$ is the
number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook
graph on that board (Mertens' $d_{R_{n,m}}(k)$).

articles.title: Symmetric formula for the rook domination polynomial
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n, m \ge 1$,
the rook domination polynomial $D_{n,m}(x)$ of the $n \times m$ board, an integer polynomial,
satisfies

$$D_{n,m}(x) = ((1+x)^n - 1)^m + ((1+x)^m - 1)^n -
(-1)^{n+m} \sum_{\ell=0}^{n} \sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^{k+\ell}
\binom{n}{\ell} \binom{m}{k} (1+x)^{k\ell}.$$

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, "Domination Polynomial of the Rook Graph", Corollary 5 (`cor:domination-polynomial`).

articles.title: Single-sum formula for the rook domination polynomial
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n, m \ge 1$,
the rook domination polynomial $D_{n,m}(x)$ of the $n \times m$ board, an integer polynomial,
satisfies

$$D_{n,m}(x) = ((1+x)^n - 1)^m -
(-1)^m \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} (-1)^k \binom{m}{k} ((1+x)^k - 1)^n.$$

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, "Domination Polynomial of the Rook Graph", Theorem 4 (`thm:domination-polynomial`).

articles.title: Domination polynomial of the rook graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the rook
domination polynomial of the $n \times m$ board is the integer polynomial
$D_{n,m}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{nm} d_{n,m}(k)\, x^k$, where $d_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element
sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that
board.

articles.title: Dominating sets of the rook graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, a finite set $S$ of
cells of the $n \times m$ board dominates the rook graph on that board if and only if for every
cell $(i, j)$, some cell of $S$ lies in row $i$ or some cell of $S$ lies in column $j$.

articles.title: Rook graph
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the rook graph on the $n \times m$ board is the
simple graph whose vertices are the cells $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which
two cells are adjacent if and only if they are distinct and lie in the same row (same $i$) or the
same column (same $j$).

articles.title: All-covered signature
articles.statement:
For a graph $R$ (the row), the all-covered signature
$\sigma_\bullet$ of $R$ is the signature that gives every vertex of $R$ the state covered; it
is a signature because it has no uncovered vertex.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Almost dominating polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a finite graph (the row), $n$ a natural number
and $\sigma$ an assignment of a domination state to each vertex of $R$. Let $H$ be the box
product of $R$ with the path on the vertices $0, \dots, n$, so that the last row of $H$ consists
of the vertices $(i, n)$. Relative to a vertex set $S$ of $H$, a vertex is occupied if it lies in
$S$, covered if it lies outside $S$ but is adjacent to a vertex of $S$, and uncovered otherwise.
The almost dominating polynomial $G^\sigma(z)$ is the polynomial $\sum_S z^{|S|}$ with integer
coefficients, the sum running over the vertex sets $S$ of $H$ such that no vertex of $H$ outside
the last row is uncovered and every vertex $(i, n)$ of the last row has state $\sigma(i)$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 2.

articles.title: Compatible row signatures
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a graph (the row) and let $\sigma$ and $\tau$
assign a domination state (uncovered, covered or occupied) to each vertex of $R$. The new row
$\tau$ is compatible with the previous row $\sigma$ when, for every vertex $i$ of $R$: if
$\sigma(i)$ is uncovered then $\tau(i)$ is occupied; if $\sigma(i)$ is occupied then $\tau(i)$
is not uncovered; and if $\tau(i)$ is covered then $\sigma(i)$ is occupied or some neighbour $j$
of $i$ in $R$ has $\tau(j)$ occupied.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 5.

articles.title: Cylinder domination polynomial as a sum of almost dominating polynomials
articles.statement:
For all
natural numbers $m$ and $n$, let $C_m$ be the cycle graph on the vertices $0, \dots, m - 1$, in
which distinct $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $i - j \equiv \pm 1 \pmod m$, and let $P_{n+1}$ be
the path on the vertices $0, \dots, n$. Then the domination polynomial of the cylinder
$C_m \mathbin{\square} P_{n+1}$ equals $\sum_\sigma G^\sigma(z)$, the sum running over the
signatures $\sigma$ of the row graph $C_m$ with no uncovered vertex, where $G^\sigma(z)$ is the
almost dominating polynomial of $C_m$ with $n + 1$ rows and last-row state $\sigma$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Lemma 4 (`jis-2024-24.7.6-lem-4`).

articles.title: Transfer-matrix formula for the domination polynomial of the cylinder
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $m$ and $n$, let $C_m$ be the cycle graph on the vertices $0, \dots, m - 1$, in which
distinct $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $i - j \equiv \pm 1 \pmod m$, and let $P_n$ be the path on
the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$. Let $\bar A$ be the domination transfer matrix of the row graph
$C_m$, indexed by the signatures of $C_m$, and let $\sigma_\bullet$ be the all-covered signature.
Then the domination polynomial of the cylinder $C_m \mathbin{\square} P_n$ is

$$\sum_\sigma (\bar A^n)_{\sigma, \sigma_\bullet},$$

the sum running over the signatures $\sigma$ of $C_m$ with no uncovered vertex.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Theorem 7 (`jis-2024-24.7.6-thm-7`).

articles.title: The domination polynomial at one counts dominating sets
articles.statement:
For every finite graph $G$, the
value at $1$ of the domination polynomial of $G$ equals the number of dominating sets of $G$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Grid domination polynomial as a sum of almost dominating polynomials
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $m$ and $n$, let $P_k$ denote the path on the vertices $0, \dots, k - 1$. Then the
domination polynomial of the grid $P_m \mathbin{\square} P_{n+1}$ equals $\sum_\sigma G^\sigma(z)$,
the sum running over the signatures $\sigma$ of the row graph $P_m$ with no uncovered vertex,
where $G^\sigma(z)$ is the almost dominating polynomial of $P_m$ with $n + 1$ rows and last-row
state $\sigma$.

The grid is taken with at least one row, so that the last row carrying $\sigma$ exists.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Lemma 4 (`jis-2024-24.7.6-lem-4`).

articles.title: Transfer-matrix formula for the domination polynomial of the grid
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $m$ and $n$, let $P_k$ denote the path on the vertices $0, \dots, k - 1$, let $A$ be the
domination transfer matrix of the row graph $P_m$, indexed by the signatures of $P_m$, and let
$\sigma_\bullet$ be the all-covered signature. Then the domination polynomial of the grid
$P_m \mathbin{\square} P_n$ is

$$\sum_\sigma (A^n)_{\sigma, \sigma_\bullet},$$

the sum running over the signatures $\sigma$ of $P_m$ with no uncovered vertex.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Theorem 7 (`jis-2024-24.7.6-thm-7`).

articles.title: Transfer-matrix formula for the domination polynomial of the torus
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $m$ and $n$ with $n \ge 1$, let $C_k$ denote the cycle graph on the vertices
$0, \dots, k - 1$, in which distinct $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $i - j \equiv \pm 1 \pmod k$,
and let $\bar A$ be the domination transfer matrix of the row graph $C_m$. Then the domination
polynomial of the torus $C_m \mathbin{\square} C_n$ equals the trace of $\bar A^n$.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is needed: for $n = 0$ the trace counts the signatures of $C_m$, while
the torus $C_m \mathbin{\square} C_0$ has no vertices, so its domination polynomial is $1$. For
$n = 1$ and $n = 2$ the cycle $C_n$ is a single vertex and a single edge respectively.

## Sources
