- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Theorem 8 (`jis-2024-24.7.6-thm-8`).

articles.title: Domination polynomial
articles.statement:
For a finite graph $G$, the domination polynomial of $G$ is the
polynomial $\sum_S z^{|S|}$ with integer coefficients, the sum running over the dominating sets
$S$ of $G$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Signatures of a row graph
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $R$ on a vertex set $V$ (the row), a
signature of $R$ is a map $\sigma$ assigning to each vertex of $V$ a domination state (uncovered,
covered or occupied) such that $\sigma$ is a domination signature for $R$, that is, no uncovered
vertex is adjacent in $R$ to an occupied vertex. This is the type of all signatures of $R$; when
$R$ is a cycle they are the paper's cyclic signatures.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 3.

articles.title: Domination states
articles.statement:
A domination state is one of three labels: uncovered, covered or
occupied.

Relative to a set $S$ of vertices of a graph, a vertex is occupied if it lies in $S$, covered if
it lies outside $S$ but is adjacent to a vertex of $S$, and uncovered otherwise.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 1.

articles.title: Transfer matrix column of the all-covered signature
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex set (the row), let $A$ be its domination transfer matrix, with entries in
$\mathbb{Z}[z]$, and let $\sigma_\bullet$ be its all-covered signature. For every signature $\tau$
of $R$, the entry $A_{\tau\sigma_\bullet}$ equals $z^{\operatorname{occ}(\tau)}$, where
$\operatorname{occ}(\tau)$ is the number of occupied vertices of $\tau$, if every covered vertex of
$\tau$ is adjacent in $R$ to an occupied vertex of $\tau$, and equals $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Domination transfer matrix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set (the row).
The transfer matrix $A$ of $R$ is the matrix with entries in $\mathbb{Z}[z]$, rows indexed by the
new signature $\tau$ and columns by the old signature $\sigma$, both ranging over the signatures
of $R$, whose entry $A_{\tau\sigma}$ is $z^{\operatorname{occ}(\tau)}$ if $\tau$ is compatible
with $\sigma$ and $0$ otherwise; here $\operatorname{occ}(\tau)$ is the number of occupied
vertices of $\tau$. When $R$ is the cycle on $m$ vertices this is Mertens' matrix $\bar A$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 6.

articles.title: Dominating sets have no uncovered vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and $S$ a finite set
of vertices of $G$. Then $S$ dominates $G$ if and only if no vertex of $G$ has domination state
uncovered relative to $S$ in $G$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 1.

articles.title: Domination signature
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$ (the row). A map
$\sigma$ assigning to each vertex of $V$ a domination state (uncovered, covered or occupied) is a
signature for $R$ if no uncovered vertex is adjacent in $R$ to an occupied vertex: for all
vertices $i, j$ adjacent in $R$, it is not the case that $\sigma(i)$ is uncovered and $\sigma(j)$
is occupied.

When $R$ is the path on $m$ vertices, signatures are the strings of length $m$ in which no
uncovered entry is next to an occupied one; when $R$ is the cycle on $m$ vertices the condition
also applies to the first and last entries (the paper's cyclic signatures).

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 3.

articles.title: The all-covered signature has no occupied vertex
articles.statement:
For every simple graph $R$ on a finite
vertex set, the number of occupied vertices of the all-covered signature of $R$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Number of occupied vertices
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set and let $\sigma$ assign a domination
state (uncovered, covered or occupied) to each element of $V$. The occupied count
$\operatorname{occ}(\sigma)$ is the number of elements $i \in V$ such that $\sigma(i)$ is occupied.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 6.

articles.title: A vertex is occupied exactly when it lies in the set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph, $S$ a
finite set of vertices of $G$ and $v$ a vertex of $G$. Then the domination state of $v$ relative
to $S$ in $G$ is occupied if and only if $v \in S$.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 1.

articles.title: Domination state of a vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph, $S$ a finite set of vertices of
$G$ and $v$ a vertex of $G$. The domination state of $v$ relative to $S$ in $G$ is occupied if
$v \in S$, covered if $v \notin S$ and $v$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $S$, and
uncovered otherwise.

## Sources

- Stephan Mertens, *Domination Polynomials of the Grid, the Cylinder, the Torus, and the King Graph*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.6, Definition 1.

articles.title: Characteristic vector of an independent set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex type
$V$ and let $A$ be a finite independent set of $G$. The characteristic vector of $A$ is the
Boolean function on $V$ that sends a vertex $v$ to true if $v \in A$ and to false otherwise.

articles.title: Pairing of Boolean vectors along a relation
articles.statement:
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite types, let $R$ be a
relation between $V$ and $W$, and let $a$ and $b$ be Boolean functions on $V$ and on $W$. The
pairing of $a$ and $b$ along $R$ is the natural number of pairs $(v, w) \in V \times W$ such that
$R(v, w)$ holds and both $a(v)$ and $b(w)$ are true.

articles.title: Transfer matrix of a generalized Zykov sum
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on finite
vertex types $V$ and $W$, and let $R$ be a relation between $V$ and $W$. The transfer matrix of
$G$ and $H$ along $R$ is indexed by pairs $(A, B)$ where $A$ is a finite independent set of $G$
and $B$ is a finite independent set of $H$. Its entry at $(A, B)$ is the Boolean value that is
true exactly when the pairing along $R$ of the characteristic vectors of $A$ and $B$ is zero,
that is, when there are no $v \in A$ and $w \in B$ with $R(v, w)$.

Only the loopless case is covered: $G$ and $H$ are simple graphs, whereas the source construction
of Bautista-Ramos and Guillén-Galván also allows loops.

articles.title: Zero indicator of a natural number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $z$, the zero indicator of $z$ is
the Boolean value that is true if $z = 0$ and false otherwise.

articles.title: Evaluating the independence polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set
$V$, and let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence polynomial,
where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. Then for every element
$x$ of a commutative ring $R$, the value of $I(G)$ at $x$ is $\sum_S x^{|S|}$, the sum running
over all independent sets $S \subseteq V$ of $G$, the empty set included.

articles.title: The two definitions of claw-free agree
articles.statement:
A simple graph on a finite vertex set is a
claw-free finite graph if and only if it is a claw-free graph in the sense defined for graphs on
arbitrary vertex sets.

articles.title: Claw-free finite graphs have no induced claw
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex set. Then $G$ is claw-free if and only if the claw $K_{1,3}$, the star graph on four
vertices whose center is adjacent to the other three, is not an induced subgraph of $G$, that is,
there is no injective map from its vertices to those of $G$ that preserves both adjacency and
nonadjacency.

articles.title: Claw-free finite graph
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is claw-free if it
has no induced claw $K_{1,3}$: there are no vertices $c, \ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3 \in V$ such that
$\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ are pairwise distinct, each is adjacent to $c$ and different from $c$,
and no two of them are adjacent.

## Sources

- Moussa Benoumhani, "On the Modes of the Independence Polynomial of the Centipede," Journal of Integer Sequences 15 (2012), Article 12.5.1, unnumbered Chudnovsky–Seymour theorem, lines 142–144, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL15/Benoumhani/benoumhani8.tex quoting M. Chudnovsky and P. Seymour, "The roots of the independence polynomial of a clawfree graph," J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 97 (2007), 350–357 (biblio lines 499–501).

articles.title: Independence polynomial of the edgeless graph
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set. For a simple
graph $G$ on $V$, let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence
polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. If $G$ is the
graph on $V$ with no edges, then $I(G) = (1 + X)^{|V|}$.

articles.title: Coefficients of the independence polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex
set $V$, and let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence
polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. Then for every
natural number $k$, the coefficient of $X^k$ in $I(G)$ is the number of independent sets of $G$
with exactly $k$ vertices.

articles.title: Chudnovsky–Seymour theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a claw-free simple graph on a finite vertex set
$V$, and let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence polynomial,
where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. Then $I(G)$, viewed as a
polynomial with real coefficients, splits over $\mathbb{R}$: it is a constant times a product of
linear factors $X - r$ with $r \in \mathbb{R}$, so all its roots are real.

## Sources

- Moussa Benoumhani, "On the Modes of the Independence Polynomial of the Centipede," Journal of Integer Sequences 15 (2012), Article 12.5.1, unnumbered Chudnovsky–Seymour theorem, lines 142–144, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL15/Benoumhani/benoumhani8.tex quoting M. Chudnovsky and P. Seymour, "The roots of the independence polynomial of a clawfree graph," J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 97 (2007), 350–357 (biblio lines 499–501).

articles.title: Independence polynomial of the complete graph
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set. For a simple
graph $G$ on $V$, let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence
polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. If $G$ is the
complete graph on $V$, then $I(G) = 1 + |V|\,X$.

articles.title: Claw-free graphs have no induced claw
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on an arbitrary vertex
set. Then $G$ is claw-free if and only if the claw $K_{1,3}$, the star graph on four vertices
whose center is adjacent to the other three, is not an induced subgraph of $G$, that is, there is
no injective map from its vertices to those of $G$ that preserves both adjacency and
nonadjacency.

articles.title: Claw-free graph
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ on a vertex set $V$, not necessarily finite, is
claw-free if it has no induced claw $K_{1,3}$: there are no vertices
$c, \ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3 \in V$ such that $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ are pairwise distinct, each
is adjacent to $c$ and different from $c$, and no two of them are adjacent.

articles.title: Sizes of maximal cliques
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$, this is the set of natural numbers $k$
such that some finite clique of $G$ with exactly $k$ vertices is maximal under inclusion among
the finite cliques of $G$, that is, no finite clique of $G$ strictly contains it.

An infinite maximal clique of $G$ contributes no size to this set.

articles.title: Triangles containing an edge
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and an edge
$uv$ of $G$, this is the finite set of triangles of $G$ that contain the edge $uv$, where a
triangle is the vertex set of a $3$-clique of $G$; that is, the $3$-cliques of $G$ containing
both $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Outside vertices see an empty or odd part of an odd independent set
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be an odd
independent set of a simple graph $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex with $v \notin S$. Then the set of
neighbours of $v$ that lie in $S$ is either empty or has an odd number of elements.

articles.title: Outside vertices have finitely many neighbours in an odd independent set
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be an
odd independent set of a simple graph $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex with $v \notin S$. Then only
finitely many neighbours of $v$ lie in $S$.

articles.title: Odd independent sets are independent
articles.statement:
If $S$ is an odd independent set of a simple graph
$G$, then $S$ is an independent set of $G$: no two distinct vertices of $S$ are adjacent.

articles.title: The empty set is odd independent
articles.statement: The empty set is odd independent in any simple graph.

articles.title: Singletons are odd independent
articles.statement:
For every vertex $a$ of a simple graph $G$, the singleton
$\{a\}$ is odd independent in $G$.

articles.title: Odd independent set
articles.statement:
A set $S$ of vertices of a simple graph $G$ is odd independent if
$S$ is an independent set of $G$ and, for every vertex $v \notin S$, the set of neighbours of $v$
that lie in $S$ is finite and is either empty or has an odd number of elements.

articles.title: Berge's lemma for matching subgraphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and
let $M$ be a matching subgraph of $G$, so that every vertex of $M$ is incident to exactly one
edge of $M$. Then $M$ has the maximum number of edges among all matching subgraphs of $G$ if and
only if there is no $M$-augmenting path: a path in $G$ of positive length between two distinct
vertices $u$ and $v$, neither of which is a vertex of $M$, whose consecutive edges alternate
between edges of $M$ and edges not in $M$.

articles.title: Berge's lemma
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $M$ be a matching
of $G$, that is, a finite set of edges of $G$ no two distinct members of which share a vertex.
Then $M$ has maximum cardinality among all matchings of $G$ if and only if there is no
$M$-augmenting path: a path in $G$ of positive length between two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$,
neither of which lies on an edge of $M$, whose consecutive edges alternate between edges of $M$
and edges not in $M$.

## Sources

- Wikipedia, Berge's theorem, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berge%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Kőnig's theorem on a finite vertex type
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a bipartite simple graph on a finite
vertex type $V$. Then there are a matching $M$ in $G$ and a vertex cover $C \subseteq V$ of $G$ such
that the number of edges of $M$ equals the number of vertices in $C$.

articles.title: Kőnig's theorem for finite bipartite graphs
articles.statement:
Every bipartite simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex
type $V$ has a matching $M$ and a vertex cover $C \subseteq V$ such that the number of edges of $M$
equals the number of vertices in $C$.

## Sources

- D. Kőnig (1931); J. Egerváry (1931) weighted form. It follows from `konig_matching_cover_general`; the instances `[DecidableEq V]` and `[DecidableRel G.Adj]` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Average degree of a finite graph
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ with
edge set $E$, the average degree of $G$ is the rational number $2|E|/|V|$; it equals $0$ when $V$
is empty.

articles.title: Negative answer to the matching cut and girth question
articles.statement:
It is not the case that for
every real number $d$ there is a natural number $g$ such that every simple graph on a finite
vertex set with at least two vertices, average degree less than $d$ and girth at least $g$ has a
matching cut. That is, there is a real number $d$ such that for every natural number $g$ some
simple graph on a finite vertex set with at least two vertices, average degree less than $d$ and
girth at least $g$ has no matching cut.

Feghali, Lucke, Paulusma and Ries (Lemma 5) construct, for every $g$, a connected 14-regular
bipartite graph of girth at least $g$ with no matching cut; these graphs give $d = 15$.

## Sources

- C. Feghali, F. Lucke, D. Paulusma and B. Ries, Matching Cuts in Graphs of High Girth and H-Free Graphs, ISAAC 2023, arXiv:2212.12317, https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.12317.

articles.title: Matching cut and girth question, affirmative form
articles.statement:
For every real number $d$ there is a
natural number $g$ such that every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set with at least two
vertices, whose average degree is less than $d$ and whose girth is at least $g$, has a matching
cut. An acyclic graph has infinite girth, so it meets the girth bound for every $g$.

## Sources

- [OPG-37364], Open Problem Garden, "Matching cut and girth".

articles.title: Matching cut
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ has a matching cut if some matching $M$ of $G$, that is,
a set of pairwise disjoint edges of $G$, is such that deleting the edges of $M$ from $G$ leaves
two vertices $u$ and $v$ that are not joined by any path. The matching may be empty, in which
case this says that $G$ itself has two vertices not joined by any path.

articles.title: Cut capacity
Flow across a cut
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set, $s, t \in V$, and
$f : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ a function conserved at every vertex $v \ne s, t$, that is,
$\sum_{u \in V} f(u, v) = \sum_{w \in V} f(v, w)$; no sign or capacity condition is imposed. Then
for every subset $S \subseteq V$ with $s \in S$ and $t \notin S$, the flow value
$\sum_{v \in V} f(s, v) - \sum_{u \in V} f(u, s)$ of $f$ equals
$\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \in V \setminus S} f(u, v) -
\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \in V \setminus S} f(v, u)$, the flow leaving $S$ minus the flow
entering $S$.

articles.title: Weak duality for flows and cuts
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set, $c : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$
a capacity function and $s, t \in V$. If $f$ is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ and $S$ is an
$s$-$t$ cut, then the flow value of $f$ is at most the capacity of $S$ for $c$.

articles.title: Flow value
articles.statement:
For a finite set $V$, a vertex $s \in V$ and a function
$f : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$, the value of $f$ is its net outflow from the source $s$,
$\sum_{v \in V} f(s, v) - \sum_{u \in V} f(u, s)$.

articles.title: Feasible flow
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set, $c : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ a capacity
function and $s, t \in V$. A function $f : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow
for $c$ if $0 \le f(u, v) \le c(u, v)$ for all $u, v \in V$ and $f$ is conserved at every vertex
$v \ne s, t$, that is, $\sum_{u \in V} f(u, v) = \sum_{w \in V} f(v, w)$.

articles.title: Source–sink cut
articles.statement:
For a finite set $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, an $s$-$t$ cut is a
subset $S \subseteq V$ with $s \in S$ and $t \notin S$.

articles.title: Max-flow min-cut theorem
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set, $c : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ a capacity
function with $c(u, v) \ge 0$ for all $u, v \in V$, and $s, t \in V$ with $s \ne t$. Then there is
a feasible $s$-$t$ flow $f$ for $c$ whose value is at least the value of every feasible $s$-$t$
flow for $c$ and at most the capacity of every $s$-$t$ cut, and there is an $s$-$t$ cut whose
capacity equals the value of $f$. In other words, the maximum value of a feasible $s$-$t$ flow
equals the minimum capacity of an $s$-$t$ cut.

## Sources

- L. R. Ford and D. R. Fulkerson, Canad. J. Math. 8 (1956), 399-404, DOI 10.4153/CJM-1956-045-5.

articles.title: Petersen's perfect matching theorem
articles.statement:
Every finite simple graph that is $3$-regular and
has no bridge, that is, no edge whose removal disconnects its endpoints, has a perfect
matching: a set of edges of the graph such that every vertex lies on exactly one of them.

## Sources

- J. Petersen, "Die Theorie der regulären graphs", Acta Mathematica 15 (1891), 193-220, DOI 10.1007/BF02392606. It follows from `petersen_bridgeless_cubic_has_perfect_matching_general`; the instance `[DecidableEq V]` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Petersen's theorem on cubic graphs
articles.statement:
Every finite simple graph that is $3$-regular
and has no bridge, that is, no edge whose removal disconnects its endpoints, has a perfect
matching: a set of edges of the graph such that every vertex lies on exactly one of them.

articles.title: Counting disjoint preference profiles
articles.statement:
Call a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women
disjoint if for every pair of positions $(r, s)$ there is exactly one man–woman pair in which the
man ranks the woman at position $r$ and the woman ranks the man at position $s$. For every natural
number $n$, the number of disjoint profiles is at most $(n^2)!$ and is divisible by $(n!)^2$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Proposition 3 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-prop-3`).

articles.title: Strict total orders are determined by their relation
articles.statement:
Let $T$ and $T'$ be strict total
orders on a set $\alpha$, with relations $\lt _T$ and $\lt _{T'}$. If $x \lt _T y \iff x \lt _{T'} y$ for all
$x, y \in \alpha$, then $T = T'$.

articles.title: Existence of stable perfect matchings
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $W$ be finite sets with the same
number of elements. Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict total order of preference on $W$ and
each $w \in W$ has a strict total order of preference on $M$. Then some perfect matching between
$M$ and $W$ is stable for these preferences.

This is the Gale–Shapley theorem, stated without decidability assumptions on $M$ and $W$.

articles.title: Gale–Shapley theorem
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $W$ be finite sets with the same number of elements.
Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict total order of preference on $W$ and each $w \in W$ has
a strict total order of preference on $M$. Then some perfect matching between $M$ and $W$ is
stable for these preferences.

## Sources

- D. Gale and L. S. Shapley, "College Admissions and the Stability of Marriage", American Mathematical Monthly 69 (1962), 9–15, DOI 10.2307/2312726. It follows from `gale_shapley_exists_stable_matching_general`; the instances `[DecidableEq M]` and `[DecidableEq W]` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: When the Gale–Shapley algorithm ends in one round
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $P$ be a
preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women. The men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ ends
in exactly one round if and only if every woman is the first choice of exactly one man.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Proposition 2 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-prop-2`).

articles.title: Gale–Shapley rounds when all men have the same preferences
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference
profile for $n$ men and $n$ women in which all men rank the women in the same order. Then the
men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ ends in exactly $n$ rounds.

## Sources

- Borodin, Duncan, Litchev, Liu, Moroz, Qian, Raghavan, Rastogi, Voigt, and Khovanova, *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Proposition 1 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-prop-1`).

articles.title: Gale–Shapley rounds with no participants
articles.statement:
For the preference profile with no men and no
women, the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm takes zero rounds.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Number of Gale–Shapley rounds
articles.statement:
For a preference profile $P$ for $n$ men and $n$ women,
the number of rounds of the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ is the least $t$ such
that every man is provisionally engaged after $t$ rounds (or $0$ if there is no such $t$).

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: One round of the Gale–Shapley algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and
$n$ women and let $t$ be a natural number. After $t + 1$ rounds of the men-proposing
Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$, a man who is provisionally engaged after $t$ rounds has made as
many proposals as after $t$ rounds, and every other man has made one proposal more than after
$t$ rounds.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: No proposals before the first round
articles.statement:
For every preference profile, after zero rounds of
the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm every man has made zero proposals.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Proposal counts in the Gale–Shapley algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men
and $n$ women. The number $p_t(i)$ of women man $i$ has proposed to after $t$ rounds of the
men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ is defined by $p_0(i) = 0$ and, for every $t$,
$p_{t+1}(i) = p_t(i)$ if man $i$ is provisionally engaged in the state $p_t$ and
$p_{t+1}(i) = p_t(i) + 1$ otherwise: in each round every man who is not provisionally engaged
proposes to his next choice.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Provisional engagement in the Gale–Shapley algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference profile for
$n$ men and $n$ women, with positions in each ranking numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$, and consider
the state of the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm in which each man $i'$ has proposed to the
women at the positions $r' < p(i')$ of his ranking. Man $i$ is provisionally engaged in this
state if $1 \le p(i) \le n$ and the woman $w$ at his position $p(i) - 1$ (the last woman he
proposed to) ranks him weakly above every man who has proposed to her: her position for $i$ is
at most her position for every man $i'$ who has $w$ at some position $r' < p(i')$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2 (description of the Gale–Shapley algorithm).

articles.title: A hell-couple belongs to every stable matching
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$
men and $n$ women and let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be stable matchings for $P$. If man $i$ and his wife
$\mu(i)$ form a hell-couple in $\mu$ (each ranks the other last), then $\nu(i) = \mu(i)$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Proposition 13 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-prop-13`).

articles.title: At most one hell-couple in a stable matching
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference profile of $n$
men and $n$ women, and let $\mu$ be a stable matching for $P$, in which man $i$ marries woman
$\mu(i)$. Then at most one man $i$ forms a hell-couple with his wife $\mu(i)$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Proposition 12 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-prop-12`).

articles.title: Irreflexivity of a strict total order
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a strict total order on a set $\alpha$,
with relation $\lt _T$. Then $a \lt _T a$ fails for every $a \in \alpha$.

articles.title: Blocking pair
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $W$ be sets. Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict total
order $\lt _m$ of preference on $W$ and each $w \in W$ has a strict total order $\lt _w$ of preference
on $M$, where $x \lt _m y$ means that $m$ prefers $x$ to $y$, and likewise for $\lt _w$. For a perfect
matching $\mu$ between $M$ and $W$, a pair $(m, w) \in M \times W$ is a blocking pair when
$w \lt _m \mu(m)$ and $m \lt _w \mu^{-1}(w)$, that is, when $m$ prefers $w$ to $\mu(m)$ and $w$ prefers
$m$ to $\mu^{-1}(w)$.

articles.title: Hell-couple
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, and let $\mu$
be a matching in which man $i$ marries woman $\mu(i)$. Man $i$ and his wife $\mu(i)$ form a
hell-couple when each ranks the other last: $i$ ranks $\mu(i)$ in his last position and
$\mu(i)$ ranks $i$ in her last position.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 6.1.

articles.title: Soulmate pair
articles.statement:
For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, man $i$ and woman $j$
are soulmates when each ranks the other first: $j$ is the first choice of $i$ and $i$ is the
first choice of $j$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Stability in terms of ranks
articles.statement:
For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, a
matching $\mu$, in which man $i$ marries woman $\mu(i)$, is stable if and only if there are no
man $i$ and woman $j$ such that $i$ ranks $j$ strictly above his wife $\mu(i)$ and $j$ ranks $i$
strictly above her husband $\mu^{-1}(j)$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Stable matching
articles.statement:
For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, a matching $\mu$, in
which man $i$ marries woman $\mu(i)$, is stable when no man and woman both strictly prefer each
other to their own spouses. Equivalently, $\mu$ is a stable perfect matching for the strict
preferences induced by the men's and the women's rankings.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Stable perfect matching
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $W$ be sets. Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict
total order of preference on $W$ and each $w \in W$ has a strict total order of preference on
$M$. A perfect matching $\mu$ between $M$ and $W$ is stable for these preferences when no pair
$(m, w) \in M \times W$ is a blocking pair for $\mu$.

articles.title: Latin squares of order zero
articles.statement:
There is exactly one Latin square of order $0$, that is,
$L_0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 4.2 (OEIS A002860).

articles.title: Number of Latin squares
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $L_n$ is the number of Latin squares of
order $n$: families $(M_0, \dots, M_{n-1})$ of permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (the rows)
such that for every position $r$ the entries $M_0(r), \dots, M_{n-1}(r)$ (column $r$) are
pairwise distinct.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 4.2 (OEIS A002860).

articles.title: Relation of a strict total order
articles.statement:
The relation of a strict total order $T$ on a set
$\alpha$ is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$, which is irreflexive, transitive,
and relates any two distinct elements in one direction or the other.

articles.title: Men's preferences induced by rankings
articles.statement:
For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$
women, each man $i$ gets the strict total order on the women in which $i$ prefers woman $a$ to
woman $b$ exactly when he ranks $a$ at an earlier position than $b$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Rank of a woman for a man
articles.statement:
For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, the rank of
woman $j$ for man $i$ is the zero-based position $r \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ at which $i$ ranks
$j$, so his favorite has rank $0$ and his least favorite has rank $n - 1$.

The paper's one-based ranking is this rank plus one.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Profiles with Latin-square men's preferences, counted by soulmate pairs
articles.statement:
For all
$n, k \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of preference profiles of $n$ men and $n$ women in which, for
every position $r$, different men rank different women at position $r$ (the men's rankings form
a Latin square), and which have exactly $k$ soulmate pairs, is

$$L_n \binom{n}{k} (n-1)^{n-k} ((n-1)!)^n,$$

where $L_n$ is the number of Latin squares of order $n$.

Here $n - 1$ and $n - k$ are truncated subtractions in $\mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Theorem 8 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-thm-8`).

articles.title: Building a strict total order from a relation
articles.statement:
A binary relation $<$ on a set $\alpha$
that is irreflexive ($a \not< a$ for all $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and
total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on
$\alpha$ whose relation is $<$.

articles.title: Men's preferences
articles.statement:
For sets $M$ (men) and $W$ (women), a preference profile of the men
assigns to each $m \in M$ a strict total order on $W$, the preferences of $m$.

articles.title: Mutually Latin profiles with $k$ soulmate pairs
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers and
let $L_n$ be the number of Latin squares of order $n$. Call the men's preferences of a preference
profile for $n$ men and $n$ women Latin when, for every position $r$, distinct men rank distinct
women at position $r$, and likewise for the women's preferences. The number of preference
profiles whose men's and women's preferences are both Latin and that have exactly $k$ soulmate
pairs is

$$\frac{L_n^2}{n!} \binom{n}{k} \sum_{i=0}^{n-k} \frac{(-1)^i (n-k)!}{i!}.$$

When $k > n$ the binomial coefficient vanishes and both sides are $0$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-thm-9`).

articles.title: Profiles with a pair of outcasts
articles.statement:
In a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women, a man
$i$ and a woman $j$ form a pair of outcasts when every man other than $i$ ranks $j$ last and every
woman other than $j$ ranks $i$ last. The number of preference profiles with at least one pair of
outcasts is $14$ if $n = 2$ and $n^4 ((n-1)!)^{2n}$ if $n \ne 2$ (this is $0$ for $n = 0$).

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Proposition 14 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-prop-14`).

articles.title: Outsiders without soulmate pairs
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, where $n - k$ is
read as $0$ when $k > n$. Consider the $n - k$ men $k, \dots, n - 1$ and the $n - k$ women
$k, \dots, n - 1$ among $n$ men and $n$ women numbered from $0$, where each of these men ranks all
$n$ women and each of these women ranks all $n$ men. The number of ways to choose these rankings
so that no man and woman among them each rank the other first is

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-k} (-1)^i \binom{n-k}{i}^2 ((n-1)!)^{2i}\, i!\, (n!)^{2(n-k-i)}.$$

This number is the paper's $S(k, n)$: the preferences of the remaining $k$ men and $k$ women are
ignored.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Lemma 4 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-lem-4`).

articles.title: Perfect matching
articles.statement:
A perfect matching between sets $M$ and $W$ is a bijection
$\mu \colon M \to W$, which matches each $m \in M$ with $\mu(m) \in W$.

articles.title: Preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, number $n$ men and
$n$ women by $0, \dots, n - 1$. A preference profile $P = (M, W)$ for them consists of a
permutation $M_i$ of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ for each man $i$ and a permutation $W_j$ of
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ for each woman $j$: $M_i(r)$ is the woman man $i$ ranks at zero-based
position $r$, and $W_j(r)$ is the man woman $j$ ranks at position $r$.

## Sources

- Borodin, Duncan, Litchev, Liu, Moroz, Qian, Raghavan, Rastogi, Voigt, and Khovanova, *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: A profile has at most $n$ soulmate pairs
articles.statement:
Every preference profile for $n$ men and $n$
women has at most $n$ soulmate pairs, since a man's soulmate is his first choice.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 4.

articles.title: Number of soulmate pairs
articles.statement:
The number of soulmate pairs of a preference profile $P$ for
$n$ men and $n$ women is the number of pairs $(i, j)$ of a man $i$ and a woman $j$ that are
soulmates in $P$, that is, each ranks the other first.

This is the paper's $k$ in $F(k, n)$, the number of profiles with exactly $k$ soulmate pairs.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 4.

articles.title: Number of profiles with exactly $k$ soulmate pairs
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the
number $F(k, n)$ of preference profiles for $n$ men and $n$ women with exactly $k$ soulmate pairs
is

$$
\binom{n}{k}^2 k!\, ((n-1)!)^{2k}
\sum_{i=0}^{n-k} (-1)^i \binom{n-k}{i}^2 ((n-1)!)^{2i}\, i!\, (n!)^{2(n-k-i)}.
$$

When $k > n$ both sides are $0$.

The sum is the paper's $S(k, n)$ of Lemma 4, which counts the preferences of the people outside
the $k$ soulmate couples that create no further soulmate pair.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Theorem 6 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-thm-6`).

articles.title: Strict preference order
articles.statement:
A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ is a binary relation
$<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$
imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). In the
Gale–Shapley development it models strict preference.

articles.title: Strict total orders are total on distinct elements
articles.statement:
Let $<$ be the relation of a strict
total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b \in \alpha$ and $a \ne b$, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.

articles.title: Transitivity of a strict total order
articles.statement:
Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a
type $\alpha$. If $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.

articles.title: Profiles with $n - 1$ soulmate pairs
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$
women with exactly $n - 1$ soulmate pairs (read as $0$ when $n = 0$). Then $P$ has exactly one
stable matching. Moreover, for every stable matching $\mu$ of $P$ and every man $i$ who has no
soulmate, the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ ends after $r + 1$ rounds, where $r$ is
the zero-based position at which man $i$ ranks his wife $\mu(i)$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Proposition 7 (`jis-2024-24.2.2-prop-7`).

articles.title: Women's preference orders of a profile
articles.statement:
For a preference profile $P$ for $n$ men and $n$
women, each woman $j$ gets the strict total order on the men in which man $a$ comes before
(is preferred to) man $b$ exactly when woman $j$ ranks $a$ at an earlier position than $b$.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: A woman's rank of a man
articles.statement:
For a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women, the rank
that woman $j$ gives man $i$ is the zero-based position at which she ranks him, that is, the
paper's ranking minus one.

## Sources

- Borodin et al., *Sequences of the Stable Matching Problem*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Women's preference profile
articles.statement:
For types $M$ and $W$, a preference profile of $W$ over $M$
assigns to each $w \in W$ a strict total order on $M$, read as the strict preference of $w$
among the elements of $M$.

articles.title: The edgeless graph is bridgeless
articles.statement:
The edgeless graph on any vertex set is vacuously
bridgeless.

articles.title: Characterization of bridgeless graphs
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ is bridgeless if and only if no
edge of $G$ is a bridge.

articles.title: Bridgeless graph
articles.statement: A simple graph is bridgeless when no edge is a bridge.

articles.title: Bridgeless from non-bridge edges
articles.statement:
If no edge of a simple graph $G$ is a bridge, then $G$ is
bridgeless.

articles.title: Edges of a bridgeless graph are not bridges
articles.statement:
Every edge of a bridgeless graph is not a
bridge.

articles.title: Cycles in a graph
articles.statement:
A cycle in a simple graph $G$ consists of a base vertex $v$ of $G$
together with a closed walk $v = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n = v$ in $G$ such that $n \ge 1$, the $n$
edges $v_{k-1} v_k$ of the walk are pairwise distinct, and the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are
pairwise distinct. In a simple graph this forces $n \ge 3$.

The base vertex and the direction of traversal are part of the data, so a single cycle subgraph
of $G$ arises from several such cycles.

articles.title: Edges of a cycle
articles.statement:
The edges of a cycle $c$ in a simple graph form the list of the edges of
its closed walk, in the order in which $c$ traverses them starting from its base vertex; each edge
is the unordered pair of its two endpoints.

articles.title: Cycle covers
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. A finite multiset $C$ of cycles in $G$ is a
cycle cover of $G$ when every edge of $G$ is an edge of at least one cycle in $C$.

articles.title: Length of a cycle
articles.statement:
The length of a cycle in a simple graph is the number of edges of its
closed walk.

articles.title: Total length of a multiset of cycles
articles.statement:
The total length of a finite multiset $C$ of cycles in
a simple graph is the sum of the lengths of the cycles in $C$, each counted with its multiplicity.

articles.title: Cycle lengths
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$, the set of cycle lengths of $G$ is the set of
natural numbers $m$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $m$.

articles.title: Longest cycle in a graph
articles.statement: A cycle is globally longest if no cycle in the graph has more edges.

articles.title: Odd cycle lengths
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$, the set of odd cycle lengths of $G$ is the set
of those cycle lengths of $G$ that are odd, that is, the odd natural numbers $m$ such that $G$
contains a cycle of length $m$.

articles.title: Edges at a vertex of an Eulerian trail
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and let $p$ be an
Eulerian trail in $G$, that is, a walk between any two vertices that uses every edge of $G$
exactly once. Then for every vertex $x$, the number of edges of $p$ that contain $x$, counted
with multiplicity along $p$, equals the degree of $x$ in $G$.

articles.title: Degree as the number of incident edges
articles.statement:
For every vertex $v$ of an edge-indexed
multigraph $M$, the degree of $v$ equals the cardinality of the set of edges of $M$ whose
endpoint pair contains $v$, where this cardinality is taken to be $0$ when the set is infinite.

articles.title: Degrees are bounded by the maximum degree
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with
finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. Then every vertex of $M$ has degree at most the
maximum degree of $M$.

articles.title: Degree in an edge-indexed multigraph
articles.statement:
The degree of a vertex $v$ in an edge-indexed
multigraph $M$ is the number of edges of $M$ incident with $v$, that is, the cardinality of the
set of edges whose endpoint pair contains $v$; it is defined to be $0$ when this set is
infinite.

articles.title: Adding edges preserves connectedness
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the
same vertex type. If the underlying simple graph of $M$ is connected, then the underlying simple
graph of the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$ is connected.

articles.title: Degrees add under disjoint sums
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same
vertex type, each with finitely many edges. Then for every vertex $v$, the degree of $v$ in the
disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$ equals the degree of $v$ in $M$ plus the degree of $v$ in $N$.

articles.title: Endpoints of edges from the first summand
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on
the same vertex type. Every edge $e$ of $M$, viewed as an edge of the disjoint sum of $M$ and
$N$, has the same endpoints as in $M$.

articles.title: Endpoints of edges from the second summand
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs
on the same vertex type. Every edge $f$ of $N$, viewed as an edge of the disjoint sum of $M$ and
$N$, has the same endpoints as in $N$.

articles.title: Disjoint sum of edge-indexed multigraphs
articles.statement:
Given edge-indexed multigraphs $M$ and $N$ on
the same vertex type $V$, with edge types $E$ and $F$, their disjoint sum is the edge-indexed
multigraph on $V$ whose edge type is the disjoint union $E \sqcup F$, where an edge coming from
$E$ has its endpoints in $M$ and an edge coming from $F$ has its endpoints in $N$.

articles.title: Edge-indexed multigraph
articles.statement:
An edge-indexed multigraph with vertex type $V$ and edge type
$E$ assigns to each edge $e \in E$ an unordered pair of endpoints in $V$, such that no edge has
two equal endpoints. Distinct edges may have the same endpoints, so parallel edges are
distinguished by their elements of $E$.

articles.title: Edge list of an extended indexed walk
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an indexed walk from $v$ to $w$ in an
edge-indexed multigraph $M$, and let $e$ be an edge of $M$ with endpoints $u$ and $v$. The edge
list of the walk from $u$ to $w$ that traverses $e$ and then follows $p$ is $e$ followed by the
edge list of $p$.

articles.title: The empty indexed walk has no edges
articles.statement:
For every vertex $v$ of an edge-indexed multigraph,
the edge list of the empty indexed walk at $v$ is the empty list.

articles.title: Edges of the forgetful walk
articles.statement:
For every indexed walk $p$ from $u$ to $v$ in an
edge-indexed multigraph, the edge list of the walk in the underlying simple graph obtained from
$p$ by forgetting edge identities is the list of the endpoint pairs of the edges of $p$, taken in
the same order.

articles.title: Edge list of an indexed walk
articles.statement:
The edge list of an indexed walk is the list of the edge
identities it traverses, in order and with repetitions: the empty walk has the empty edge list,
and the walk that traverses an edge $e$ and then follows an indexed walk $p$ has edge list $e$
followed by the edge list of $p$.

articles.title: Handshake lemma for edge-indexed multigraphs
articles.statement:
In an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely
many vertices and finitely many edges, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is even.

articles.title: Euler circuits in edge-indexed multigraphs whose non-isolated vertices are connected
articles.statement:
Let
$M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. Suppose
that the subgraph of the underlying simple graph of $M$ induced on its non-isolated vertices is
connected, and that every vertex of $M$ has even degree. Then there are a vertex $u$ and a closed
indexed walk from $u$ to $u$ that is Eulerian, that is, it traverses every edge of $M$ exactly
once.

A connected graph has at least one vertex, so the hypothesis requires $M$ to have an edge.

articles.title: Euler circuits in edge-indexed multigraphs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with
finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. If the underlying simple graph of $M$ is
connected and every vertex of $M$ has even degree, then there are a vertex $u$ and a closed
indexed walk from $u$ to $u$ that is Eulerian, that is, it traverses every edge of $M$ exactly
once.

articles.title: Euler circuits in simple graphs whose non-isolated vertices are connected
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
finite simple graph in which every vertex has even degree, and suppose that the subgraph of $G$
induced on its non-isolated vertices is connected (in particular nonempty, so $G$ has at least
one edge). Then $G$ has a closed Eulerian trail, that is, a closed walk that uses every edge of
$G$ exactly once.

Isolated vertices are irrelevant to an Euler tour.

articles.title: Euler circuits in connected even graphs
articles.statement:
Every finite connected simple graph in which every
vertex has even degree has a closed Eulerian trail, that is, a closed walk that uses every edge of
the graph exactly once.

articles.title: Degree counts incident edges
articles.statement:
In an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many edges, the
degree of every vertex $v$ equals the number of edges incident with $v$.

articles.title: Incidence is membership in the endpoint pair
articles.statement:
In an edge-indexed multigraph, a vertex $v$
is incident with an edge $e$ if and only if $v$ belongs to the unordered pair of endpoints of
$e$.

articles.title: Incidence
articles.statement:
In an edge-indexed multigraph, a vertex $v$ is incident with an edge $e$ when
$v$ belongs to the unordered pair of endpoints of $e$.

articles.title: Indexed walk
articles.statement:
In an edge-indexed multigraph, an indexed walk is a walk that records which
edge it traverses at each step. Indexed walks are defined inductively: for every vertex $v$ there
is the empty indexed walk from $v$ to $v$, and if $e$ is an edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$ and
$p$ is an indexed walk from $v$ to $w$, then traversing $e$ from $u$ to $v$ and then following
$p$ is an indexed walk from $u$ to $w$.

articles.title: Reachability among non-isolated vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and let $u$ and $v$ be
non-isolated vertices of $G$, that is, vertices with at least one neighbour. If $v$ is reachable
from $u$ in $G$, then $v$ is reachable from $u$ in the subgraph of $G$ induced on the set of
non-isolated vertices.

articles.title: Characterization of Eulerian indexed walks
articles.statement:
An indexed walk is Eulerian exactly when it
is a trail whose edge list contains every edge identity of the multigraph.

articles.title: Eulerian indexed walk
articles.statement:
An indexed walk is Eulerian when it is a trail, that is, it uses
no edge identity twice, and every edge identity of the multigraph occurs in its edge list.

articles.title: Characterization of indexed trails
articles.statement:
An indexed walk is a trail exactly when its edge
list has no duplicates.

articles.title: Indexed trail
articles.statement:
An indexed walk $p$ in an edge-indexed multigraph is a trail when its edge
list has no repeated entries, that is, $p$ traverses each edge of the multigraph at most once.

articles.title: Forgetting edge identities preserves length
articles.statement:
For an indexed walk $p$, the walk in the
underlying simple graph obtained by forgetting edge identities has the same length as $p$, namely
the number of entries in the edge list of $p$.

articles.title: Adjacency in the line graph of a multigraph
articles.statement:
Two edge identities $e_1$ and $e_2$ are
adjacent in the line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph exactly when $e_1 \ne e_2$ and some
vertex is incident with both of them.

articles.title: Line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph
articles.statement:
The line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph is
the simple graph whose vertices are the edge identities, two of them being adjacent when they are
distinct and share an endpoint. In particular, parallel edges are adjacent.

articles.title: Maximum degree of a multigraph
articles.statement:
For an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices
and finitely many edge identities, the maximum degree is the largest degree of a vertex, and $0$
when there are no vertices.

Finiteness of the edge identities matters: the degree of a vertex is the cardinality of its set
of incident edges, which is taken to be $0$ for an infinite set, so without it a vertex of
infinite degree could be reported as having degree $0$.

articles.title: Support of a walk extended at the front
articles.statement:
If $e$ is an edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$ and
$p$ is an indexed walk starting at $v$, then the support of the walk that traverses $e$ from $u$
to $v$ and then follows $p$ is $u$ followed by the support of $p$.

articles.title: Support of the empty indexed walk
articles.statement:
The support of the empty indexed walk at a vertex $v$
is the one-element list $[v]$.

articles.title: Forgetting edge identities preserves the vertex sequence
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an edge-indexed
multigraph and $p$ an indexed walk in $M$ from $u$ to $v$. The walk from $u$ to $v$ in the
underlying simple graph of $M$ obtained from $p$ by forgetting edge identities visits the same
vertices as $p$, in the same order: the two supports are equal as lists.

articles.title: Vertex list of an indexed walk
articles.statement:
The support of an indexed walk $p$ from $u$ to $v$ in
an edge-indexed multigraph is the list of the vertices that $p$ visits, in order and with
repetitions, including both endpoints: the empty walk at $w$ has support $[w]$, and a walk that
starts at $u$ with an edge and continues with an indexed walk $q$ has support $u$ followed by
the support of $q$.

articles.title: From an indexed walk to a walk in the underlying graph
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an edge-indexed
multigraph. An indexed walk $p$ in $M$ from $u$ to $v$ yields a walk from $u$ to $v$ in the
underlying simple graph of $M$ by forgetting edge identities: the empty indexed walk at $w$ goes
to the empty walk at $w$, and an indexed walk that first traverses an edge $e$ with endpoints
$\{u, x\}$ and then continues with an indexed walk $q$ goes to the walk that first steps from $u$
to $x$, an edge of the underlying graph because $e$ has these endpoints, and then follows the
image of $q$.

articles.title: Adjacency in the underlying graph
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph. Two vertices $u$
and $v$ are adjacent in the underlying simple graph of $M$ if and only if some edge $e$ of $M$ has
endpoint pair $\{u, v\}$.

articles.title: Underlying simple graph of an edge-indexed multigraph
articles.statement:
The underlying simple graph of an
edge-indexed multigraph $M$ with vertex set $V$ is the simple graph on $V$ whose edges are the
unordered pairs $\{u, v\}$ that are the endpoint pair of some edge of $M$; such pairs have
$u \ne v$ because $M$ is loopless. It forgets edge multiplicities.

articles.title: Cardinality bound for contracting the complement
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite set and
$D \subseteq V$. If the complement $V \setminus D$ has at least two elements, then $D$ together
with one new vertex has fewer elements than $V$, that is, $|D| + 1 < |V|$.

This counts the vertices of the graph obtained by contracting $V \setminus D$ to a single
vertex.

articles.title: Preimage of the contraction vertex under the collapse map
articles.statement:
For a set $D \subseteq V$ and a
vertex $v \in V$, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex sends $v$
to the contraction vertex if and only if $v \notin D$.

articles.title: Preimages of retained vertices under the collapse map
articles.statement:
For a set $D \subseteq V$, a vertex
$v \in V$ and an element $a \in D$, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the
contraction vertex sends $v$ to $a$ if and only if $v = a$.

articles.title: The collapse map fixes the retained set
articles.statement:
For a set $D \subseteq V$, the collapse map from
$V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex sends each $v \in D$ to $v$ itself.

articles.title: The collapse map sends the complement to the contraction vertex
articles.statement:
For a set
$D \subseteq V$, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex sends each
vertex $v \notin D$ to the contraction vertex.

articles.title: The collapse map is surjective
articles.statement:
For a set $D \subseteq V$ whose complement $V \setminus D$
is nonempty, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex is
surjective.

articles.title: Collapsing the complement of a set
articles.statement:
For a set $D \subseteq V$, the collapse map sends $V$
to $D$ together with one new vertex, the contraction vertex: each $v \in D$ is sent to itself,
and each $v \notin D$ is sent to the contraction vertex.

articles.title: Contracting the complement preserves 2-connectivity
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a 2-vertex-connected
graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $D \subseteq V$ be a set with at least two elements
that induces a connected subgraph of $G$ and whose complement $V \setminus D$ is nonempty. Then
the graph obtained from $G$ by contracting $V \setminus D$ to a single vertex is
2-vertex-connected.

articles.title: Neighbors of the contraction vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on $V$, let $D \subseteq V$, and
contract $V \setminus D$ to a single vertex. A vertex $a \in D$ is adjacent to the contraction
vertex in the contracted graph if and only if $a$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex
$v \notin D$.

articles.title: Contraction preserves adjacency among retained vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on $V$, let
$D \subseteq V$, and contract $V \setminus D$ to a single vertex. Two vertices $a, b \in D$ are
adjacent in the contracted graph if and only if they are adjacent in $G$.

articles.title: Contracting the complement of a vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$
and let $D \subseteq V$. Contracting the complement of $D$ to a single vertex gives the simple
graph whose vertices are the elements of $D$ together with one new vertex $\ast$, in which two
vertices $a, b \in D$ are adjacent exactly when they are adjacent in $G$, and a vertex $a \in D$
is adjacent to $\ast$ exactly when $a$ has a neighbour in $G$ outside $D$. The new vertex $\ast$
is present even when $D = V$, and is then isolated.

articles.title: Fleischner's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph that is 2-vertex-connected, that is,
$G$ has at least three vertices and stays connected after deleting at most one vertex. Let $H$ be
the square of $G$: the graph on the same vertices in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if
and only if they are adjacent in $G$ or have a common neighbour in $G$. Then $H$ is Hamiltonian:
it has a cycle that passes through every vertex exactly once.

## Sources

- Herbert Fleischner, "The Square of Every Two-Connected Graph Is Hamiltonian," Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 16 (1974), 29–34, DOI 10.1016/0095-8956(74)90091-4, https://doi.org/10.1016/0095-8956(74)90091-4. Proof: the strengthened vertex-rooted induction of A. Georgakopoulos, "A short proof of Fleischner's theorem", Discrete Math. 309 (2009), 6632–6634.

articles.title: Strong square cycle at a vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let
$x \in V$. Then $G$ has a strong square cycle at $x$ if the square $G^2$ of $G$ has a Hamiltonian
cycle that starts and ends at $x$ and whose two edges at $x$, its first and its last edge, are
edges of $G$.

articles.title: Characterization of strong square cycles
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on a finite vertex set $V$
and let $x \in V$. Then $G$ has a strong square cycle at $x$ if and only if the square $G^2$ of
$G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle $p$ that starts and ends at $x$ such that $x$ is adjacent in $G$ to
the second vertex of $p$ and the second-to-last vertex of $p$ is adjacent in $G$ to $x$.

articles.title: Strengthened Fleischner theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph that is
2-vertex-connected, that is, $G$ has at least three vertices and stays connected after deleting at
most one vertex. Let $G^2$ be the square of $G$: the graph on the same vertices in which two
distinct vertices are adjacent if and only if they are adjacent in $G$ or have a common neighbour
in $G$. Then for every vertex $x$ of $G$, the graph $G^2$ has a Hamiltonian cycle whose two edges
at $x$ are edges of $G$.

articles.title: Říha's cycle lemma
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite $2$-vertex-connected simple graph. Then for
every vertex $x$ of $G$ there is a cycle $c$ through $x$ and a vertex $y \ne x$ that is bound
to $c$: $y$ lies on $c$ and every neighbor of $y$ in $G$ lies on $c$.

articles.title: Characterization of bound vertices
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a closed walk in a simple graph $G$. A
vertex $y$ is bound to $c$ if and only if $y$ lies on $c$ and every neighbor of $y$ in $G$ lies
on $c$.

articles.title: Bound vertices of a closed walk
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a closed walk in a simple graph $G$. A vertex
$y$ is bound to $c$ when $y$ lies on $c$ and every neighbor of $y$ in $G$ lies on $c$.

articles.title: Špacapan's counterexample to prism-Hamiltonicity
articles.statement:
The prism-Hamiltonicity conjecture for
3-connected planar graphs is false: there is a finite simple graph $G$ that is
$3$-vertex-connected and straight-line planar whose prism $G \mathbin{\square} K_2$ is not
Hamiltonian.

## Sources

- S. Špacapan, A counterexample to prism-hamiltonicity of 3-connected planar graphs, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 148 (2021), 46–52, https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.06683.

articles.title: Prism-Hamiltonicity conjecture for 3-connected planar graphs
articles.statement:
For every finite simple
graph $G$ that is $3$-vertex-connected and straight-line planar, the prism
$G \mathbin{\square} K_2$, the Cartesian product of $G$ with the complete graph on two
vertices, is Hamiltonian.

articles.title: Dirac's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with $n \ge 3$ vertices in which every
vertex has degree at least $n/2$. Then $G$ is Hamiltonian, that is, it has a cycle that visits
every vertex exactly once.

## Sources

- G. A. Dirac, Some Theorems on Abstract Graphs, Proc. London Math. Soc. s3-2 (1952), 69–81, DOI 10.1112/plms/s3-2.1.69.

articles.title: A cyclic listing of the vertices gives a Hamiltonian cycle
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex set $V$, and let $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$ be a list of vertices with $v_0 = v_n$ in
which $v_{i-1}$ and $v_i$ are adjacent in $G$ for each $1 \le i \le n$. If $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are
pairwise distinct, every vertex of $V$ is among them, and $n \ge 3$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian: it
has a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once.

articles.title: Ore's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ with $|V| \ge 3$. If
$\deg u + \deg v \ge |V|$ for every pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices $u$ and $v$, then $G$
is Hamiltonian.

## Sources

- O. Ore, Note on Hamilton Circuits, Amer. Math. Monthly 67 (1960), 55, DOI 10.2307/2308928.

articles.title: Concatenation of paths meeting at one endpoint is a path
articles.statement: Two paths that meet only at their common endpoint `m` concatenate to a path.

articles.title: Edge-disjoint paths
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph with vertices $s$ and $t$. A family
$P_0, \dots, P_{n-1}$ of paths from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ is edge-disjoint when, for all indices
$i \ne j$, no edge of $P_i$ is an edge of $P_j$.

articles.title: Internally vertex-disjoint paths
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph with vertices $s$ and $t$,
and let $P_0, \dots, P_{n-1}$ be a family of paths from $s$ to $t$ in $G$, indexed by
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The family is internally vertex-disjoint when for all indices $i \ne j$,
every vertex lying on both $P_i$ and $P_j$ is $s$ or $t$.

articles.title: Edge cuts separating two vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let
$s$ and $t$ be vertices of $G$. A finite set $C$ of unordered pairs of vertices is an $s$-$t$ edge
cut when every element of $C$ is an edge of $G$ and $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the graph
obtained from $G$ by deleting the edges in $C$.

articles.title: Vertex cuts are walk separators
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set, let $s$
and $t$ be vertices of $G$, and let $C$ be a set of vertices of $G$. Then $C$ is an $s$-$t$ vertex
cut if and only if $s \notin C$, $t \notin C$, and every walk from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ passes
through a vertex of $C$.

articles.title: Vertex cuts separating two vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set, let
$s$ and $t$ be vertices of $G$, and let $C$ be a set of vertices of $G$. Then $C$ is an $s$-$t$
vertex cut when $s \notin C$, $t \notin C$, and $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the graph
obtained from $G$ by deleting every edge that has an endpoint in $C$.

articles.title: Menger's theorem for edge cuts and edge-disjoint paths
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex set and let $s$ and $t$ be distinct vertices of $G$. Then there is a natural number $k$ such
that there exist $k$ edge-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$ and an $s$-$t$ edge cut with exactly $k$
edges, every family of edge-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$ has at most $k$ members, and every
$s$-$t$ edge cut has at least $k$ edges. In words, the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths from
$s$ to $t$ equals the minimum size of an $s$-$t$ edge cut.

## Sources

- K. Menger, Zur allgemeinen Kurventheorie, Fund. Math. 10 (1927), 96-115, DOI 10.4064/FM-10-1-96-115.

articles.title: Menger's theorem for vertex cuts and internally disjoint paths
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a
finite vertex set and let $s$ and $t$ be distinct, nonadjacent vertices of $G$. Then there is a
natural number $k$ such that there exist $k$ internally vertex-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$ and
an $s$-$t$ vertex cut with exactly $k$ vertices, every family of internally vertex-disjoint
paths from $s$ to $t$ has at most $k$ members, and every $s$-$t$ vertex cut has at least $k$
vertices. In words, the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$
equals the minimum size of an $s$-$t$ vertex cut.

## Sources

- K. Menger, Fund. Math. 10 (1927), DOI 10.4064/fm-10-1-96-115.

articles.title: Menger's theorem, vertex form
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let
$s$ and $t$ be distinct, nonadjacent vertices of $G$. Then there is a natural number $n$ with
the following two properties. First, there is a set $C$ of exactly $n$ vertices with
$s \notin C$ and $t \notin C$ such that every walk from $s$ to $t$ passes through a vertex of
$C$, and every set of vertices with these three properties has at least $n$ elements. Second,
there are $n$ paths $P_1, \dots, P_n$ from $s$ to $t$ (walks that repeat no vertex) such that
every vertex lying on both $P_i$ and $P_j$ for some $i \ne j$ is $s$ or $t$, and every finite
family of paths from $s$ to $t$ with this property has at most $n$ members. Thus the minimum
number of vertices other than $s$ and $t$ whose removal separates $s$ from $t$ equals the
maximum number of pairwise internally disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$.

## Sources

- K. Menger, *Zur allgemeinen Kurventheorie*, Fund. Math. 10 (1927), 96–115, doi:10.4064/fm-10-1-96-115; statement as in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menger%27s_theorem (`menger-s1`).

articles.title: Breadth-first search with a round limit
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set,
a natural number $n$ and a set $s$ of vertices, this applies rounds of breadth-first search to
$s$ (each round adds all neighbours of the current vertices), stopping after $n$ rounds or as
soon as a round adds no new vertex, whichever comes first, and returns the resulting set.

articles.title: One round of breadth-first search
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and a
set $s$ of vertices, this is the set of vertices that lie in $s$ or are adjacent to some vertex
of $s$, that is, $s$ together with all neighbours of its vertices.

articles.title: Parent vertex towards a root in a connected graph
articles.statement:
In a connected graph every vertex `v ≠ s` has a neighbor `p` one step closer to `s`
(a parent of `v` in a breadth-first tree rooted at `s`).

articles.title: Infinitely connected graphs
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ is infinitely connected if it has at
least two vertices and, for any two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, there is an infinite set of
paths from $u$ to $v$ in $G$ that are pairwise internally disjoint.

In particular, a graph with at most one vertex is not infinitely connected.

articles.title: Internally disjoint walks
articles.statement:
Two walks $p$ and $q$ in a simple graph $G$ are internally
disjoint if no vertex is an interior vertex of both, where the interior vertices of a walk are
the entries of its vertex sequence other than the first and the last.

articles.title: Vertices reachable from a vertex
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ and
a vertex $u$, this is the set obtained from $\{u\}$ by breadth-first search with at most $|V|$
rounds, stopping early as soon as a round adds no new vertex.

It consists exactly of the vertices reachable from $u$ in $G$.

articles.title: Characterization of the graph square
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on the same vertex
set. Then $H$ equals the square of $G$ if and only if, for all vertices $u$ and $v$, the vertices
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $H$ exactly when $u \ne v$ and either $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$
or there is a vertex $w$ with $u$ adjacent to $w$ and $w$ adjacent to $v$ in $G$.

articles.title: Minimum degree in the square of a 2-connected graph
articles.statement:
In a 2-vertex-connected simple graph
on a finite vertex set with at least five vertices, every vertex has at least four neighbors in
the square of the graph.

articles.title: Skipping a vertex of a walk in the graph square
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and let
$u, w, v, x_1, \dots, x_k$ (with $k \ge 0$) be a sequence of vertices in which consecutive
vertices are adjacent in $G$. If $u \ne v$, then in the sequence $u, v, x_1, \dots, x_k$
consecutive vertices are adjacent in the square of $G$.

articles.title: The square of a connected graph is connected
articles.statement:
If a simple graph $G$ is connected, then
the square of $G$ is connected.

articles.title: Adjacency in the graph square
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, the
vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the square of $G$ if and only if $u \ne v$ and either $u$
and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ or there is a vertex $w$ with $u$ adjacent to $w$ and $w$ adjacent
to $v$ in $G$.

articles.title: Adding edges preserves a Hamiltonian square
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on the same
finite vertex set such that every edge of $G$ is an edge of $H$. If the square of $G$ is
Hamiltonian, then the square of $H$ is Hamiltonian.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the graph square
articles.statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on the same vertex set
such that every edge of $G$ is an edge of $H$. Then every edge of the square of $G$ is an edge of
the square of $H$.

articles.title: A cyclic listing by square adjacencies gives a Hamiltonian square
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple
graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$ be vertices with $n \ge 3$ and
$v_0 = v_n$, such that $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are pairwise distinct and every vertex of $V$ is among
them. If for each $i < n$ the vertices $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}$ are distinct and either adjacent in
$G$ or have a common neighbor in $G$, then the square of $G$ is Hamiltonian.

articles.title: Square of a graph
articles.statement:
The square of a simple graph $G$ is the simple graph on the same vertex
set in which two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when they are adjacent in $G$ or have
a common neighbor in $G$, that is, a vertex $w$ adjacent in $G$ to both $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Vertex count of a $k$-vertex-connected graph
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. If a simple
graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is $k$-vertex-connected, then $V$ has more than $k$
elements.

articles.title: Deleting one vertex from a $k$-vertex-connected graph with $k \ge 2$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ be a
natural number and let $G$ be a $k$-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$.
Then for every vertex $v$, the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus \{v\}$ is connected.

articles.title: Deleting fewer than $k$ vertices from a $k$-vertex-connected graph
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural
number and let $G$ be a $k$-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$. Then for
every set $S$ of fewer than $k$ vertices, the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus S$ is
connected.

articles.title: A $k$-vertex-connected graph with $k \ge 1$ is connected
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ be a natural
number. Every $k$-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set is connected.

articles.title: Cycles through each vertex of a 2-vertex-connected graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a 2-vertex-connected
simple graph on a finite vertex set. Then for every vertex $x$ of $G$ there is a cycle in $G$
that starts and ends at $x$.

articles.title: Characterization of $k$-vertex-connectivity by vertex deletion
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural
number and let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$. Then $G$ is $k$-vertex-connected
if and only if $V$ has more than $k$ elements and, for every set $S$ of fewer than $k$ vertices,
the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus S$ is connected.

articles.title: Characterization of 2-vertex-connected graphs
articles.statement:
A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set
$V$ is 2-vertex-connected if and only if $V$ has more than two elements, $G$ is connected, and
for every vertex $v$ the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus \{v\}$ is connected.

articles.title: $k$-vertex-connected graph
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. A simple graph $G$ on a finite
vertex set $V$ is $k$-vertex-connected if $V$ has more than $k$ elements and, for every set $S$ of
fewer than $k$ vertices, the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus S$ is connected.

articles.title: Degrees in a 2-vertex-connected graph are at least two
articles.statement:
Every vertex of a 2-vertex-connected
simple graph on a finite vertex set has degree at least two.

articles.title: Total turning of a boundary orbit is bounded by its length
articles.statement:
The total signed turning around a boundary orbit is at most the orbit length in absolute
 value.

articles.title: Boundary indicator of an edge
articles.statement: `1` if exactly one of `x` and `y` lies in `S`, and `0` otherwise.

articles.title: Lattice connectivity in the complement implies king connectivity
articles.statement: Sites connected by a lattice path in `Kᶜ` are connected by king moves in `Kᶜ`.

articles.title: King-move graph on the complement of a set
articles.statement: The graph of king moves on the complement of `K`.

articles.title: Cumulative turn along a boundary-tracing orbit
articles.statement: The cumulative turn, in `ZMod 4`, over the first `k` steps of the `dartNext K`-orbit of `e`.

articles.title: Next boundary dart direction is rotated by the turn
articles.statement: The direction of `dartNext K e` is the direction of `e` rotated by `turn K e` quarter turns.

articles.title: Successor map on boundary darts
articles.statement: The successor map restricted to boundary darts of `K`.

articles.title: Successor of a boundary dart
articles.statement:
The successor of the dart `e` along the boundary of `K`. Write `r` for `e.dir` rotated
clockwise by a quarter turn. If `e.head + r ∈ K` (a reflex corner of `K`), the successor shares the
head of `e`; if only `e.tail + r ∈ K`, it is the translate of `e` by `r`; otherwise (a convex corner
of `K`) it starts at `e.tail` in direction `r`.

articles.title: Minimal period of a boundary dart
articles.statement: The minimal period of the boundary dart `a` under the successor map.

articles.title: Closed walk around a boundary dart orbit
articles.statement: The closed walk in `dartSuccGraph K` that runs once around the orbit of `a`.

articles.title: Successor graph on boundary darts
articles.statement: The graph on boundary darts of `K` in which each dart is adjacent to its successor.

articles.title: Dart of the square lattice
articles.statement:
An oriented edge of the square lattice: a pair of nearest-neighbour sites. This is the same data
as Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.Dart` of `hypercubicLattice 2`; see
`StatMech.Lattice.Dart.equivSimpleGraphDart`.

articles.title: Dart direction after k steps is rotated by the cumulative turn
articles.statement:
After `k` boundary-tracing steps the direction of a dart is its initial direction rotated by the
 cumulative turn `cumTurn K e k`.
